It achieves SOTA on shot sequence prediction and outperforms prior methods in user studies for full film editing.
AI.motivation: To automate video montage (turning raw footage into coherent cinematic sequences) by learning the implicit "grammar" of film editing from data, avoiding hand-coded rules, and without generating new video frames.
AI.method: Trains a long-context autoregressive transformer on a large corpus of movies to capture statistical patterns of film editing. At inference, uses a footage-constrained decoding algorithm to select the best next shot from input raw footage according to learned patterns.
AI.result: Outperforms previous SOTA on next shot prediction for shot sequence ordering. User study shows FilmGPT-based editing significantly outperforms previous approaches on the full film editing task.
AI.conclusion: FilmGPT is effective for automated video montage and applicable to a range of tasks including automatic video segment trimming and human-in-the-loop film editing, without generating new frames.

title: Tactile: Giving Computer-Using Agents Hands and Feet
summary: Computer-use agents are becoming capable software operators, but their interface to desktop applications is still often a brittle motor layer: they look at screenshots, predict coordinates, click, and hope that the visible state changed as intended. This collapses target grounding, action execution, and outcome verification into a single ambiguous operation. We present Tactile, an open-source tool layer that gives agents a more reliable "hands and feet" for desktop use. Tactile converts heterogeneous UI evidence--operating-system accessibility semantics, OCR-grounded text, and visual fallback regions--into action-grounded interface states: compact target candidates with source labels, roles or text, state, geometry, executable affordances, and verification cues. Agents operate through an observe-ground-act-verify loop that prefers native semantic actions when available, falls back to OCR-grounded coordinates when visible text is the best evidence, and keeps full provenance for replay and failure attribution. On macOSWorld-style tasks, adding Tactile improves Codex Success@100 from 41.1% to 50.0% overall and from 45.2% to 55.3% on accessibility-adapted tasks; a 96-task cross-agent subset shows consistent gains across Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, and Goose. These results suggest that reliable computer use requires not only stronger models, but also a reusable execution substrate that exposes software actions as semantic, verifiable, and auditable objects rather than anonymous screen coordinates.

AI.tldr: Tactile is an open-source tool layer that provides agents with a reliable "hands and feet" for desktop use by converting heterogeneous UI evidence (accessibility semantics, OCR text, visual regions) into action-grounded interface states with verification cues, improving Codex Success@100 from 41.1% to 50.0% on macOSWorld-style tasks and showing consistent gains across multiple agent frameworks.
AI.motivation: Current computer-use agents rely on a brittle motor layer—looking at screenshots, predicting coordinates, clicking, and hoping for the intended state change—which collapses target grounding, action execution, and outcome verification into a single ambiguous operation, making desktop automation unreliable.
AI.method: Tactile converts heterogeneous UI evidence (OS accessibility semantics, OCR-grounded text, visual fallback regions) into action-grounded interface states with compact target candidates, source labels, roles, state, geometry, executable affordances, and verification cues. Agents operate through an observe-ground-act-verify loop that prefers native semantic actions, falls back to OCR-grounded coordinates when needed, and maintains full provenance for replay and failure attribution.
AI.result: Adding Tactile improves Codex Success@100 from 41.1% to 50.0% overall and from 45.2% to 55.3% on accessibility-adapted tasks on macOSWorld-style tasks. A 96-task cross-agent subset shows consistent gains across Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, and Goose.
AI.conclusion: Reliable computer use requires not only stronger models but also a reusable execution substrate that exposes software actions as semantic, verifiable, and auditable objects rather than anonymous screen coordinates.

title: Active Real-World Factor-Based Evaluation for Generalist Robot Policies
summary: Generalist robot manipulation policies trained on large, diverse datasets have shown remarkable promise across a wide range of tasks. However, rigorously evaluating these policies remains a fundamental challenge. Real-world performance depends on a large combinatorial space of task factors including object poses and camera viewpoints, making full, exhaustive evaluation intractable. Additionally, real hardware evaluation is slow and resource-intensive, so current practice is to use narrow test suites that can miss critical failure modes and misrepresent true deployment readiness. We propose an active evaluation framework that addresses this challenge by treating policy evaluation as a sequential experimental design problem. Our approach fits a probabilistic surrogate model over a structured space of task factors and adaptively selects evaluation configurations to maximize information gain over the policy's performance distribution, allowing for sample-efficient characterization of policy behavior across unseen conditions and a systematic identification of failure-prone regions. We conduct 2331 real-world evaluations across 3 tasks with 3 factor variations and find that our approach typically saves the evaluator at least 20-40% of trials compared to typical random testing.

AI.tldr: Proposes an active evaluation framework for generalist robot manipulation policies that uses probabilistic surrogate modeling and adaptive selection of evaluation configurations to achieve sample-efficient characterization of policy performance, identifying failure modes with 20-40% fewer trials than random testing.
AI.motivation: Real-world evaluation of generalist robot policies is intractable due to the combinatorial space of task factors (object poses, camera viewpoints), and current narrow test suites miss critical failure modes, misrepresenting deployment readiness.
AI.method: Treats policy evaluation as a sequential experimental design problem: fits a probabilistic surrogate model over a structured space of task factors, then adaptively selects evaluation configurations to maximize information gain about the policy's performance distribution.
AI.result: Conducted 2331 real-world evaluations across 3 tasks with 3 factor variations; the approach saves evaluators at least 20-40% of trials compared to typical random testing.
AI.conclusion: Active evaluation enables sample-efficient characterization of policy behavior across unseen conditions and systematic identification of failure-prone regions, improving evaluation rigor for generalist robot policies.

title: VIABench: A Comprehensive Video Benchmark Collected from Blind Individuals for Visual Impairment Assistance
summary: Visually impaired individuals (VIIs) encounter significant daily challenges due to limited access to visual information. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive results on general vision and language tasks, their practical utility in real-world blind assistance still remains largely underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce VIABench, a comprehensive video benchmark specifically designed to evaluate MLLMs in Visually Impaired Assistance scenarios using first-person videos recorded or shared by VIIs themselves. VIABench defines three core tasks, each targeting a distinct requirement in visual assistance. Proactive Reminder: Assesses the model's ability to interpret ongoing video content while proactively anticipating and verbally describing upcoming navigation-critical events; Visual Question Answering (VQA): Evaluates the model's capacity to answer user-posed questions about the environment or objects within the video; Vision-Guided Interaction: Tests context-aware reasoning to accomplish intentional interactions between user and environment. To ensure a robust and fair evaluation, we propose a rigorous benchmarking pipeline that supports both online (real-time) and offline settings. Our experiments demonstrate that current MLLMs still struggle to deliver comprehensive support for VIIs, especially in the Proactive Reminder task, which demands accurate anticipation and real-time responsiveness. We hope VIABench will drive future research toward developing customized MLLMs for real-world assistance, ultimately improving navigation and interaction experiences for visually impaired individuals. Code and data will be released at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/VIABench.

AI.tldr: VIABench is a video benchmark evaluating MLLMs on visually impaired assistance using first-person videos, covering Proactive Reminder, VQA, and Vision-Guided Interaction tasks; current MLLMs struggle significantly, especially in proactive anticipation tasks.
AI.motivation: Visually impaired individuals face major daily challenges due to limited visual information access, and while MLLMs show promise, their practical utility in real-world blind assistance remains largely underexplored, motivating the need for a dedicated benchmark.
AI.method: The authors introduce VIABench, a video benchmark using first-person videos recorded or shared by VIIs, defining three core tasks (Proactive Reminder, VQA, Vision-Guided Interaction) and a benchmarking pipeline supporting both online (real-time) and offline settings.
AI.result: Experiments show current MLLMs still struggle to deliver comprehensive support for VIIs, especially in the Proactive Reminder task requiring accurate anticipation and real-time responsiveness.
AI.conclusion: VIABench aims to drive future research toward developing customized MLLMs for real-world visually impaired assistance, improving navigation and interaction experiences.

title: Step-Level Preference Learning for Generative Agents in Social Simulations
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based generative agents simulate human behavior through long-horizon decision-making processes that comprise intermediate steps such as planning, memory retrieval, reflection, and action selection. However, fine-grained human annotations of these intermediate steps remain scarce, and existing agents are not grounded in human preferences over such intermediate decisions. To address this gap, we introduce \method, an interactive simulation interface that enables us to collect step-level human preference supervision over agent decision trajectories, leading to a dataset of 57K fine-grained annotations. We conduct step-level preference learning on open-weight language models using supervised finetuning and direct preference optimization on this data, consistently improving simulation fidelity, coordination, and interaction quality, and inducing more socially effective agent behavior. Our results show that step-level human supervision is an effective training signal for improving both local decision quality and long-horizon agent behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an interactive simulation interface to collect step-level human preference supervision over agent decision trajectories, creating a dataset of 57K fine-grained annotations. Using supervised finetuning and direct preference optimization on open-weight LLMs, the authors achieve improved simulation fidelity, coordination, and interaction quality in generative agents.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained human annotations of intermediate decision steps (planning, memory retrieval, reflection, action selection) in LLM-based generative agents are scarce, and existing agents lack grounding in human preferences over such intermediate decisions.
AI.method: The authors develop an interactive simulation interface to collect step-level human preference supervision, yielding a 57K annotation dataset. They apply supervised finetuning and direct preference optimization on open-weight language models using this data.
AI.result: Step-level preference learning consistently improves simulation fidelity, coordination, and interaction quality, and induces more socially effective agent behavior.
AI.conclusion: Step-level human supervision is an effective training signal for improving both local decision quality and long-horizon agent behavior in generative agents.

title: Depth-Dependent Hidden-State Collapse in Dynamical System Autoencoders for LiDAR Point-Cloud Classification
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Submitted to the 2026 IEEE High Performance Extreme Computing Conference (HPEC 2026)
summary: We study Dynamical System Autoencoders (DSAE) for LiDAR point-cloud classification using spatial coordinates and Product Coefficient feature augmentations. The experiments compare separately trained DSAE architectures at encoder depths $K=1,\ldots,5$ and evaluate the resulting hidden representations with Random Forest, kNN, and a majority-class Dummy baseline. The main finding is a hidden-state collapse at $K=5$. For both xyz and xyz plus Product Coefficient inputs, the hidden-state standard deviation falls to the order of $10^{-5}$, while all three classifiers attain the same macro F1 score of $0.224688$. We prove that between-class hidden scatter is bounded by total hidden scatter, which in turn is controlled by the reported hidden-state variance. Thus a nearly constant hidden representation cannot retain substantial class-separating structure. Product Coefficients neither improve pre-collapse macro F1 nor prevent the $K=5$ collapse in the present DSAE setting. These results identify large-depth representation collapse as a concrete failure mode for DSAE LiDAR classification.

AI.tldr: Dynamical System Autoencoders (DSAE) for LiDAR point-cloud classification suffer from hidden-state collapse at encoder depth K=5, where hidden-state variance drops to ~10^-5, leading all classifiers to produce identical macro F1 scores of 0.224688. Product Coefficient feature augmentations neither improve performance nor prevent collapse.
AI.motivation: To investigate the effectiveness of DSAE architectures for LiDAR point-cloud classification and identify potential failure modes when increasing encoder depth, particularly examining whether Product Coefficient feature augmentations can enhance classification performance.
AI.method: DSAE architectures with varying encoder depths (K=1 to 5) were trained separately on LiDAR point-cloud data using spatial coordinates (xyz) and Product Coefficient-augmented inputs. Hidden representations were evaluated using Random Forest, kNN, and a Dummy baseline classifier.
AI.result: Hidden-state collapse occurs at K=5, with standard deviation dropping to ~10^-5. All three classifiers yield identical macro F1=0.224688 at K=5. Product Coefficients do not improve pre-collapse F1 nor prevent collapse. A theoretical bound shows between-class scatter is limited by total hidden scatter controlled by hidden-state variance.
AI.conclusion: Large-depth representation collapse is a concrete failure mode for DSAE LiDAR classification, and Product Coefficients are insufficient to mitigate this issue.

title: ReBind: Multi-Reference Video Editing via Structured Instructions with Explicit Reference Relationships
summary: Recent diffusion-based video generation models have made significant progress in multi-reference image-conditioned video editing. However, existing methods still struggle to coordinate information from multiple visual sources accurately. We identify a critical deficiency in existing approaches. Existing editing instructions lack explicit reference relationships, and most multimodal large language models (MLLMs) cannot generate them reliably. To address this problem, we propose ReBind, a systematic framework that introduces semantic instructions with embedded reference tokens as the intermediate representation for multi-reference image-conditioned video editing. Our key insight is embedding reference tokens at semantic positions to eliminate ambiguity and establish precise bindings between visual attributes and their sources. We develop ReBind-Instruct, a specialized MLLM that learns to establish explicit bindings between visual attributes and their reference sources through a two-stage progressive scheme for precise reference relationships. We further develop ReBind-Edit, which enables lightweight adaptation of text-to-video models to coordinate multiple references by binding visual attributes to their designated sources. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReBind substantially outperforms general-purpose MLLMs in instruction quality and achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source methods on reference image conditioned video editing. Our project webpage: https://rebind-mrv2v.github.io/.

AI.tldr: ReBind introduces a systematic framework for multi-reference image-conditioned video editing that uses semantic instructions with embedded reference tokens to establish precise bindings between visual attributes and their sources, achieving state-of-the-art performance among open-source methods.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-reference video editing methods struggle to coordinate information from multiple visual sources accurately because editing instructions lack explicit reference relationships, and most MLLMs cannot generate them reliably.
AI.method: ReBind proposes ReBind-Instruct (a specialized MLLM trained via two-stage progressive scheme to learn explicit bindings between visual attributes and reference sources) and ReBind-Edit (a lightweight adaptation of text-to-video models that binds visual attributes to designated sources).
AI.result: ReBind substantially outperforms general-purpose MLLMs in instruction quality and achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source methods on reference image conditioned video editing.
AI.conclusion: Embedding reference tokens at semantic positions eliminates ambiguity and establishes precise bindings between visual attributes and their sources, enabling more accurate multi-reference image-conditioned video editing.

title: Interleaved Noise Injection Improves Clean, Corrupted, and OOD Performance
summary: Noise injection is a well-known technique in stochastic optimization. We report its surprising effectiveness with an interleaved (on-off-on-off...) rather than the usual monotonic decay schedule. We present a theoretical analysis of noise injection, which confirms that corruption by impulse noise approximates a Jacobian regularization, whereas Gaussian noise acts as a curvature penalty. This regularization behavior has been invoked to explain why noise injection increases model robustness. But the interleaved nature of our proposed schedule produces superior results even for the optimization objective: mixing phases of noisy data permits the optimizer to escape local minima and increase exploration without the risk of catastrophically forgetting the important features from the clean data. To stabilize this training scheme against the rapid changes of the loss when switching between clean and noisy data, we introduce a gradient-norm stabilization technique that scales noisy updates based on clean gradient magnitudes. We compare this method with other common augmentation methods and find substantial improvements in corruption tolerance and robustness to real-world distribution shifts on CIFAR-100-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R for ResNet and ViT architectures, with the best results being achieved by stacking our method on top of other augmentations. Through saliency and attention maps we show that the effect of interleaved noise injection stems from penalizing the failure modes encouraged by the inductive bias of the models: impulse noise works against the locality bias of convolutional (ResNet) architectures, and Gaussian noise reduces the tendency of attention-based models to pick up large-scale spurious features. Interleaved noise injection is therefore an effective tool to improve the test performance on clean, noisy, and out-of-distribution data at essentially zero computational cost.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes interleaved noise injection (on-off-on-off schedule) for stochastic optimization, showing it outperforms monotonic decay schedules. Theoretical analysis reveals impulse noise approximates Jacobian regularization while Gaussian noise acts as curvature penalty. A gradient-norm stabilization technique is introduced to handle loss fluctuations when switching between clean and noisy data. The method improves corruption tolerance and robustness on CIFAR-100-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R across ResNet and ViT architectures, with zero additional computational cost.
AI.motivation: To improve upon traditional monotonic decay noise injection schedules by leveraging an interleaved schedule that balances exploration (noisy phases) and exploitation (clean phases) without catastrophic forgetting, while understanding the distinct regularization effects of impulse vs. Gaussian noise.
AI.method: Interleaved noise injection schedule (alternating clean and noisy data phases), theoretical analysis of noise types (impulse → Jacobian regularization, Gaussian → curvature penalty), gradient-norm stabilization to scale noisy updates by clean gradient magnitudes, and evaluation on ResNet/ViT architectures with corruption benchmarks.
AI.result: Substantial improvements on CIFAR-100-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R for both ResNet and ViT architectures; best results when stacked on top of other augmentations. Impulse noise helps counteract locality bias in CNNs, while Gaussian noise reduces large-scale spurious feature reliance in attention-based models.
AI.conclusion: Interleaved noise injection is an effective, zero-cost method to improve test performance on clean, noisy, and out-of-distribution data by penalizing inductive bias failure modes specific to each architecture.

title: GlobalForge: Towards Robust AI-Generated Image Detection
summary: AI-generated image (AIGI) detectors achieve strong accuracy on clean benchmarks, but their performance drops sharply after images are propagated through real-world channels. We trace this fragility to what these detectors actually learn: they overfit to local artifacts left by generators in small spatial neighborhoods, which are easily destroyed by common propagation degradations such as JPEG compression and blur. Instead, we shift the discriminative cue from fragile local artifacts to more robust global structure. Building on this, we propose GlobalForge, a framework with two complementary modules. The Local Information Bottleneck (LIB) suppresses local components to block shortcut learning, while the Global Structural Reasoning (GSR) module forces every token to gather evidence from distant regions. Both modules are trained jointly under a contrastive structural loss based on degradation that keeps the resulting features stable under degradation. To support fine-grained robustness evaluation, we further introduce RealDeg-Bench, covering 7 common degradation operators and multi-step compound chains. GlobalForge improves average BAcc on 8 in-the-wild benchmark groups by $\mathbf{5.89\%}$ over the previous state-of-the-art, and is clearly ahead of representative baselines on RealDeg-Bench under both single and compound degradations. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GlobalForge-BE0F/.

AI.tldr: AI-generated image detectors overfit to fragile local artifacts and fail under real-world degradations. GlobalForge addresses this by suppressing local shortcuts and enforcing global structural reasoning, achieving +5.89% average BAcc over state-of-the-art on 8 in-the-wild benchmarks, validated on the new RealDeg-Bench covering 7 single and compound degradations.
AI.motivation: Existing AIGI detectors achieve high accuracy on clean benchmarks but degrade sharply after images pass through real-world propagation channels (e.g., JPEG compression, blur). The paper identifies the root cause: detectors overfit to local generator-specific artifacts that are easily destroyed by common degradations.
AI.method: GlobalForge consists of two modules: (1) Local Information Bottleneck (LIB) suppresses local spatial components to block shortcut learning from fragile artifacts; (2) Global Structural Reasoning (GSR) forces every token to gather evidence from distant regions. Both are trained jointly under a contrastive structural loss based on degradation to ensure feature stability. The authors also introduce RealDeg-Bench with 7 degradation operators and multi-step compound chains for fine-grained robustness evaluation.
AI.result: GlobalForge improves average BAcc by 5.89% over the previous state-of-the-art on 8 in-the-wild benchmark groups, and outperforms representative baselines on RealDeg-Bench under both single and compound degradations.
AI.conclusion: Shifting discriminative cues from fragile local artifacts to robust global structure is an effective strategy for building AIGI detectors that generalize under real-world degradations. The proposed modules and benchmark provide a foundation for robust forensic analysis.

title: Contextualized Evaluation of Vision Language Models through Dynamic, Multi-turn Interactions
summary: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made substantial advances on benchmarks, yet their real-world effectiveness remains uncertain. This gap stems from the fundamental misalignment between benchmarks in controlled, static settings and the dynamic, interactive, and contextualized nature of real-world applications. To bridge this gap, we propose CEDI (Contextualized Evaluations of MLLMs through Dynamic, multi-round Interactions), a framework that recasts evaluation as a three-party interaction between an evaluatee model, an automated examiner, and a grader. The examiner conducts multi-turn, semi-structured conversation guided by a graph-based representation of the task. By navigating state-space transitions, CEDI deploys diverse strategies, from clarification requests to adversarial probes, to elicit performance evidence. We apply CEDI to visual hallucinations. Empirical results across multiple models, diverse settings, datasets, and domains show that contextualized, interactive evaluations reveal not only significantly more hallucinations than conventional static evaluation but also ones that more closely resemble those arising in practical use cases. We further show that hallucinations often accumulate over long contexts, through self-reinforcing dialogue history, and models are particularly vulnerable to questions requiring premise rejection or refusal. Together, these findings highlight CEDI as a step toward realistic, systematic, and ecologically valid assessments of MLLMs' capabilities. Code is available at github.com/williamium3000/cedi.

AI.tldr: CEDI is a framework that evaluates MLLMs through dynamic, multi-round interactions instead of static benchmarks, revealing more hallucinations that better reflect real-world usage.
AI.motivation: Traditional static benchmarks misalign with the dynamic, interactive, and contextualized nature of real-world MLLM applications, making their real-world effectiveness uncertain.
AI.method: CEDI recasts evaluation as a three-party interaction (evaluatee model, automated examiner, grader), using graph-based state-space navigation to conduct multi-turn, semi-structured conversations with diverse strategies like clarification requests and adversarial probes.
AI.result: Contextualized interactive evaluations reveal significantly more hallucinations than static evaluations, and these hallucinations more closely resemble real-world cases. Hallucinations accumulate over long contexts via self-reinforcing dialogue history, with models vulnerable to premise rejection/refusal questions.
AI.conclusion: CEDI represents a step toward more realistic, systematic, and ecologically valid assessments of MLLM capabilities.

title: Non-vacuous Generalization Bounds for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
summary: While reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is widely used to improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), the generalizability of the resulting models remains poorly understood. In this work, we establish the first non-vacuous generalization bounds for parameter-efficient RLVR fine-tuning at the billion-parameter scale. Our approach adapts PAC-Bayes compression bounds to this setting, and addresses the inherent stochasticity of token generation by applying the Gumbel-max reparameterization trick. To operationalize these bounds, we propose the Progressive RLVR framework, which integrates RLVR with on-policy distillation, TinyLoRA, and model quantization. Progressive RLVR empirically retains 84-97% performance of standard LoRA fine-tuning while producing models that are 14,796x more compressible. We show that this framework yields non-vacuous generalization bounds in four domains: mathematical problem-solving, programming, general-knowledge reasoning, and Text-to-SQL. Our bounds exceed the accuracy of the base model by 9-51% and lie within 6-11% of the accuracy of the fine-tuned models.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes the first non-vacuous generalization bounds for parameter-efficient RLVR fine-tuning of large language models by adapting PAC-Bayes compression bounds with Gumbel-max reparameterization, and proposes Progressive RLVR (integrating on-policy distillation, TinyLoRA, and quantization) which retains 84-97% of LoRA performance while being 14,796x more compressible, achieving bounds within 6-11% of fine-tuned model accuracy across math, programming, reasoning, and Text-to-SQL domains.
AI.motivation: While RLVR is widely used to improve LLM reasoning capabilities, the generalizability of resulting models remains poorly understood; no prior work has established non-vacuous generalization bounds for parameter-efficient RLVR fine-tuning at billion-parameter scale.
AI.method: Adapts PAC-Bayes compression bounds by applying Gumbel-max reparameterization to handle token generation stochasticity. Proposes Progressive RLVR framework combining RLVR, on-policy distillation, TinyLoRA, and model quantization to produce highly compressible models amenable to these bounds.
AI.result: Progressive RLVR retains 84-97% of standard LoRA fine-tuning performance while achieving 14,796x better compressibility. Non-vacuous bounds exceed base model accuracy by 9-51% and lie within 6-11% of fine-tuned model accuracy across all four evaluated domains.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach provides the first non-vacuous generalization guarantees for parameter-efficient RLVR fine-tuning at scale, demonstrating that theoretical bounds can be practically tight for billion-parameter LLMs.

title: Team RAS in 11th ABAW Competition: Multimodal Ambivalence Recognition Approach
summary: Automatic recognition of ambivalence and hesitancy is challenging because these states may be expressed through inconsistent linguistic, acoustic, facial, and contextual patterns, while top-performing systems often rely on computationally expensive ensembles. We present a single text-centered multimodal approach for video-level ambivalence and hesitancy recognition for the 11th Affective & Behavior Analysis in-the-Wild (ABAW) Challenge. The proposed approach combines linguistic, acoustic, facial, and scene features using text-centered multimodal fusion model. Text Residual Fusion treats text as the anchor modality and applies gated residual adjustments based on the other modalities. Experiments on the Behavioural Ambivalence/Hesitancy (BAH) corpus confirm that text is the strongest unimodal modality. The Text Residual Fusion model achieves an average Macro F1-score (MF1) of 75.14% across the Development and Public Test subsets. On the Private Test subset, it reaches an MF1 of 78.24%, outperforming the text model by 4.03%. These results demonstrate that complementary multimodal information can improve recognition performance without requiring a large model ensemble.

AI.tldr: A single text-centered multimodal approach (Text Residual Fusion) for ambivalence/hesitancy recognition achieves 78.24% MF1 on Private Test, outperforming text-only models by 4.03% without expensive ensembles.
AI.motivation: Ambivalence and hesitancy recognition is challenging due to inconsistent multimodal patterns, and top systems rely on computationally expensive ensembles.
AI.method: Text Residual Fusion: treats text as the anchor modality and applies gated residual adjustments based on linguistic, acoustic, facial, and scene features for video-level recognition.
AI.result: Achieves 75.14% MF1 on Dev/Public Test and 78.24% MF1 on Private Test, outperforming text-only model by 4.03%.
AI.conclusion: Complementary multimodal information via text-centered fusion improves recognition performance without requiring large model ensembles.

title: VLT: A Vision-Language-Time Series Multimodal Foundation Model for Industrial Intelligence
comment: 18 pages, 13 figures, and 13 tables, including supplementary material. Haiteng Wang and Jingheng Yan contributed equally to this work
summary: Industrial time series serve as the foundation for Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) to ensure the reliability and safety of industrial equipment such as aero-engines. However, existing approaches are typically limited to single-modality modeling, which restricts their generalization in complex scenarios. Although recent advances in large language models (LLMs) provide new opportunities for multimodal learning, bridging continuous time-series signals and discrete textual semantics remains an open challenge. To this end, we propose VLT, a multimodal foundation model that jointly models time-series, frequency-spectrum visual representations, and textual knowledge. A key insight is to utilize the frequency spectrum as a visual bridge to connect continuous temporal signals with discrete semantics. Specifically, a Time-aware Mixture-of-Experts (Time-MoE) is designed to capture heterogeneous temporal dynamics, while a Frequency-Text Augmented Learner enables joint modeling of spectral and semantic features within a shared representation space. Furthermore, a time-centric gradient alignment mechanism is introduced to mitigate cross-modal optimization conflicts via gradient normalization and reliability-aware dynamic reweighting. Extensive experiments on multiple industrial datasets demonstrate that VLT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior robustness and generalization under few-shot, noisy, and incomplete-modality settings.

AI.tldr: VLT is a multimodal foundation model for industrial time series that jointly models time-series, frequency-spectrum visual representations, and textual knowledge using a frequency spectrum as a visual bridge, achieving superior robustness and generalization across few-shot, noisy, and incomplete-modality settings.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for industrial time-series analysis are limited to single-modality modeling, restricting generalization in complex scenarios. Bridging continuous time-series signals and discrete textual semantics remains an open challenge despite advances in LLMs for multimodal learning.
AI.method: VLT employs (1) a Time-aware Mixture-of-Experts (Time-MoE) for capturing heterogeneous temporal dynamics, (2) a Frequency-Text Augmented Learner for joint modeling of spectral and semantic features in a shared representation space using frequency spectrum as a visual bridge, and (3) a time-centric gradient alignment mechanism to mitigate cross-modal optimization conflicts via gradient normalization and reliability-aware dynamic reweighting.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple industrial datasets show VLT outperforms state-of-the-art methods with superior robustness and generalization under few-shot, noisy, and incomplete-modality settings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multimodal approach effectively bridges continuous time-series signals and discrete textual semantics via frequency spectrum representation, achieving superior generalization for PHM applications like aero-engine reliability monitoring.

title: Adaptive Runge-Kutta Step Control Buys Training Loss, Not Generalization: An Honest Compute-Matched Study of RK-Adam Optimizers
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. Code, logs, and result JSONs: https://github.com/akigogikar/RK4Optimizer
summary: Interpreting optimizers as gradient-flow discretizations has motivated applying higher-order Runge-Kutta (RK) integrators to neural networks. We build a representative Adam variant (Bogacki-Shampine 3(2) RK pair, FSAL reuse, local-error step control) and evaluate it under a strict compute-matched protocol giving every method the same gradient-evaluation budget - an accounting this literature rarely enforces. Under it the RK variant loses to plain Adam on training loss in both minibatch and full-batch (RK's best-case) training. Instrumenting it shows the "adaptivity" is illusory: normalized error stays far below tolerance, the step size pins at its growth cap from step one (98-100 percent of steps), and no rtol x hmax x h0 setting makes it act; tolerances spanning 100x give bit-identical trajectories. The method is exactly fixed-step Adam with an averaged gradient at 3-4x cost. Repairing it (true reject branch; error on the applied map) reverses the full-batch result - about 40x lower training loss than tuned Adam - and a fixed-step control isolates adaptivity (an emergent warmup-and-growth schedule) as the mechanism. But the gain is fragile to the initial step size and does not reach test accuracy. A pre-registered follow-up rules out the obvious explanations: deeper minimization does not overfit, and an explicit temperature knob only hurts - leaving a trajectory effect, the controller selecting a minimum generalizing 1.3-3.4 points below first-order descent at equal depth. An n=10 study confirms one secondary effect: gradient averaging is a genuine implicit regularizer, beating lr-matched Adam and AdamW on 10/10 seeds - yet RMSprop and NAdam match or beat it at a third the per-step cost. Higher-order adaptive integration buys deeper deterministic minimization and a small regularization effect, but nothing a cheaper, well-tuned first-order baseline does not already provide.

AI.tldr: A compute-matched evaluation shows that a Runge-Kutta variant of Adam (Bogacki-Shampine 3(2) pair with FSAL and local-error step control) is actually fixed-step Adam with gradient averaging at 3-4x cost; repairing the adaptive controller yields deeper minimization but fragile generalization that cheaper first-order methods match.
AI.motivation: To rigorously test whether interpreting optimizers as ODE integrators and applying higher-order Runge-Kutta methods to neural networks yields practical benefits over standard first-order optimizers like Adam.
AI.method: Build a representative Adam variant using the Bogacki-Shampine 3(2) RK pair with FSAL reuse and local-error step control; evaluate under a strict compute-matched protocol (equal gradient-evaluation budget); diagnose the adaptive controller's behavior; repair the controller with a true reject branch and error on the applied map; conduct a pre-registered follow-up with n=10 seeds comparing against first-order baselines.
AI.result: The RK variant is exactly fixed-step Adam with an averaged gradient at 3-4x cost; the "adaptivity" is illusory as normalized error stays far below tolerance and step size is pinned at its growth cap 98-100% of steps. Repairing the controller reverses full-batch results (~40x lower training loss than tuned Adam) but the gain is fragile to initial step size. The RK variant's gradient averaging beats lr-matched Adam and AdamW on 10/10 seeds, but RMSprop and NAdam match or beat it at one-third the per-step cost.
AI.conclusion: Higher-order adaptive integration buys deeper deterministic minimization and a small regularization effect, but nothing a cheaper, well-tuned first-order baseline already provides.

title: Pretraining Multiple Instance Learning Networks with Multi-Teacher Distillation from Pathology Slide Foundation Models
summary: Multiple instance learning (MIL) has become the main paradigm for whole-slide image (WSI) analysis in computational pathology. However, existing MIL aggregators are still typically trained from scratch for each downstream task, relying on limited slide-level labels to learn both aggregation mechanisms and downstream discriminative representations simultaneously. As a result, they often suffer from unstable optimization, overfitting, and limited transferability. Similar to pretrained ResNet and Vision Transformer models in natural image learning, MIL also requires reusable pretrained initialization. However, high-quality slide-level pretraining data remain scarce, and MIL models are usually lightweight and weakly supervised, making large-scale pretraining difficult in practice. To address this challenge, we propose a distillation-based pretraining framework for MIL, which leverages two slide-level foundation models, TITAN and CARE, as teachers to transfer their representational knowledge into a diverse set of MIL architectures. To effectively balance supervision from different teachers, we further introduce an angular dispersion normalized distillation loss. The distilled weights are then used as initialization for downstream adaptation. We conduct systematic evaluations on 15 benchmark datasets under both linear probing and full-parameter fine-tuning, and further validate its advantages in few-shot scenarios. Experimental results show that pretraining generally improves MIL aggregators over from scratch training, especially in linear-probing and few-shot settings, while maintaining the computational efficiency of lightweight MIL models. Code is available at https://github.com/fu0201/MIL_Pretrained.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a distillation-based pretraining framework for multiple instance learning (MIL) in computational pathology, using two slide-level foundation models (TITAN and CARE) as teachers. An angular dispersion normalized distillation loss balances supervision from different teachers. The pretrained weights serve as initialization for downstream tasks, and experiments on 15 benchmarks show improvements over from-scratch training, especially in linear-probing and few-shot settings.
AI.motivation: Existing MIL aggregators are trained from scratch for each downstream task with limited slide-level labels, leading to unstable optimization, overfitting, and limited transferability. Unlike natural image learning where pretrained models like ResNet and ViT are standard, MIL lacks reusable pretrained initialization due to scarce high-quality slide-level pretraining data and the lightweight, weakly supervised nature of MIL models.
AI.method: The authors propose a distillation-based pretraining framework for MIL that uses two slide-level foundation models (TITAN and CARE) as teacher models to transfer representational knowledge into diverse MIL architectures. They introduce an angular dispersion normalized distillation loss to balance supervision from different teachers. The distilled weights are then used as initialization for downstream adaptation.
AI.result: Systematic evaluations on 15 benchmark datasets under linear probing and full-parameter fine-tuning, as well as few-shot scenarios, show that pretraining generally improves MIL aggregators over from-scratch training, especially in linear-probing and few-shot settings, while maintaining computational efficiency of lightweight MIL models.
AI.conclusion: The proposed distillation-based pretraining framework effectively provides reusable initialization for MIL models in computational pathology, improving performance and transferability without sacrificing efficiency.

title: RetroAgent: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured Memory for Agentic Retrosynthesis Planning
summary: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning seeks to decompose a target molecule into commercially available building blocks through a sequence of feasible reactions. The vast combinatorial search space makes this task challenging even for expert chemists. Traditional methods combine tree search with offline-trained value networks that score candidates in isolation, without reasoning about complete multi-step routes. Recent work leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) for this task, but relies on simple interfaces that limit exploration of the full search space. We introduce RetroAgent, an LLM agent that bridges symbolic search and neural reasoning through a harness with structured memory. Through memory and chemistry tools, the agent observes the full search state, including explored routes, available alternatives, and properties of intermediates, enabling informed decisions grounded in both global progress and domain knowledge. Experiments on in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate that RetroAgent delivers strong performance and generalization.

AI.tldr: RetroAgent is an LLM agent that integrates symbolic search with neural reasoning via structured memory and chemistry tools to improve multi-step retrosynthesis planning, achieving strong performance and generalization on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning faces a vast combinatorial search space that challenges even expert chemists. Existing methods either use tree search with offline value networks that lack reasoning over complete routes, or employ LLMs with simple interfaces that limit full search space exploration.
AI.method: RetroAgent uses a harness with structured memory to enable the LLM agent to observe the full search state, including explored routes, available alternatives, and properties of intermediates, combining symbolic search with neural reasoning through memory and chemistry tools.
AI.result: RetroAgent delivers strong performance and generalization on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Bridging symbolic search and neural reasoning via structured memory enables LLM agents to make informed decisions grounded in global progress and domain knowledge, improving retrosynthesis planning effectiveness.

title: A Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning Framework for Fine-Tuning Discrete Diffusion Models
summary: We formulate reinforcement learning (RL) in continuous time with discrete state spaces and possibly arbitrary action spaces via a stochastic control approach, where the state dynamics are modeled as a controlled continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC). We consider policy optimization problems and derive the corresponding policy gradient methods, leading to continuous-time variants of proximal policy optimization (PPO) and group relative policy optimization (GRPO). As a primary application, we develop a complete continuous-time RL framework for fine-tuning score-based discrete diffusion models. The proposed framework enables reward-driven optimization without requiring differentiability on the reward signals. In contrast to the existing GRPO-based approaches that only rely on terminal rewards, our formulation allows intermediate reward or advantage signals to be incorporated throughout the denoising trajectory. Importantly, when specialized to masked diffusion models (MDMs), our framework encompasses a rich class of policy parameterizations over the vocabulary simplex with analytically tractable probability ratios, providing a unified perspective on exploration and policy optimization in MDMs. For masked diffusion large language models (dLLMs), we further propose trajectory subsampling techniques to efficiently estimate computationally prohibitive trajectory likelihoods, reducing the computational cost of computing per-position probability ratios. We showcase the effectiveness of our methods on both low-dimensional entropy-regularized optimization problems and RL post-training of dLLMs on mathematical reasoning and coding tasks.

AI.tldr: A continuous-time RL framework for fine-tuning discrete diffusion models, deriving CTMC-based variants of PPO and GRPO that enable reward-driven optimization without differentiable rewards, support intermediate reward signals, and introduce trajectory subsampling for efficient likelihood estimation in diffusion LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing GRPO-based approaches for diffusion model fine-tuning rely solely on terminal rewards and require differentiable reward signals. A continuous-time RL formulation is needed to incorporate intermediate reward signals throughout the denoising trajectory and enable reward-driven optimization without reward differentiability.
AI.method: Formulates RL in continuous time with discrete state spaces via controlled CTMCs; derives continuous-time policy gradient methods (CT-PPO, CT-GRPO); applies to score-based discrete diffusion models; proposes trajectory subsampling for efficient likelihood estimation in masked diffusion LLMs.
AI.result: Effectiveness demonstrated on low-dimensional entropy-regularized optimization problems and RL post-training of diffusion LLMs on mathematical reasoning and coding tasks.
AI.conclusion: The continuous-time RL framework unifies exploration and policy optimization in masked diffusion models, enables non-differentiable reward signals and intermediate advantage signals, and provides computationally tractable trajectory likelihood estimation via subsampling for dLLMs.

title: Variational Inference for Bird's Eye View Segmentation in Autonomous Driving
summary: The bird's eye view (BEV) has emerged as a pivotal approach for environmental perception in autonomous driving, providing a unified spatial representation for vehicles. Nevertheless, despite BEV's significance in addressing the challenges inherent to autonomous driving, effectively fusing data from multiple camera sensors and operating in complex external driving environments remains a considerable challenge. To mitigate this issue, we recast the BEV segmentation problem within a variational inference framework. In this paper, we propose a novel transformer-based variational flow transformation network for BEV segmentation, denoted as TVB. Our architecture implicitly learns the mapping from multiple camera views to a unified canonical BEV map during training by exploiting posterior BEV supervision. TVB employs a conditional variational auto encoder (CVAE) as its backbone and produces multiple BEV map candidates. To augment the realism of the generated BEV maps, we integrate normalizing flows into the map generation process, enabling the construction of more complex and expressive probability distributions. Furthermore, we design a BEV-attention fusion (BAF) module that harnesses attention mechanisms to adaptively integrate the multiple candidate BEV maps. Experimental results, evaluated on both the nuScenes and OPV2Vdatasets, demonstrate that our proposed method achieves superior performance in multi-camera view BEV segmentation and lane environment perception.

AI.tldr: TVB is a transformer-based variational flow transformation network that reformulates BEV segmentation as a variational inference problem, using CVAE with normalizing flows and a BEV-attention fusion module to generate and adaptively integrate multiple BEV map candidates, achieving superior performance on nuScenes and OPV2V datasets.
AI.motivation: BEV perception in autonomous driving faces challenges in fusing multi-camera data and operating in complex environments; existing methods struggle to effectively learn the mapping from multiple views to a unified BEV space.
AI.method: Formulates BEV segmentation as a variational inference problem; proposes a CVAE-based backbone that learns implicit multi-view to BEV mapping with posterior supervision; integrates normalizing flows for richer probability distributions; designs a BEV-attention fusion (BAF) module to adaptively combine multiple candidate BEV maps via attention mechanisms.
AI.result: Superior performance demonstrated on nuScenes and OPV2V datasets for multi-camera BEV segmentation and lane environment perception tasks.
AI.conclusion: The variational flow transformation framework with attention-based fusion effectively addresses multi-camera fusion and environmental complexity in BEV segmentation for autonomous driving.

title: WrAFT: a Modularized Automated Writing Evaluation System for Argumentative Essays
summary: This study presents WrAFT, a Writing Assessment and Feedback Tool, that delivers both accurate and reliable scores and effective comprehensive feedback to argumentative essays. WrAFT adopts a modular design by dividing automated writing evaluation (AWE) tasks into scoring, surface-level feedback, and deep-level feedback. In building the system, various Large Language Models (LLMs) have been evaluated, including LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.7, through both direct prompting and supervised fine-tuning approaches. A proprietary dataset of 480 TOEFL Independent Writing essays with official benchmark scores was utilized. Benchmark-based evaluation shows that WrAFT achieves state-of-the-art performance in scoring, with a quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.84 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.44 against official scores on a scale of 0-5. Human evaluation of system-generated feedback also reveals high approval ratings: 96.14 percent for surface-level feedback, 93.03 percent for deep-level macro feedback, and 94.69 percent for deep-level micro feedback. An interactive user interface has been developed for the system and is publicly available and free to use.

AI.tldr: WrAFT is a modular AWE system using LLMs (LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o, Claude 3.7) for scoring and feedback on argumentative essays, achieving SOTA scoring (QWK 0.84, RMSE 0.44) and high human approval ratings (>93%) on a TOEFL essay dataset.
AI.motivation: To develop an automated writing evaluation tool that simultaneously provides accurate scoring and comprehensive feedback (surface-level and deep-level) for argumentative essays, addressing the limitations of existing AWE systems that often lack effective deep-level feedback.
AI.method: Modular design separating scoring, surface-level feedback, and deep-level feedback; evaluated multiple LLMs (LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o, Claude 3.7) via direct prompting and supervised fine-tuning; used proprietary dataset of 480 TOEFL Independent Writing essays with official benchmark scores.
AI.result: Achieved QWK of 0.84 and RMSE of 0.44 for scoring against official scores (0-5 scale); human evaluation yielded 96.14% approval for surface-level feedback, 93.03% for deep-level macro feedback, and 94.69% for deep-level micro feedback.
AI.conclusion: WrAFT achieves state-of-the-art scoring performance and highly rated comprehensive feedback, with a publicly available interactive interface, demonstrating the effectiveness of modular AWE design leveraging LLMs.

title: xHC: Expanded Hyper-Connections
summary: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of Transformers into $N$ parallel streams, providing a form of memory scaling beyond model width and depth. Manifold-Constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes this formulation at scale. The large gains from $N{=}1$ to $N{=}4$ suggest residual-stream expansion as a promising scaling axis. However, existing HC-family methods typically stop at $N{=}4$. Our experiments reveal why: scaling mHC beyond this point yields diminishing performance gains and rapidly increasing training cost. We attribute this limitation to two bottlenecks: insufficient write-back information for an expanding number of streams and residual-mixing generation whose cost scales cubically with $N$. To address both bottlenecks, we propose xHC (Expanded Hyper-Connections), the first HC-family method to achieve meaningful expansion beyond $N{=}4$. xHC combines temporal feature augmentation for richer write-back with a sparse residual-stream architecture that updates only $k=4$ of the $N=16$ streams while retaining dense access to the full residual state. Across 18B and 28B MoE models, xHC delivers strong and consistent downstream improvements. On an 18B MoE model, xHC improves the average downstream score by 4.0 points over mHC, while adding only modest training FLOPs over the vanilla baseline. Scaling-law experiments show that the vanilla and mHC require $1.50\times$ and $1.19\times$ the compute of xHC, respectively, to reach the same loss. Practical large-$N$ training also requires controlling memory traffic from the expanded residual state. We therefore introduce xHC-Flash, which reduces the per-sublayer memory traffic from $73.5C$ to $40C$, comparable to the $34C$ required by mHC at $N{=}4$, while retaining the gains of full xHC. Together, xHC and xHC-Flash make large-$N$ residual-stream expansion effective and practical for LLM pre-training.

AI.tldr: xHC (Expanded Hyper-Connections) enables effective residual-stream expansion beyond N=4 by addressing write-back and residual-mixing bottlenecks, achieving strong downstream improvements with practical memory efficiency via xHC-Flash.
AI.motivation: Existing HC-family methods (e.g., mHC) suffer from diminishing returns and rapidly increasing training cost when scaling the number of residual streams N beyond 4, due to two bottlenecks: insufficient write-back information and cubically-scaling residual-mixing generation cost.
AI.method: xHC combines temporal feature augmentation for richer write-back with a sparse residual-stream architecture that updates only k=4 of N=16 streams while retaining dense access to the full residual state. xHC-Flash reduces per-sublayer memory traffic from 73.5C to 40C.
AI.result: On 18B and 28B MoE models, xHC improves downstream scores by 4.0 points over mHC with modest training FLOPs. Vanilla and mHC require 1.50× and 1.19× the compute of xHC to reach the same loss. xHC-Flash reduces memory traffic to 40C (vs. 34C for mHC at N=4).
AI.conclusion: xHC and xHC-Flash make large-N residual-stream expansion effective and practical for LLM pre-training, overcoming prior scaling limitations.

title: VideoSEMA: a scalable and efficient Mamba-like attention for video understanding
summary: We present for video understanding (classification) a split space-time attention model, VideoSEMA, consisting of a scalable and efficient Mamba-like attention (SEMA) block in space and a softmax temporal attention in time. In each frame, SEMA attention applies a local window attention in parallel with a global averaging in a Mamba macro-architecture, which is called Mamba-like. Under certain rank conditions, we prove that the computationally cheaper split space-time attention is equivalent to full space-time attention. On benchmark K400 data sets, VideoSEMA out-performs heavier vision transformer and Mamba models. On benchmark SSv2 data, VideoSEMA leads in top-1 accuracy among models of similar parameter sizes. As image resolution scales up from standard $224^2$ to $1024^2$ on K400 and without fine-tuning, VideoSEMA degrades much more gracefully than VideoMamba in accuracy. It is promising to extend VideoSEMA to longer videos with a dilated/sparse temporal attention.

AI.tldr: VideoSEMA introduces a split space-time attention model for video classification that combines a Mamba-like local-global attention in space with softmax temporal attention, achieving state-of-the-art results on K400 and SSv2 while being more efficient and robust to resolution scaling than ViT and Mamba baselines.
AI.motivation: To design a scalable and efficient video understanding model that avoids the quadratic complexity of full space-time attention by splitting spatial and temporal modeling, while maintaining provable equivalence to full attention under rank conditions.
AI.method: VideoSEMA uses a SEMA block (local window attention + global averaging in a Mamba-like macro-architecture) for spatial modeling, and softmax temporal attention for temporal modeling. The split space-time approach is proven equivalent to full space-time attention under certain rank conditions.
AI.result: Outperforms heavier ViT and Mamba models on K400; leads in top-1 accuracy on SSv2 among similar-sized models; degrades more gracefully than VideoMamba when resolution scales from 224² to 1024² without fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: VideoSEMA is a promising efficient architecture for video classification, with potential to extend to longer videos via dilated/sparse temporal attention.

title: Are LLM-Generated GPU Kernels Production-Ready? A Trace-Driven Benchmark and Optimization Agent
comment: Both artifacts are released as open source: Atrex-Bench (https://github.com/alibaba/atrex-bench) and Atrex-Kernel-Agent (https://github.com/alibaba/atrex-kernel-agent)
summary: Existing GPU kernel generation benchmarks draw problems from synthetic or curated sources that diverge from deployed workloads. We present Atrex-Bench, a benchmark whose 30 operators and 440 shapes are sampled directly from full-cluster production inference traces of compute-limited, memory-rich GPUs. Each problem carries an importance weight derived from its share of observed GPU time, weighted by application card-hours and computed separately for the serving phases in which it runs, together with a per-problem roofline ceiling, so the aggregate score emphasizes the kernels that consume the most serving time. Evaluating six frontier coding agents on Atrex-Bench shows that even the best vanilla model reaches only ${\sim}10\%$ of the hardware roofline on production operators; and correctness alone overstates capability, since much of the apparent pass rate comes from PyTorch fallbacks rather than kernels the model wrote. To close this gap, we co-release Atrex-Kernel-Agent (AKA), a profile-driven kernel-optimization agent that combines iterative measure-revise search, optimization dropout for escaping stalled search contexts, and a layered GPU-optimization knowledge base (298 reference-kernel files and 244 optimization-knowledge documents, plus external upstream reference projects for API/ISA lookup). In a controlled case study, the agent converts zero-FlyDSL fallbacks into real kernels that match or exceed hand-tuned production baselines.

AI.tldr: Atrex-Bench is a production-grounded GPU kernel benchmark with 30 operators and 440 shapes sampled from real inference traces, weighted by serving-time importance. Evaluation of frontier coding agents shows they reach only ~10% roofline, and correctness overstates capability due to PyTorch fallbacks. The co-released Atrex-Kernel-Agent (AKA) combines iterative measure-revise search, optimization dropout, and a layered GPU-optimization knowledge base to convert fallbacks into real kernels matching hand-tuned baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing GPU kernel benchmarks use synthetic or curated workloads that do not reflect real deployment, leading to poor evaluation of code generation agents for production-relevant kernels.
AI.method: (1) Atrex-Bench: 30 operators and 440 shapes sampled from full-cluster production inference traces, with importance weights from observed GPU time and per-problem roofline ceilings. (2) Atrex-Kernel-Agent (AKA): profile-driven optimization with iterative measure-revise search, optimization dropout to escape local optima, and a layered knowledge base (298 reference kernels, 244 optimization documents, external API/ISA references).
AI.result: Frontier coding agents reach only ~10% of hardware roofline on production operators; apparent pass rates are inflated by PyTorch fallbacks. AKA converts zero-FlyDSL fallbacks into real kernels that match or exceed hand-tuned production baselines.
AI.conclusion: Production-grounded benchmarking reveals significant gaps in current kernel-generation agents, and the proposed AKA agent demonstrates that profile-driven, knowledge-augmented optimization can close this gap.

title: Muse: Representation Geometry of Muon Beyond Normalized Momentum
summary: Muon-style optimizers apply a polar map to matrix momentum, but their updates also depend on the representation of each parameter block before orthogonalization. We study this representation choice as a form of optimizer geometry and introduce {\method}, a family of Muon-style optimizers that shares the same momentum rule and Newton--Schulz backend across native, nearest-square, skinny, and vector representations. Each Frobenius-isometric representation induces a distinct polar steepest-descent geometry, in which the shorter matrix dimension determines the number of supported singular channels, the pullback scaling, and the constants in stochastic nonconvex convergence bounds. In a teacher--student model, curvature collapse and an isotropic Marchenko--Pastur spectral profile connect early-stage dissipation to the represented nuclear-to-squared-Frobenius norm ratio. Pretraining experiments on LLaMA2-130M and LLaMA2-600M, together with fixed-momentum diagnostics, show that balanced non-native representations can match the performance of the native representation, whereas reducing the shorter dimension weakens the scaling and singular-channel support, leading to behavior that increasingly resembles normalized momentum.

AI.tldr: This paper studies representation-induced geometry in Muon-style optimizers, showing that Frobenius-isometric representations of matrix momentum affect singular channel count, pullback scaling, and convergence bounds. Experiments on LLaMA2 models show balanced non-native representations can match native performance, while reducing the shorter dimension degrades scaling and resembles normalized momentum.
AI.motivation: To understand how the choice of matrix representation before orthogonalization in Muon-style optimizers affects optimization geometry and practical performance, and to systematically explore alternative representations beyond the native parameter shape.
AI.method: The authors introduce {method}, a family of Muon-style optimizers sharing momentum rules and Newton-Schulz backend across native, nearest-square, skinny, and vector representations. They analyze each Frobenius-isometric representation's polar steepest-descent geometry and study spectral properties via a teacher-student model. Pretraining experiments on LLaMA2-130M and LLaMA2-600M with fixed-momentum diagnostics validate theoretical findings.
AI.result: Balanced non-native representations can match native performance; reducing the shorter dimension weakens scaling and singular-channel support, increasingly resembling normalized momentum. Curvature collapse and isotropic Marchenko-Pastur spectral profile in a teacher-student model connect early-stage dissipation to the represented nuclear-to-squared-Frobenius norm ratio.
AI.conclusion: The representation geometry in Muon-style optimizers is consequential: the shorter matrix dimension determines singular channel count, pullback scaling, and convergence constants. Non-native representations can be viable if balanced, but overly skinny representations degrade toward normalized momentum-like behavior.

title: Causal-Adversarial Probing of Clinical Covariates for Prostate MRI Grading
summary: Deep learning models for prostate MRI-based cancer grading may encode clinical covariates that either reflect useful disease-related signal or non-generalising shortcut information, but their role is usually assumed. We propose a causal-reasoning framework for probing covariate dependence in MRI-based International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) Grade Group prediction. Rather than treating mpMRI as a direct cause of grade, we model MRI appearance and ISUP grade as observations of latent tumour pathology, and test whether candidate clinical variables act as nuisance correlates, disease-related proxies, or irrelevant covariates in the learned representation. We implement this using an adversarial framework that suppresses the decodability of individual clinical covariate at a time while preserving MRI-based grade prediction. The approach is developed and evaluated on 2,903 prostate MRI examinations, with external validation on 576 patients. We report a set of interesting and previously under-explored imaging-to-clinical-variable interactions in the context of deep learning generalisation. For examples, in binary ISUP Grade Group $\geq2$ classification, suppressing age, BMI, and alcohol use improved AUC by 1.23%, 0.84%, and 1.42%, respectively (all p < 0.05), suggesting reduced non-generalising covariate information; In contrast, suppressing PSA and prostate volume degraded AUC by 1.91% and 7.61% (all p < 0.001), indicating that these variables carried task-relevant signal. These findings show that adversarial covariate suppression can provide a practical representation-level analysis for distinguishing potentially harmful dependence from informative signal in prostate MRI grading models.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a causal-reasoning framework with adversarial covariate suppression to probe whether clinical variables in MRI-based prostate cancer grading models serve as harmful shortcuts or useful disease-related signals, revealing that suppressing age/BMI/alcohol use improves performance while suppressing PSA/prostate volume degrades it.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for prostate MRI cancer grading may inadvertently encode clinical covariates that either reflect useful disease-related signal or non-generalising shortcut information, but their role is usually assumed rather than rigorously tested.
AI.method: A causal-reasoning framework is proposed where MRI appearance and ISUP grade are modeled as observations of latent tumour pathology, not direct cause-effect. An adversarial framework suppresses decodability of individual clinical covariates one at a time while preserving MRI-based grade prediction, enabling distinction between nuisance correlates, disease-related proxies, and irrelevant covariates.
AI.result: On 2,903 prostate MRI exams (external validation on 576): suppressing age, BMI, and alcohol use improved AUC by 1.23%, 0.84%, and 1.42% (p<0.05), indicating non-generalising shortcut information; suppressing PSA and prostate volume degraded AUC by 1.91% and 7.61% (p<0.001), indicating these carry task-relevant signal.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial covariate suppression provides a practical representation-level analysis for distinguishing harmful dependence from informative signal in prostate MRI grading models, revealing previously under-explored imaging-to-clinical-variable interactions important for deep learning generalisation.

title: Towards an Intention Abstraction Layer for Autonomous Industrial Systems
summary: Modern industrial environments increasingly run many autonomous subsystems at once - schedulers, energy managers, vehicle fleets - each pursuing its own goals while sharing the same physical resources. Because high-level human intentions are translated into low-level control logic and then discarded, no running component can tell whether it is still doing what was actually intended, and goal conflicts surface only after they have caused a missed target or a shutdown. We propose the Intention Abstraction Layer (IAL), a domainagnostic middleware that represents intentions as first-class, persistent, and explainable runtime objects: a large language model grounded in a formal OWL ontology parses naturallanguage goals into structured intentions, a consistency monitor detects conflicts at registration time, before execution, and a transparency module explains them in natural language. We report a first proof of concept in which two autonomous agents register conflicting production and energy intentions, and the IAL flags and explains the conflict before it reaches the execution layer. The result is a mechanism that shifts behavioral assurance for cooperating autonomous systems from post-hoc failure analysis to pre-execution, intention-level checking.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the Intention Abstraction Layer (IAL), a middleware that represents intentions as persistent runtime objects using LLMs and OWL ontologies, enabling pre-execution conflict detection and explanation for cooperating autonomous systems.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent industrial environments, high-level human intentions are lost after translation to low-level control logic, preventing runtime verification of goal alignment and causing undetected conflicts until failures occur.
AI.method: IAL uses an LLM grounded in a formal OWL ontology to parse natural-language goals into structured intentions, a consistency monitor detects conflicts at registration time before execution, and a transparency module explains conflicts in natural language.
AI.result: A proof of concept demonstrates two autonomous agents registering conflicting production and energy intentions; the IAL successfully flags and explains the conflict before it reaches the execution layer.
AI.conclusion: The IAL shifts behavioral assurance for cooperating autonomous systems from post-hoc failure analysis to pre-execution, intention-level checking.

title: CASP: Learning-Augmented Offline Approximation with Verifiable Certificates and Bounded-Loss PAC Guarantees
summary: Machine-learned predictions can speed up offline NP-hard optimization, but asking a predictor what to do amounts to asking it to solve the problem, and committing an unchecked prediction forfeits every worst-case guarantee. CASP (Certificate-Augmented Solution Pruning) instead asks which parts of the search space may be ignored, and accepts each answer only after a sound polynomial-time verifier has checked it, so correctness never depends on prediction quality. We develop the learning theory of this design. The verifier makes the induced loss class uniformly bounded, so certificate parameters are learnable from $\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log K)$ samples ($K$ the maximum instance size), whereas the unverified commitment class admits no distribution-free rate and, under cost spread $R$, none below $Ω(R/\varepsilon^2)$. Filtering noisy predictions by verifiable confidence dominates the standard min-combiner, with a margin we compute in closed form, and the prediction stays useful even given the LP, because it breaks ties on degenerate optimal faces, where every symmetric LP policy, meaning one whose commitments depend on the instance only through the verifiable confidence values, provably stalls. Experiments on five problems test the theory's quantitative predictions. With trained predictors, unverified pruning loses up to $26%$ of the optimum under distribution shift, while the verified deployment of the same predictions loses nothing.

AI.tldr: CASP (Certificate-Augmented Solution Pruning) uses a sound polynomial-time verifier to check predictions about which parts of the search space to ignore, ensuring worst-case guarantees regardless of prediction quality. The paper develops learning theory showing certificate parameters are learnable from few samples, while unverified commitment has no distribution-free rate. Experiments across five problems show verified predictions lose nothing under distribution shift, while unverified pruning loses up to 26% of optimum.
AI.motivation: Machine-learned predictions can speed up NP-hard optimization, but committing to unchecked predictions forfeits worst-case guarantees. The paper aims to design a framework that leverages predictions for efficiency while preserving correctness guarantees through sound verification.
AI.method: CASP asks a predictor which parts of the search space may be ignored, then accepts each answer only after a sound polynomial-time verifier checks it. The paper develops learning theory for this design, analyzing sample complexity, comparing to unverified commitment, and examining the role of confidence filtering and symmetric LP policies.
AI.result: Certificate parameters are learnable from $\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log K)$ samples, while unverified commitment admits no distribution-free rate and has a lower bound of $\Omega(R/\varepsilon^2)$. Filtering noisy predictions by verifiable confidence dominates the standard min-combiner. Under distribution shift, unverified pruning loses up to 26% of optimum while verified deployment loses nothing.
AI.conclusion: The verified prediction framework (CASP) provides a theoretically grounded approach to incorporating ML predictions into NP-hard optimization without sacrificing worst-case guarantees, with favorable sample complexity and robustness to distribution shift.

title: Multimodality as Supervision: Self-Supervised Specialization to the Test Environment via Multimodality
summary:
Cross-modal learning, i.e., learning to predict one modality from another, is a fundamental mechanism for self-supervision via leveraging multimodality. Many practical applications, e.g., deploying a household robot, involve devices that are equipped with a rich set of sensors that enable multimodal sensing in their test environment. This presents an opportunity to apply cross-modal learning to the multimodal data sensed by these devices to learn representations. Findings in developmental psychology also suggest that biological agents leverage it to build an effective representation of their surroundings.
  To study this, we propose a controlled setup, where we restrict a user device to just a given test environment. It results in a specialization setup where we attempt to develop a performant model for this specific test environment. Under this setup, we develop Test-Space Training (TST), which performs multimodal data collection in the test environment and performs self-supervised pre-training on it. We evaluate these models on various downstream tasks in the same environment.
  Under this setup, we find various interesting insights, such as collecting rich multimodal data only from the test environment and leveraging cross-modal learning, we can achieve competitive results with generalist models (e.g., DINOv2 and CLIP) pre-trained on large-scale internet datasets. This enables an alternative scenario where the need for external Internet-scale datasets for pre-training models is reduced. We also present a set of analyses and ablations that raise intriguing points on substituting data with (multi)modality, and how varying pre-training data enables a tradeoff between a model's abilities to specialise to a test environment, and generalize to held-out spaces.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Test-Space Training (TST), a cross-modal learning approach where models are self-supervised pre-trained solely on multimodal data collected from a specific test environment. Results show that TST can achieve competitive performance with large-scale generalist models like DINOv2 and CLIP, reducing the need for Internet-scale pre-training datasets. The study also explores tradeoffs between specialization to a test environment and generalization to unseen spaces.
AI.motivation: To explore whether cross-modal learning using only in-situ multimodal sensor data from a specific test environment can produce performant representations, drawing inspiration from developmental psychology and enabling an alternative to large-scale Internet dataset pre-training.
AI.method: Proposes Test-Space Training (TST), which constrains the model to a single test environment, collects multimodal data from that environment using device sensors, performs self-supervised cross-modal pre-training on this data, and then evaluates on downstream tasks within the same environment.
