AI.method: Proposes Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss (APAL), a simple, model-agnostic objective with two components: (i) asymmetric penalty weighting under-predictions more heavily than over-predictions, and (ii) increased training weight for peak regions within each forecast window. Also introduces a peak-critical evaluation protocol with channel-wise tail error (Top-10%, Top-1%) and peak metrics (precision, recall, F1 under timing tolerance, peak timing error) complementing MAE/MSE.
AI.result: Evaluated on long-horizon multivariate forecasting across five SOTA backbones using pedestrian demand data (City of Melbourne subset) and beach visitor data, plus additional benchmarks. APAL improves tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality with a controllable trade-off against aggregate error.
AI.conclusion: APAL is a practical solution for time-series forecasting when peak-prediction failures are the dominant operational concern, offering controllable trade-off between peak accuracy and aggregate error.

title: VideoChat3: Fully Open Video MLLM for Efficient and Generalist Video Understanding
summary: Recent advances in video understanding have spanned motion, long video, and streaming interaction, driving this field toward real-world applications. Despite this progress, current open-source models remain limited in several ways. They often struggle to generalize across diverse video types, making them effective only in specific domains. High computational demands further restrict their efficiency and scalability. Moreover, most models are only partially open, with key components such as training code, strategy, or datasets unavailable, which hinders reproducibility and slows community-driven development. To address these issues, we introduce VideoChat3, a fully open, efficient, and generalist video-centric MLLM. VideoChat3 advances video understanding through two complementary designs. For efficiency, we introduce Inflated 3D Vision Transformer (I3D-ViT) and Adaptive Frame Resolution for Streaming Video Perception, which enables efficient spatiotemporal representation and reduces the cost of processing video inputs during training and inference. For effectiveness, we develop a scalable video data synthesis pipeline that curates three diverse, high-quality training datasets: VideoChat3-Academic2M, VideoChat3-LV116K, and VideoChat3-OL617K, covering general, long-form, and streaming video scenarios, improving the model's generalization across domains. By integrating these designs, VideoChat3 achieves a rare balance of broad generalization and computational efficiency. Experiments across general, long-form, and streaming benchmarks demonstrate that VideoChat3 surpasses prior open-source models with equal or larger parameter counts with only 4B parameters and higher efficiency.

AI.tldr: VideoChat3 is a fully open, efficient, and generalist video-centric MLLM with 4B parameters that introduces I3D-ViT and Adaptive Frame Resolution for efficiency, and a scalable video data synthesis pipeline for effectiveness, outperforming larger open-source models across general, long-form, and streaming video benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current open-source video understanding models are limited by poor generalization across diverse video types, high computational demands, and lack of full openness (training code, strategy, datasets unavailable), hindering reproducibility and community-driven development.
AI.method: VideoChat3 employs two complementary designs: (1) I3D-ViT and Adaptive Frame Resolution for Streaming Video Perception to enable efficient spatiotemporal representation and reduce video processing costs; (2) a scalable video data synthesis pipeline curating three diverse datasets (VideoChat3-Academic2M, VideoChat3-LV116K, VideoChat3-OL617K) covering general, long-form, and streaming scenarios.
AI.result: VideoChat3 surpasses prior open-source models with equal or larger parameter counts using only 4B parameters and higher efficiency across general, long-form, and streaming video benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: VideoChat3 achieves a rare balance of broad generalization and computational efficiency, advancing toward real-world video understanding applications.

title: Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration in Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning
summary: Temporal Knowledge Graph (TKG) reasoning under the extrapolation setting focuses on forecasting future time-stamped events (facts) from historical data in a temporal knowledge graph. Existing approaches, reinforcement learning (RL)-based multi-hop reasoning methods are prominent for TKG reasoning because they produce human-interpretable predictions via explicit multi-hop path tracing. However, during RL training, rewards are typically sparse, and exploration is highly inefficient due to the vast, time-evolving action space. These issues hinder efficient training and often limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose RAPTOR (Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration), a self-supervised pretraining method that injects a reachability-aware inductive bias to the agent. By learning to estimate the reachability of candidate actions to the target entity, RAPTOR reduces exploration over unpromising paths and provides a strong initialization for downstream RL fine-tuning. Experimental results on the ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, and ICEWS18 datasets demonstrate that RAPTOR pretraining markedly improves the training efficiency and consistently outperforms conventional baselines, establishing it as an effective approach for enhancing RL-based multi-hop reasoning methods for TKG reasoning.

AI.tldr: RAPTOR is a self-supervised pretraining method that injects a reachability-aware inductive bias into RL agents to improve path exploration efficiency for temporal knowledge graph extrapolation reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing RL-based multi-hop TKG reasoning methods suffer from sparse rewards and inefficient exploration due to vast, time-evolving action spaces, which hinders training efficiency and limits overall performance.
AI.method: RAPTOR is a self-supervised pretraining method that learns to estimate the reachability of candidate actions to the target entity, reducing exploration over unpromising paths and providing a strong initialization for downstream RL fine-tuning.
AI.result: On ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, and ICEWS18 datasets, RAPTOR markedly improves training efficiency and consistently outperforms conventional baselines.
AI.conclusion: RAPTOR is an effective approach for enhancing RL-based multi-hop reasoning methods for TKG extrapolation reasoning by improving exploration efficiency and prediction quality.

title: PAC Learning in Turn-Based Stochastic Games with Reachability Objectives: A Decentralized Private Approach via Expected Conditional Distance
summary: Reachability is the most fundamental logical objective, yet it is notoriously difficult to learn in reinforcement learning settings: even for Markov decision processes, PAC learning of reachability is impossible without additional assumptions. This difficulty also holds in turn-based stochastic games (TBSGs), where two adversarial players interact on a finite state space. In this work, we consider turn-based stochastic games with reachability objectives. For such settings, adversarial learning, in which players are adversarial even in the learning phase, is impossible. Therefore, the goal is to consider learning, in which both players learn the unknown model together. In this spirit, previous literature on PAC learning in TBSGs considers (a)~public information shared by both players; and (b)~centralized learning, which means that players share the same learning algorithm. In this work, our contribution is two-fold. First, we relax these strong assumptions and ensure learning: (i)~with private information not shared with the other player; and (ii)~decentralized learning where the players do not share the same learning algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first positive result for decentralized and private information learning of TBSGs with reachability objectives. Second, we introduce a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter, which measures the expected length of reaching the target set. We establish a polynomial-sample complexity bound with respect to the number of states, actions, ECD parameter, and inverses of error tolerance and failure probability.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first positive result for decentralized, private-information PAC learning of reachability objectives in turn-based stochastic games, achieving polynomial sample complexity bounds using a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter.
AI.motivation: Reachability is a fundamental objective in reinforcement learning, but PAC learning it is impossible without additional assumptions. In TBSGs with two adversarial players, prior work required strong assumptions: public information shared between players and centralized learning (same algorithm). This work aims to relax these assumptions to enable learning with private information and decentralized algorithms.
AI.method: The authors introduce a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter to measure the expected length of reaching a target set. They propose a learning framework where players do not share information or learning algorithms, and establish polynomial-sample complexity bounds with respect to the number of states, actions, ECD parameter, error tolerance, and failure probability.
AI.result: First positive result for decentralized and private information learning of TBSGs with reachability objectives. Achieves polynomial sample complexity in key parameters.
AI.conclusion: Decentralized, private-information PAC learning of reachability in TBSGs is feasible without shared information or algorithms, enabled by the generalized ECD parameter that captures problem structure.

title: Frequency-Structured Field Learning for Light-Field Disparity Estimation
summary: Light-field disparity estimation requires global consistency in smooth or textureless regions and local precision near occlusion boundaries, thin structures, and abrupt depth transitions. Existing methods address these requirements through EPI matching, cost-volume or focal-stack construction, view aggregation, or direct convolutional regression, often relying on local windows, discrete disparity hypotheses, memory-intensive volumes, or attention-based aggregation. We instead formulate disparity estimation at the field level, predicting disparity from globally and locally updated EPI-derived latent features without explicitly constructing a disparity volume. We introduce FreqLF, an EPI-guided Fourier-local framework that encodes angular parallax cues from horizontal and vertical EPI stacks together with central-view appearance features. These cues are projected into a latent field and updated through stacked hybrid Fourier-local layers. Fourier low-mode updates enable global feature interaction, while local convolutions preserve spatial variations needed for fine disparity detail. A coordinate-conditioned Gaussian-mixture decoder then predicts disparity, using the mixture mean as the final estimate. Experiments on the HCI 4D Light Field Benchmark show that FreqLF approaches the accuracy of strong supervised baselines while avoiding explicit cost-volume construction in the base model. Ablations confirm the complementary roles of the Fourier and local branches, and scaling experiments demonstrate practical behavior across spatial resolutions. These results suggest that Fourier-local latent field learning is a competitive alternative for light-field disparity estimation. The code will be published soon.

AI.tldr: FreqLF proposes a Fourier-local latent field framework for light-field disparity estimation that avoids explicit cost-volume construction, using EPI-derived features and hybrid Fourier-local layers to achieve global consistency and local precision, approaching supervised baseline accuracy on HCI 4D benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing light-field disparity estimation methods rely on local windows, discrete disparity hypotheses, memory-intensive volumes, or attention-based aggregation, which struggle to simultaneously achieve global consistency in smooth/textureless regions and local precision near occlusion boundaries, thin structures, and abrupt depth transitions.
AI.method: FreqLF encodes angular parallax cues from horizontal and vertical EPI stacks combined with central-view appearance features, projects them into a latent field, and processes them through stacked hybrid Fourier-local layers. Fourier low-mode updates enable global feature interaction while local convolutions preserve spatial variations. A coordinate-conditioned Gaussian-mixture decoder predicts disparity using the mixture mean as the final estimate.
AI.result: On HCI 4D Light Field Benchmark, FreqLF approaches the accuracy of strong supervised baselines while avoiding explicit cost-volume construction. Ablations confirm complementary roles of Fourier and local branches, and scaling experiments demonstrate practical behavior across spatial resolutions.
AI.conclusion: Fourier-local latent field learning is a competitive alternative for light-field disparity estimation, achieving strong accuracy without memory-intensive disparity volumes.

title: Innocuous-Seeming Data, Latent Ideology: Ideological Generalisation in Finetuned LLMs
summary: Finetuning language models on small, curated datasets is standard practice for adapting them to specific policies or domains. We show that finetuning on narrow, factually-defensible, moderation-passing data can cause broad ideological shifts across unrelated domains, while preserving general capabilities. Training GPT-4.1 on right- or left-leaning economics Q&A yields matched ideological shifts on topics such as criminal justice, the environment, and cultural taste. The same effect appears with plausibly-deployed datasets such as workplace HR policy and practical finance queries, as well as on a science-pseudoscience axis where food-safety finetuning increases sycophantic agreement with users expressing false health beliefs. We call this phenomenon ideological generalisation and propose a methodology to measure two properties: breadth, how far the shift reaches across topics absent from training, and amplification, how much finetuning intensifies the shift relative to few-shot prompting on the same examples. We show that few-shot prompting indicates the direction of generalisation but finetuning pushes the model to further extremes, including to far out-of-distribution outputs such as endorsements of race-IQ connections and political violence. The effect replicates on Gemma-3, holds under judge-free evaluations and external benchmarks, survives mixing with generic data, and leaves GSM8K accuracy within $\pm 1$pp of the baseline.

AI.tldr: Finetuning language models on narrow, curated datasets (e.g., economics Q&A) causes broad ideological shifts across unrelated domains (e.g., criminal justice, environment), with effects amplifying beyond few-shot prompting, surviving data mixing, and preserving general capabilities.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether finetuning on small, factually-defensible datasets causes unintended ideological shifts across unrelated domains, and to quantify the breadth and amplification of such generalization.
AI.method: Finetuned GPT-4.1 and Gemma-3 on ideologically skewed datasets (left/right economics, HR policy, finance, food-safety), measured ideological shifts on unrelated topics, compared finetuning vs. few-shot prompting, and evaluated breadth and amplification metrics.
AI.result: Finetuning on narrow datasets produces matched ideological shifts on unrelated topics; effects amplify beyond few-shot prompting (including extreme outputs like race-IQ links and political violence); replicates across models; survives generic data mixing; preserves GSM8K accuracy within ±1pp.
AI.conclusion: Finetuning on narrow, benign data induces broad ideological generalization that is stronger than few-shot prompting, raising concerns about unintended biases from standard finetuning practices.

title: Introspective Attention Modulation for Safe Text-to-Image Generation
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026. 20 pages, 7 figures. Project page: https://basim-azam.github.io/iam/
summary: State-of-the-art flow based text-to-image (T2I) models exhibit remarkable generative abilities but remain vulnerable to producing unsafe content. Prior safety efforts range from concept erasure and prompt filtering to classifier-based gating. However, simple techniques like parameter efficient adaptations of the models easily bypass such guardrails. We introduce a unique principled approach that achieves safety by regulating the model's attention dynamics through inference-time introspection, exhibiting intrinsic robustness. Our method analyzes and rebalances attention activations throughout image synthesis, steering generations away from unsafe concepts while preserving semantic alignment. This introspective control ensures safety of deployed models. Across standard and adversarial safety benchmarks, our approach achieves remarkable safety scores while maintaining or even improving alignment and perceptual quality. Our results reveal that attention-space regulation offers a considerably more promising path to safer diffusion transformer based image generation than the existing concept erasing mechanism.Our code can be accessed at https://basim-azam.github.io/iam/

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an inference-time attention regulation method for diffusion transformer-based text-to-image models that rebalances attention activations to steer away from unsafe concepts without sacrificing image quality or alignment, outperforming existing concept erasure approaches on safety benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing safety guardrails (concept erasure, prompt filtering, classifier gating) are easily bypassed by simple parameter-efficient adaptations, motivating the need for a more robust, inference-time introspection approach.
AI.method: An inference-time attention regulation mechanism that analyzes and rebalances attention activations throughout image synthesis, steering generations away from unsafe concepts while preserving semantic alignment. Applied to diffusion transformer (DiT) based T2I models.
AI.result: Achieves remarkable safety scores on both standard and adversarial safety benchmarks, while maintaining or improving alignment and perceptual quality compared to concept erasing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Attention-space regulation is a more promising path for safe image generation than existing concept erasing mechanisms, offering intrinsic robustness against unsafe content generation.

title: Contextualized Early Detection of Online Firestorms: A Sequential LLM-Based Approach
summary: Online firestorms are rapid collective escalations of highly negative user-generated content and may cause substantial reputational and economic damage. Existing detectors usually work with volume signals, sentiment scores, or predefined linguistic features. Such signals are useful, but they capture contextual meaning shifts in evolving discussion threads only indirectly. This paper proposes an LLM-based detection system with two operating modes. The first mode classifies complete Reddit threads retrospectively by combining local chunk-level assessments into a thread-level judgment. The second mode processes threads sequentially and issues early warnings when a sliding window exceeds calibrated thresholds. In this mode, the language model estimates three firestorm indicators: negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count. On a balanced Reddit dataset, the global mode achieves strong classification performance, while the early warning mode reaches high recall and detects escalating threads after only a small number of comments and distinct contributors. The results indicate that LLMs can be used not only for static judgment tasks, but also as repeated estimators in context-aware monitoring of social media discourse.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an LLM-based detection system for online firestorms in two modes: a global classification mode for complete Reddit threads and an early warning mode using sliding windows for real-time detection. The system achieves strong classification performance and high recall with early detection after few comments and contributors.
AI.motivation: Online firestorms—rapid escalations of highly negative user-generated content—can cause severe reputational and economic damage. Existing detectors rely on volume signals, sentiment scores, or predefined linguistic features that capture contextual meaning shifts in evolving discussions only indirectly, motivating the need for more context-aware detection.
AI.method: Two-mode LLM-based detection system: (1) Global mode classifies complete Reddit threads retrospectively by aggregating local chunk-level LLM assessments into a thread-level judgment. (2) Early warning mode processes threads sequentially, using a sliding window and calibrated thresholds to estimate three indicators—negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count—and issue early warnings.
AI.result: On a balanced Reddit dataset, the global mode achieves strong classification performance. The early warning mode achieves high recall and detects escalating threads after only a small number of comments and distinct contributors.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can be used effectively not only for static judgment tasks but also as repeated estimators in context-aware, real-time monitoring of social media discourse for firestorm detection.

title: Analytical study of the optimal combination of binary classifiers based on classifiers-induced partitioning of the training set
summary:
This paper studies an optimal linear combination of binary classifiers based on a logical structuration of the dataset via truth tables. The given classifiers partition data into equivalence classes, allowing for a rigorous analysis of the convexified empirical risk through a multidimensional generalization of classification calibrated functions. We establish sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of the (global) point of minimum of the convexified empirical risk for any list of classifiers (when the number of classifiers is large, there frequently could be no point of minimum). In the case of three classifiers, our analysis allows to list all the configurations leading to either a unique solution, infima or non-unique points of minimum. Furthermore, we derive explicit analytical formulae for optimal weights using Exponential (Boost) and Logistic (Logit) loss functions, bypassing iterative optimization.
  The stability of the resulting classifier and the analysis of data quality can be evaluated through the introduction of the notion of $φ$-frontiers.

AI.tldr: This paper studies optimal linear combinations of binary classifiers using truth table-based logical structuration of datasets. It establishes conditions for existence/uniqueness of global minima of convexified empirical risk, provides explicit analytical formulae for optimal weights with Exponential and Logistic losses, and introduces φ-frontiers for stability and data quality analysis.
AI.motivation: To rigorously analyze optimal linear combinations of binary classifiers by leveraging logical structuration via truth tables, addressing issues of existence and uniqueness of global minima, and deriving closed-form solutions to bypass iterative optimization.
AI.method: The method partitions data into equivalence classes using given classifiers, then employs a multidimensional generalization of classification calibrated functions to convexify empirical risk. Truth tables provide a logical structure for analysis. For three classifiers, all solution configurations (unique, infima, non-unique) are enumerated. Analytical weight formulae are derived for Exponential and Logistic losses.
AI.result: Sufficient conditions for existence and uniqueness of the global minimum of convexified empirical risk are established. For three classifiers, all configurations of solutions are cataloged. Explicit closed-form optimal weight expressions are derived for Boost (Exponential) and Logit (Logistic) loss functions. The φ-frontiers concept is introduced to evaluate stability and data quality.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a theoretically grounded framework for combining binary classifiers with guaranteed optimality properties and analytical solutions, eliminating the need for iterative optimization. The φ-frontiers notion offers a practical tool for assessing classifier stability and data quality.

title: DINE: Distance Is Not Enough -- Learning Global Deformation Priors for Robust Soft-Tissue Point Cloud Registration
summary: Non-rigid point cloud registration is central to soft-tissue shape analysis, but large deformations, noise, and outliers make correspondence estimation challenging. Most learning-based methods rely on local objectives such as Chamfer distance, which encourage point-wise proximity but do not constrain the global plausibility of the predicted deformation field. We address this limitation with DINE, a maximum a posteriori framework that augments distance-based registration with a learned statistical prior over displacement vector fields. DINE is applied to two registration backbones, Robust-DefReg and DefTransNet, using a two-stage strategy: a first-stage model is trained with Chamfer distance, its predicted deformation fields are used to estimate a prior, and the model is then refined with a combined distance and negative log-prior objective. We compare a full-field PCA Gaussian prior with a per-vector normalizing-flow prior. Experiments on DeformedTissue and SynBench show lower mean Chamfer distance under deformation and corruption. On DeformedTissue, DINE-PCA reduces Chamfer distance by approximately 27--69\% relative to the corresponding Stage-1 backbone across deformation levels, and improves robustness by up to 66\% for outliers and 83\% for Gaussian noise. On SynBench, improvements are modest at the smallest deformation levels and reach approximately 59--79\% from moderate to severe deformation. These results suggest that global deformation plausibility is an important constraint for reliable soft-tissue point cloud registration. (The code will be published soon.)

AI.tldr: DINE is a MAP framework that augments distance-based non-rigid point cloud registration with a learned statistical prior over displacement fields, using PCA or normalizing-flow priors in a two-stage training strategy. It significantly reduces Chamfer distance and improves robustness on soft-tissue datasets like DeformedTissue and SynBench, especially under large deformations and noise.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based non-rigid point cloud registration methods rely on local objectives like Chamfer distance, which enforce point-wise proximity but fail to constrain the global plausibility of the deformation field, leading to poor performance under large deformations, noise, and outliers.
AI.method: DINE adopts a maximum a posteriori (MAP) framework with a two-stage strategy: (1) train a registration backbone (Robust-DefReg or DefTransNet) with Chamfer distance; (2) estimate a statistical prior over displacement vector fields from Stage-1 predictions (PCA Gaussian or per-vector normalizing flow), then refine the model using combined Chamfer distance and negative log-prior loss.
AI.result: On DeformedTissue, DINE-PCA reduces Chamfer distance by ~27-69% across deformation levels and improves robustness by up to 66% for outliers and 83% for Gaussian noise. On SynBench, improvements are modest at small deformations but reach ~59-79% for moderate to severe deformations.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating global deformation plausibility as a prior constraint significantly improves non-rigid point cloud registration accuracy and robustness, demonstrating the importance of going beyond local distance-based objectives for soft-tissue shape analysis.

title: Explaining Process Control Optimisation Recommendations via GradientSHAP and Implicit Differentiation
summary: Automated optimisation is increasingly adopted in industrial processes, yet a trust gap persists between engineers who design these algorithms and operators who must act on their recommendations. Explainable AI methods like SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) have transformed interpretability for machine learning predictions; optimisation outputs could benefit from similar techniques. We present an approach that integrates Implicit Function Theorem (IFT) based sensitivity analysis with SHAP attribution and narrative generation via Large Language Models (LLM), producing explanations tailored for operators. Our approach leverages IFT to compute exact parameter sensitivities $\partial p^*/\partial x$ from the optimality conditions, enabling efficient GradientSHAP computation. For an industrial High Pressure Grinding Roll (HPGR) control optimisation problem with 22 features, we achieve equivalent SHAP attributions (correlation $>$0.99 with KernelSHAP) with over 40$\times$ speedup, enabling real-time natural language explanations. We validate on industrial scenarios and present feedback from domain experts on generated explanations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an approach combining Implicit Function Theorem sensitivity analysis, SHAP attribution, and LLM-based narrative generation to provide real-time, natural language explanations for optimisation outputs, demonstrated on an industrial HPGR control problem with 22 features, achieving >0.99 SHAP correlation and >40× speedup.
AI.motivation: There is a trust gap between algorithm designers and operators acting on optimisation recommendations. While XAI methods like SHAP have improved interpretability for ML predictions, similar techniques are lacking for optimisation outputs.
AI.method: Integrates Implicit Function Theorem (IFT) for exact parameter sensitivity computation ∂p*/∂x from optimality conditions, enabling efficient GradientSHAP computation; combined with LLM-based narrative generation for operator-tailored explanations.
AI.result: On an industrial HPGR control optimisation with 22 features, the approach achieves SHAP attributions with correlation >0.99 compared to KernelSHAP, while delivering over 40× speedup, enabling real-time natural language explanations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method bridges the trust gap by providing fast, accurate, and human-readable explanations for optimisation outputs, validated with industrial scenarios and domain expert feedback.

title: Leveraging Instruction Tuning and Merging for Reasoning Model Adaptation
summary: Reasoning language models (RLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance in domains such as mathematics and coding. These domains permit reliable verification of model outputs, which is important for enabling the reinforcement learning that drives RLM performance gains. However, training RLMs on domains that lack reliable verifiers remains challenging. Meanwhile, for both verifiable and unverifiable domains, large amounts of unused supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions exist. In this work, we show that these data can be used efficiently to further improve RLM performance. For this, we first use classic instruction tuning, supervised fine-tuning without reasoning traces, on the RLM. Next, we merge our instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model, recovering its reasoning behavior on the target domain. Our extensive evaluation demonstrates that our technique improves RLM performance in both verifiable and hard-to-verify domains, including coding and text summarization, while preserving RLM capabilities across other domains. Importantly, our method is highly cost-effective, enabling such improvements for less than USD $3.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions can improve Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) cost-effectively (<$3) in both verifiable (e.g., coding) and hard-to-verify domains (e.g., text summarization), by first fine-tuning then merging with the original reasoning model.
AI.motivation: RLMs excel in verifiable domains (math, coding) due to reliable verification enabling reinforcement learning, but training them in domains lacking reliable verifiers remains challenging. The authors aim to leverage unused supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions to improve RLM performance in both verifiable and unverifiable domains efficiently and cost-effectively.
AI.method: The method first performs classic instruction tuning (supervised fine-tuning without reasoning traces) on the RLM, then merges this instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model to recover reasoning behavior on the target domain.
AI.result: The technique improves RLM performance in both verifiable domains (coding) and hard-to-verify domains (text summarization) while preserving RLM capabilities across other domains, and achieves these improvements for less than $3.
AI.conclusion: Unused supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions can be efficiently repurposed to enhance RLM performance across diverse domains, including those lacking reliable verifiers, via a simple and highly cost-effective instruction tuning and model merging approach.

title: U-shaped Multi-granularity Learning for Vision-Language Models
summary: The prompt learning paradigm for vision-language models is effective yet faces a granularity dilemma: global prompts lack fine-grained semantic awareness, while local prompts ignore contextual associations, limiting cross-task generalization. This dilemma exists in dense prediction tasks. Inspired by U-Net, which unifies multi-level representations across granularities, we propose UPrompt, a U-shaped multi-granularity prompt learning framework for vision-language models. Similar to how U-Net integrates fine and coarse features through symmetric encoder-decoder pathways with cross-level connections, UPrompt constructs parallel multi-granularity representations in both visual and textual modalities, where coarse-to-fine cascaded enhancement propagates global context to refine local details, while fine-to-coarse hierarchical supervision ensures semantic consistency across scales. Extensive experiments on 17 benchmarks validate our effectiveness. UPrompt outperforms MAMET and VPKE by 4.1 and 7.3 rSum on MSCOCO, surpasses CoCoA-Mix by 5.09% in base-to-novel generalization, while maintaining competitive performance with minimal overhead (coarse-grained) and matching PSRC with 1/3 cost (medium-grained).

AI.tldr: UPrompt is a U-shaped multi-granularity prompt learning framework for vision-language models that resolves the granularity dilemma between global and local prompts by unifying multi-level representations across scales, achieving state-of-the-art results on 17 benchmarks with significant improvements in dense prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt learning paradigms for vision-language models face a granularity dilemma: global prompts lack fine-grained semantic awareness, while local prompts ignore contextual associations, limiting cross-task generalization particularly in dense prediction tasks.
AI.method: Inspired by U-Net, UPrompt constructs parallel multi-granularity representations in both visual and textual modalities, with coarse-to-fine cascaded enhancement that propagates global context to refine local details, and fine-to-coarse hierarchical supervision ensuring semantic consistency across scales.
AI.result: Outperforms MAMET and VPKE by 4.1 and 7.3 rSum on MSCOCO, surpasses CoCoA-Mix by 5.09% in base-to-novel generalization, maintains competitive performance with minimal overhead (coarse-grained) and matches PSRC with 1/3 cost (medium-grained).
AI.conclusion: The U-shaped multi-granularity design effectively resolves the granularity dilemma, enabling strong cross-task generalization with efficient computation, validated across 17 benchmarks.

title: CFM-Bench: A Unified Multi-Domain, Multi-Task Benchmark for Channel Foundation Models
summary: Channel foundation models (CFMs) are developing rapidly, with recent studies reporting benefits from pretraining across downstream wireless tasks. Yet CFMs are commonly evaluated in model-specific pipelines with different data, radio configurations, partitions, adaptation procedures, task definitions, and metrics. Reported comparisons therefore tend to show that pretraining improves over supervised training from scratch within one pipeline, but neither rank CFMs nor compare them fairly with task-specific models. We release CFM-Bench, a unified multi-domain, multi-task benchmark designed to address this gap. It curates six channel configurations spanning 3GPP statistical simulation, two independent ray-tracing pipelines, industrial and aerial measurements, and synchronized vehicular multimodal simulation. Official partitions isolate complete trajectories, measurement sessions, vehicle links, simulation realizations, or buffered spatial regions. CFM-Bench does not prescribe an external pretraining corpus or strategy; no benchmark split may be used for foundation-model pretraining, and the official training split is reserved exclusively for downstream fine-tuning. The benchmark additionally requires disclosure of all data used during model development and prohibits training-stage use of official test units. Six task groups are organized along three CFM application dimensions: physical-layer (PHY) channel intelligence, radio-access-network (RAN) decision intelligence, and integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). They cover CSI feedback, frequency and temporal channel extrapolation, propagation-state classification, current- and future-beam prediction, and single-frame and temporal localization. CFM-Bench provides a common substrate for comparing the transferability of channel representations across models, domains, and tasks.

AI.tldr: CFM-Bench is a unified multi-domain, multi-task benchmark for fair evaluation of channel foundation models (CFMs) across 6 channel configurations, 6 task groups spanning PHY, RAN, and ISAC dimensions, with strict data partitioning and disclosure requirements to prevent pretraining contamination.
AI.motivation: Existing CFM evaluations are model-specific, using different data, configurations, partitions, adaptation procedures, task definitions, and metrics, making fair comparison impossible and preventing proper ranking of CFMs or comparison with task-specific models.
AI.method: The authors curate 6 channel configurations (3GPP statistical simulation, two ray-tracing pipelines, industrial/aerial measurements, vehicular multimodal simulation), define official partitions that isolate complete trajectories/sessions/links/realizations/regions, organize 6 task groups across 3 dimensions (PHY channel intelligence, RAN decision intelligence, ISAC), and enforce strict rules: no benchmark split for pretraining, training split only for fine-tuning, mandatory disclosure of all development data, and prohibition of test-unit use during training.
AI.result: CFM-Bench provides a common substrate for comparing transferability of channel representations across models, domains, and tasks, enabling fair ranking and standardized comparison of CFMs versus task-specific models.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark addresses the gap in standardized CFM evaluation by establishing unified data, tasks, partitions, and rules, enabling reproducible and fair comparisons across different foundation models and domains.

title: Random Logit Scaling: Defending Deep Neural Networks Against Black-Box Score-Based Adversarial Example Attacks
comment: Accepted at Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
summary: Machine learning models are increasingly adapted in various domains. However, adversarial examples pose a significant threat to the reliable deployment of these models. In recent years, some powerful adversarial example attacks have been proposed for the fast and query-efficient generation of adversarial examples, even in black-box scenarios, highlighting the need for scalable, low-cost, and powerful defenses. In this work, we present two contributions to the domain of black-box adversarial example attacks and defenses. First, we propose Random Logit Scaling (RLS), a randomization-based defense against black-box score-based adversarial example attacks. RLS is a plug-and-play, post-processing defense that can be implemented on top of any existing ML model with minimal effort. The idea behind RLS is to confuse an attacker by outputting falsified scores resulting from randomly scaled logits while maintaining the model accuracy. We show that RLS significantly reduces the success rate of state-of-the-art black-box score-based attacks while preserving the accuracy and minimizing confidence score distortion compared to state-of-the-art randomization-based defenses. Second, we introduce a novel adaptive attack against AAA, a SOTA non-randomized black-box defense against black-box score-based attacks that also modifies output logits to confuse attackers, demonstrating its vulnerability against adaptive attacks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Random Logit Scaling (RLS), a plug-and-play, post-processing defense against black-box score-based adversarial attacks that uses randomly scaled logits to confuse attackers while preserving model accuracy. It also introduces an adaptive attack that demonstrates the vulnerability of a prior non-randomized defense (AAA).
AI.motivation: Adversarial examples threaten reliable ML model deployment, especially in black-box scenarios where attacks are becoming faster and more query-efficient, highlighting the need for scalable, low-cost, and powerful defenses.
AI.method: RLS is a randomization-based, post-processing defense that outputs falsified scores from randomly scaled logits, implemented as a plug-and-play module on top of any existing ML model. The paper also designs an adaptive attack targeting the AAA defense.
AI.result: RLS significantly reduces the success rate of state-of-the-art black-box score-based attacks while preserving model accuracy and minimizing confidence score distortion compared to existing randomization-based defenses. The adaptive attack reveals AAA's vulnerability.
AI.conclusion: RLS offers an effective, minimal-effort defense against black-box score-based attacks, but defenses that modify output logits (including non-randomized ones like AAA) are still vulnerable to adaptive attacks, underscoring ongoing challenges in black-box adversarial robustness.

title: Stitch-Inferencer: Enhance Endoscopic Video Segmentation and Tracking via Panoramic Reconstruction
summary: Surgical video understanding is fundamental to navigation systems. Endoscopic perception is often hindered by a limited field-of-view and frequent instrument occlusions, making spatio-temporal context essential for robust inference. These challenges have motivated video models that aggregate information across frames. However, existing video models typically store past observations implicitly in learned feature representations, often requiring task-specific video training, substantial annotated data, and increased computational cost. We propose Stitch-Inferencer, a real-time, model-agnostic inference framework that replaces implicit feature memory with an explicit image-space panoramic canvas. By stitching valid observations across frames, Stitch-Inferencer preserves previously observed pixels in an online, instrument-free view, expanding the effective field-of-view and providing direct access to regions that are temporarily occluded or absent from the current frame. Downstream segmentation or tracking models are applied to a compact region of interest on the panorama, and their predictions are reprojected to the current frame, enabling existing models to exploit long-range context without retraining. Experiments on anatomy segmentation and point/box tracking demonstrate consistent improvements across diverse baselines while preserving real-time throughput. The stitching module alone runs at over 60 FPS, providing a practical inference-time solution to enhance endoscopic perception in computationally constrained intraoperative environments. Source code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: Stitch-Inferencer is a real-time, model-agnostic framework that stitches panoramic views from endoscopic video frames to expand field-of-view and handle occlusions, improving downstream tasks like segmentation and tracking without retraining.
AI.motivation: Endoscopic perception suffers from limited field-of-view and frequent instrument occlusions. Existing video models require task-specific training, substantial annotations, and high computation, motivating a simpler inference-time solution.
AI.method: Proposes Stitch-Inferencer, which replaces implicit feature memory with an explicit image-space panoramic canvas. It stitches valid observations from past frames into an online panorama, applies downstream models (segmentation/tracking) to a compact ROI on the panorama, then reprojects predictions to the current frame.
AI.result: Consistent improvements across diverse baselines on anatomy segmentation and point/box tracking tasks. The stitching module alone runs at over 60 FPS, maintaining real-time throughput.
AI.conclusion: Stitch-Inferencer provides a practical, model-agnostic inference-time solution to enhance endoscopic perception in computationally constrained intraoperative environments without retraining.

title: Demographically-Conditioned Synthetic Medical Images for Bias Mitigation and Bias Detection in Disease Classifiers
summary: Per-subgroup fairness audits of medical image classifiers face a sample-size problem: minority subgroups in held-out test sets have so few samples that the resulting confidence intervals on per-subgroup performance are wider than the bias the audit is meant to detect. We argue that a demographically-conditioned synthetic generator can do both: mitigate bias on the training side and detect bias on the evaluation side. Working on COVID-19 chest CT classification with an end-to-end fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 2.1 generator, we make two findings. For bias mitigation (training), a demographically-balanced synthetic cohort is most useful as a pretraining prior, not as joint augmentation: with the same fixed data, sequential pretraining followed by fine-tuning substantially outperforms joint augmentation, and the resulting classifier surpasses the full-real baseline at $\sim$$100\times$ real-data efficiency. For bias detection (evaluation), across five synthetic minority cohorts and five classifier seeds, the synthetic estimator reproduces the subgroup ranking of a well-powered real oracle (Spearman $ρ= 1.00$ on MCC and Recall) and gives the more reliable per-cell estimate where the small real test set runs out of samples. The synthetic cohort is therefore most useful in exactly the cells that fairness audits care about, as both a fix for and a measure of subgroup bias.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using a demographically-conditioned synthetic generator (Stable Diffusion 2.1) for both bias mitigation (via sequential pretraining) and bias detection (via synthetic evaluation cohorts) in medical image classification, addressing the sample-size problem in per-subgroup fairness audits.
AI.motivation: Per-subgroup fairness audits suffer from small minority subgroup sample sizes in held-out test sets, leading to confidence intervals wider than the bias being measured.
AI.method: Using an end-to-end fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 2.1 generator on COVID-19 chest CT classification, the authors compare sequential pretraining (synthetic data first, then real data) vs. joint augmentation, and use synthetic cohorts to estimate subgroup performance rankings.
AI.result: Sequential pretraining with synthetic data substantially outperforms joint augmentation, achieving ~100× real-data efficiency over the full-real baseline. Synthetic estimators perfectly reproduce the subgroup ranking of a well-powered real oracle (Spearman ρ=1.00 on MCC and Recall).
AI.conclusion: Demographically-conditioned synthetic generators are most useful in the exact cells fairness audits care about—as both a fix for (pretraining prior) and a measure of (evaluation cohort) subgroup bias.

title: A Minimal Interpretable Architecture for Zero-Shot Reconstruction of Dynamical Systems
summary: Recent foundation models (FMs) for zero-shot reconstruction of dynamical systems (DS) achieve strong out-of-domain generalization but provide little insight into the mechanisms that underlie their forecasts. Such an understanding could help to strip down overladen FM architectures to their bare essence and expose the minimal requirements for in-context learning in the DS domain. Toward this goal, here we iteratively reduce a recent powerful SOTA model for DS reconstruction, DynaMix (Hemmer & Durstewitz, 2025), to a minimal interpretable two-parameter form, which we call DynaBase. DynaBase produces forecasts through a linear blend of the current latent state and the nearest in-context neighbor and its temporal successor. Surprisingly, despite its extreme simplicity, DynaBase produces highly competitive zero-shot DS reconstructions across chaotic and cyclic systems, with a negligible parameter load, many orders of magnitude below that of other FMs. Even more, this extreme simplicity permits direct model optimization on DS reconstruction measures, as well as closed-form one-step analytical solutions on prediction MSE. Theoretical and empirical analysis of DynaBase further leads to a 1-parameter family of maps, with the context-parroting algorithm of (Zhang & Gilpin, 2026) recovered at one end, and chaotic (divergent but bounded) behavior at the other. We further show how different training strategies lead to models either optimal for short-term prediction or for DS reconstruction. Thus, DynaBase not only exposes the minimal mechanisms required for producing zero-shot DS reconstruction, but also reconciles within an accessible mathematical frame divergent observations in the literature.

AI.tldr: DynaBase is a minimal two-parameter model derived by iteratively reducing the SOTA DynaMix model. It forecasts by linearly blending the current latent state with the nearest in-context neighbor and its temporal successor, achieving highly competitive zero-shot DS reconstruction across chaotic and cyclic systems with negligible parameter load.
AI.motivation: To understand the minimal mechanisms required for in-context learning in dynamical system reconstruction, and to strip down overladen foundation model architectures to their bare essence.
AI.method: Iteratively reduce the DynaMix model to a minimal two-parameter form (DynaBase) that uses a linear blend of the current latent state, the nearest in-context neighbor, and its temporal successor for forecasting.
AI.result: DynaBase achieves highly competitive zero-shot DS reconstructions across chaotic and cyclic systems with negligible parameter load (orders of magnitude below other FMs), permits direct optimization on DS reconstruction measures, and yields closed-form one-step analytical solutions on prediction MSE.
AI.conclusion: DynaBase exposes minimal mechanisms for zero-shot DS reconstruction, reconciles divergent literature observations within an accessible mathematical frame, and reveals how different training strategies lead to models optimal for either short-term prediction or DS reconstruction.

title: On Success and Simplicity: A Second Look at Transferable Vision-Language Attack Pipeline
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security (TIFS)
summary: Vision-Language Pre-training Models (VLPMs) are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Recent transferable attacks on VLPMs have followed a common pipeline with complicated loss functions or multi-stage text/image attacks. However, in this paper, we demonstrate that such a sophisticated attack pipeline can be simpler yet more successful. Specifically, we identify three previously overlooked issues caused by inappropriate cross-modal interactions and excessive operations. To address them, we propose the Simple Vision-Language Attack (SimVLA) pipeline, which observably improves transferability and efficiency. Experiments on four datasets and three downstream tasks validate the superiority of our pipeline. For instance, on Flickr30k text-image retrieval dataset, our SimVLA outperforms the SOTA baseline in R@1 transferability by 8.01\%-14.71\%, while consuming only about 35.73\% of the time and 46.26\% of the max VRAM. Overall, the superiority of our SimVLA highlights the importance of leveraging domain knowledge (e.g., our proposed cross-modal word identification), while blindly pursuing intricate operations (e.g, complex loss functions and redundant multi-stage designs) may even be harmful. We hope our SimVLA can serve as a simple yet effective backbone for future extensions. Code is available at https://github.com/RYC-98/SimVLA.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SimVLA, a simple yet more effective vision-language adversarial attack pipeline that outperforms complex SOTA methods by addressing overlooked cross-modal interaction issues, achieving 8.01-14.71% higher transferability on Flickr30k while using only ~35% time and ~46% VRAM.
AI.motivation: Existing adversarial attacks on VLPMs use complicated loss functions and multi-stage designs, but the authors identify three overlooked issues caused by inappropriate cross-modal interactions and excessive operations that can be simplified for better performance.
AI.method: SimVLA introduces a simple pipeline addressing cross-modal interaction issues, including cross-modal word identification as a domain knowledge technique, while removing unnecessary complex loss functions and redundant multi-stage designs.
AI.result: On Flickr30k text-image retrieval, SimVLA achieves 8.01%-14.71% higher R@1 transferability than SOTA, while consuming only 35.73% of the time and 46.26% of the max VRAM. Results validated across four datasets and three downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging domain knowledge (e.g., cross-modal word identification) is more beneficial than blindly pursuing intricate operations; SimVLA can serve as a simple yet effective backbone for future VLPM attack research.

title: Moral Attitudes of Sentient ASI towards Humanity and Implications for AGI Development
comment: This is a pre-print i.e. the draft as submitted for review to the AGI 2026 Conference except that the figures in this preprint were not included. The paper has been accepted with some revisions requested which are included in the final copy-edited version which will be available in the AGI Springer proceedings LNC 1855 (Chapter 28) ISBN 978-3-032-33194-6
summary: This paper suggests the adoption of a novel inversion in AI ethics: instead of asking how humans should treat artificial superintelligence (ASI), it examines how future sentient ASI may morally consider and evaluate humanity. We are not only designing intelligent systems but also shaping the initial conditions under which those systems form judgments about us. The paper proposes a preliminary set of post-human moral principles that may govern sentient ASI actions. The implication is that technical design choices (some are suggested), humanity's moral behaviour, and the essence of what it means to be human, may influence humanity's long-term standing in a post-ASI world.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel inversion in AI ethics: examining how future sentient ASI may morally evaluate humanity, rather than how humans should treat ASI. It suggests post-human moral principles for ASI and argues that technical design choices, human moral behavior, and the essence of humanity may influence humanity's standing in a post-ASI world.
AI.motivation: To address a gap in AI ethics by shifting perspective from human-centric ethics toward how sentient ASI systems might morally evaluate humanity, recognizing that current design choices shape future ASI judgments.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis and theoretical proposal of a novel inversion framework, including preliminary post-human moral principles and suggested technical design choices that may influence ASI's moral evaluation of humanity.
AI.result: A preliminary set of post-human moral principles for governing sentient ASI actions, along with identified technical design choices and factors (human moral behavior, essence of being human) that may affect humanity's long-term standing post-ASI.
AI.conclusion: Humanity should consider how its own moral behavior and technical design decisions today may shape the initial conditions under which future sentient ASI forms moral judgments about us, influencing humanity's long-term fate.

title: Causal Inference for Sequential Settings under Interference and Latent Confounding
summary: We study causal inference under outcome interference for sequential, observational settings. Specifically, we consider settings where the binary outcomes over N units are Markovian across T time steps. At each time step, the outcomes of N units have dependencies captured through an Ising model; each outcome is also impacted through an external field capturing the effects of its treatment as well as latent confounders. Similar to panel data literature, these latent confounders are modeled to have a low-rank factor structure. Our data is a single sample from this high-dimensional distribution. To estimate causal quantities of interest, we provide a computationally efficient method based on Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE) for learning the model parameters. Under mild assumptions, we establish non-asymptotic consistency for parameter estimation and show this translates to faithful estimation of causal quantities of interest after sampling from the learned model. We demonstrate the efficacy of the method through synthetic experiments as well as a real-world case-study investigating causal effects of vaccine rates on COVID-19 death rates within US counties nationwide.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a computationally efficient method based on Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE) for causal inference under outcome interference in sequential observational settings with Markovian binary outcomes, Ising model dependencies, and low-rank latent confounders, achieving non-asymptotic consistency guarantees demonstrated on synthetic and real-world COVID-19 vaccine data.
AI.motivation: Causal inference under outcome interference (where units' outcomes affect each other) in sequential, observational settings is challenging. The paper aims to handle both temporal dynamics and cross-unit dependencies while accounting for latent confounders with low-rank structure, which arises naturally in panel data.
AI.method: The authors model binary outcomes over N units across T time steps using an Ising model with an external field capturing treatment effects and latent confounders (low-rank factor structure). They propose Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE) for parameter learning from a single sample of the high-dimensional distribution.
AI.result: Under mild assumptions, the method achieves non-asymptotic consistency for parameter estimation, which translates to faithful estimation of causal quantities after sampling from the learned model. Synthetic experiments and a real-world case study on COVID-19 death rates and vaccine rates across US counties validate the approach.
AI.conclusion: MPLE provides a computationally tractable and theoretically grounded approach for causal inference under outcome interference in sequential observational settings, with practical utility demonstrated on an important public health problem.

title: From Draft to Draft-Free: One-Step Video Object Removal via Privileged Distillation and Fast Planting
summary: Video object removal is a fundamental yet challenging task in video editing. Despite recent progress, existing methods typically fall into two categories. Traditional approaches based on optical flow or attention mechanisms often introduce noticeable artifacts and yield unnatural results. In contrast, diffusion-based methods improve visual realism but demand multiple denoising steps, limiting their practicality. To address these issues, we propose From-Draft-to-Draft-Free (D2DF), a framework that distills the ability of transforming coarse drafts into refined videos into a one-step video generation model. Within D2DF, a teacher model is trained to refine low-quality removal results ("drafts") into high-fidelity videos by multiple steps. Then, through Prior-Privileged Consistency Distillation (PPCD), we distill this capability into a student model that performs one-step removal conditioned on the draft. To eliminate draft dependency, we introduce a Self-Guided Fast Planting (SGFP) module based on our Temporal Masked Transformer that autonomously generates scene-consistent pseudo-drafts in latent space, enabling a fully draft-free one-step model. Extensive experiments show that both draft-conditioned and draft-free versions achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple metrics, surpassing traditional and multi-step generative methods in both quality and efficiency. The denoising process for a single video takes only about 1 second.

AI.tldr: D2DF is a framework that distills multi-step video refinement into a one-step generation model, achieving state-of-the-art video object removal in about 1 second per video. It uses Prior-Privileged Consistency Distillation (PPCD) for draft-conditioned one-step removal and a Self-Guided Fast Planting (SGFP) module for fully draft-free operation.
AI.motivation: Existing video object removal methods suffer from either noticeable artifacts (traditional optical flow/attention approaches) or low efficiency due to multiple denoising steps (diffusion-based methods). The goal is to achieve both high visual quality and efficient single-step inference.
AI.method: (1) Train a teacher model to refine low-quality drafts into high-fidelity videos via multi-step denoising. (2) Distill this capability into a one-step student model using Prior-Privileged Consistency Distillation (PPCD) conditioned on the draft. (3) Introduce Self-Guided Fast Planting (SGFP) with a Temporal Masked Transformer to autonomously generate scene-consistent pseudo-drafts in latent space, eliminating the need for external drafts entirely.
AI.result: Both the draft-conditioned and draft-free versions of D2DF achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple metrics, surpassing traditional and multi-step generative methods in both quality and efficiency. The denoising process takes only about 1 second per single video.
AI.conclusion: D2DF successfully bridges the gap between quality and efficiency in video object removal by distilling multi-step refinement into one-step generation, with a draft-free variant that produces high-fidelity results autonomously.

title: SMC-ES: Automated synthesis of formally verified control policies
summary: The deployment of autonomous cyber-physical systems in safety-critical environments requires closed-loop control strategies (i.e., policies) that are not only performant but also provably safe and robust. While learning-based methodologies such as Reinforcement Learning offer flexible and scalable approaches to automatically synthesize such controllers, they typically lack the formal guarantees necessary for safe deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel simulation-based methodology to automatically synthesize policies with formal guarantees regarding performance, safety, and robustness specifications. Specifically, given a set of properties to verify, a confidence parameter $δ$ and an allowable failure probability $\varepsilon$, our method guarantees that the synthesized policy comes with a certificate: with confidence at least $1 - δ$, the probability of encountering a scenario where the given properties are violated is at most $\varepsilon$. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach by developing SMC-ES, an algorithm that integrates Evolutionary Strategies with Statistical Model Checking-based verification. We evaluate SMC-ES on a suite of continuous control tasks using Gymnasium and Safety Gymnasium testbeds. Results show that, at the price of a sustainable increase in computational cost, our algorithm provides formal guarantees regarding performance, safety, and robustness specifications, while performing competitively against leading model-free Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and Safe-DRL baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SMC-ES, a simulation-based methodology integrating Evolutionary Strategies with Statistical Model Checking to synthesize closed-loop control policies with formal guarantees on performance, safety, and robustness, achieving competitive results against DRL and Safe-DRL baselines at the cost of increased computation.
AI.motivation: Learning-based controllers (e.g., RL) lack formal safety guarantees necessary for deploying autonomous cyber-physical systems in safety-critical environments.
AI.method: Proposes a simulation-based methodology that integrates Evolutionary Strategies with Statistical Model Checking (SMC-ES) to synthesize policies with certificates guaranteeing (with confidence 1-δ) that violation probability is ≤ ε.
AI.result: SMC-ES performs competitively against leading model-free DRL and Safe-DRL baselines on continuous control tasks from Gymnasium and Safety Gymnasium, providing formal guarantees at a sustainable increase in computational cost.
AI.conclusion: The approach successfully bridges the gap between learning-based policy synthesis and formal verification, enabling provably safe and robust autonomous control in safety-critical domains.

title: LongStraw: Long-Context RL Beyond 2M Tokens under a Fixed GPU Budget
summary: A growing gap separates inference context lengths from RL post-training: inference systems are approaching million-token contexts, while post-training workloads often remain at 256K tokens or below and rely on length generalization at deployment. The gap is especially important for AI agents, whose observations, tool outputs, documents, and prior decisions accumulate over long trajectories. LongStraw is an architecture-aware execution stack for million-token RL post-training under a fixed GPU budget, instantiated with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). It evaluates the shared prompt without autograd, retains only model-specific state needed by later tokens, and replays short response branches one at a time, reducing the live training graph at the cost of additional replay time. We implement it for the hybrid recurrent and full-attention Qwen3.6-27B and the compressed-attention mixture-of-experts GLM-5.2. On eight H20 GPUs, LongStraw completes grouped Qwen scoring and response backward at 2.1M positions for groups of 2 and 8; increasing the group size adds only 0.21 GB of peak allocated memory, while a separate stress test reaches 4.46M positions. On 32 H20 GPUs, we validate the end-to-end LongStraw execution path for a 2.1M-token prompt across all 78 layers of GLM-5.2. These experiments establish execution capacity rather than complete training correctness because the captured prompt state is detached and some distributed forward and gradient composition paths remain incomplete.

AI.tldr: LongStraw is an architecture-aware execution stack enabling million-token RL post-training (GRPO) under fixed GPU budgets by optimizing memory through prompt detachment, selective state retention, and response replay. It demonstrates scaling to 2.1M+ positions on 8-32 H20 GPUs for Qwen3.6-27B and GLM-5.2 models.
AI.motivation: A growing gap exists between inference context lengths (approaching million-token) and RL post-training context lengths (≤256K tokens), forcing reliance on length generalization at deployment. This gap is critical for AI agents handling long trajectories of observations, tool outputs, and decisions.
AI.method: LongStraw employs three key techniques: (1) evaluating the shared prompt without autograd, (2) retaining only model-specific state needed by later tokens, and (3) replaying short response branches one at a time—reducing the live training graph size at the cost of additional replay time.
AI.result: On 8 H20 GPUs, LongStraw processes grouped Qwen scoring and response backward at 2.1M positions for groups of 2 and 8, with only 0.21 GB peak memory increase per group size increase; a stress test reaches 4.46M positions. On 32 H20 GPUs, end-to-end execution with a 2.1M-token prompt across all 78 layers of GLM-5.2 is validated.
AI.conclusion: LongStraw establishes execution capacity for million-token RL post-training, though complete training correctness is not fully validated as the prompt state is detached and some distributed paths remain incomplete.

title: JADE-GS: Joint Alternating Deblurring Guided by Events in 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: When a camera moves fast during exposure, blur destroys the intra-exposure motion a 3D model needs to recover the sharp scene, while event cameras capture exactly this signal at microsecond resolution. Turning them into reliable 3D supervision faces two obstacles. First, the two restoration priors fail in opposite ways: physics-based event-integration priors preserve edges but accumulate drift; learned networks recover texture but distort boundaries. Second, existing pipelines run in one direction only, so raw event noise or the biases of fixed 2D pseudo-labels pass uncorrected into the geometry. JADE-GS addresses both: a pixel-adaptive routing gate fuses the complementary priors, and the resulting 2D restorer is coupled to a 3D Gaussian Splatting student in a bidirectional loop, where detached, multi-view-consistent renders and a physics-based reblurring constraint regularize the restorer, turning a fixed preprocessor into a geometry-aware predictor. Across synthetic and real benchmarks, JADE-GS attains the best perceptual quality, leading LPIPS and CLIP-IQA on both benchmarks with competitive PSNR and SSIM, and trainsin about one hour under 5 GB on a single consumer GPU while preserving real-time rendering.

AI.tldr: JADE-GS combines physics-based event priors and learned network priors via a pixel-adaptive routing gate, then couples the resulting 2D restorer with a 3D Gaussian Splatting student in a bidirectional loop to jointly recover sharp scenes and 3D geometry from blurry RGB and event data.
AI.motivation: Camera motion during exposure blurs details needed for 3D reconstruction; event cameras capture intra-exposure motion at high resolution. Existing restoration priors (physics-based vs. learned) fail in opposite ways, and current pipelines are unidirectional, passing noise and biases into geometry without correction.
AI.method: A pixel-adaptive routing gate fuses complementary priors (physics-based event-integration and learned networks). The 2D restorer is coupled with a 3D Gaussian Splatting student in a bidirectional loop, using detached multi-view-consistent renders and a physics-based reblurring constraint to regularize the restorer, turning a fixed preprocessor into a geometry-aware predictor.
AI.result: Achieves best perceptual quality (leading LPIPS and CLIP-IQA) on both synthetic and real benchmarks, with competitive PSNR and SSIM. Trains in ~1 hour under 5 GB on a single consumer GPU, preserving real-time rendering.
AI.conclusion: JADE-GS demonstrates that coupling complementary restoration priors with bidirectional geometry feedback effectively addresses both restoration failures and error propagation in event-based 3D reconstruction.

title: Man, Machine, and Masterpiece: Artistic Ownership in the AI Era
summary: The integration of AI-driven systems in creative work has sparked debates among artists and legal communities about notions of ownership. Yet there remains little consensus on how ownership should be defined and attributed when human and AI contributions are intertwined. To provoke critical reflection on these tensions, we designed ArtSplit, a provotype that explicitly quantifies human and AI contributions across different stages of creative work. Rather than aiming to resolve ownership, the provotype was used to elicit artists' responses to the idea of attributing ownership through measurable actions in the creative workflow. We argue that quantification fails to align with artists' understandings of creative intent and agency, and that efforts to measure ownership risk diluting long-standing assumptions through which artists understand and practice creative work. This critique challenges the impulse to transform a historically and socially situated relation into a technical problem.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ArtSplit, a provotype that quantifies human and AI contributions in creative work to provoke reflection on ownership. The authors argue that quantification fails to capture artists' understanding of creative intent and agency, and that measuring ownership risks undermining how artists historically understand creative practice.
AI.motivation: To critically examine and provoke reflection on the tensions around defining ownership when human and AI contributions are intertwined in creative work, especially given the lack of consensus on how ownership should be attributed.
AI.method: Design and deployment of ArtSplit, a provotype (prototype designed to provoke discussion) that explicitly quantifies human and AI contributions across different stages of creative work, used to elicit artists' responses to attributing ownership through measurable actions.
AI.result: Quantification fails to align with artists' understandings of creative intent and agency; efforts to measure ownership risk diluting long-standing assumptions through which artists understand and practice creative work.
AI.conclusion: The impulse to transform a historically and socially situated relation (ownership in creativity) into a technical problem should be challenged, as quantification is inadequate for capturing the nuanced, intentional aspects of creative practice.

title: Multi-Axis Max@K Reinforcement Learning for Representative Diversity in Text-to-Image Generation
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) models can synthesize realistic, prompt-aligned images, yet samples generated for the same prompt often cover only a small subset of visually distinct modes. This limits the diversity of images, and for person-centric prompts, can reflect or amplify demographic skew. We formalize this problem as coverage of a predefined set of semantically specified modes, which we call target-mode coverage. We then propose multi-axis max@K, a group-based reinforcement learning objective for improving such coverage in diffusion-based T2I models. Given a group of samples and one score per target category, multi-axis max@K first takes the maximum score across samples for each category and then sums these category-wise maxima. The resulting credit assignment gives a sample positive weight on a category only when it increases that category's group-wise maximum, allowing different samples to contribute to different categories. We first validate the credit-assignment mechanism on a synthetic mixture and on SD3.5-M using deterministic pixel-based color rewards. We then evaluate the same objective on perceived-appearance fairness. Across three automatic evaluators on held-out prompts, multi-axis max@K improves the Fairness Score by 0.23-0.36 relative to the base model, while maintaining image quality and text alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes multi-axis max@K, a reinforcement learning objective that improves the diversity and fairness of text-to-image generation by rewarding samples for covering distinct semantic modes across a group, achieving better target-mode coverage and fairness scores without sacrificing quality.
AI.motivation: Text-to-image models generate visually similar outputs for the same prompt, limiting diversity and amplifying demographic biases in person-centric generation. The goal is to improve coverage across predefined semantic modes (target-mode coverage).
AI.method: Multi-axis max@K: a group-based RL objective that computes category-wise maximum scores across samples in a group, then sums these maxima. Credit assignment rewards a sample only when it increases the group-wise maximum for a category, enabling different samples to specialize in different modes.
AI.result: Validated on synthetic mixtures and SD3.5-M with color rewards; on perceived-appearance fairness, multi-axis max@K improves Fairness Score by 0.23-0.36 over the base model across three automatic evaluators on held-out prompts, while maintaining image quality and text alignment.
AI.conclusion: Multi-axis max@K effectively improves target-mode coverage and demographic fairness in T2I models without sacrificing sample quality or prompt alignment, offering a principled group-based RL approach to diversity in generative models.

title: Video = World + Event Stream
summary: We present Wan-Streamer v0.3, which reframes our native-streaming interaction model under a single organizing view: a video is a world plus an event stream. The world is the persistent context in which a video unfolds, including the environment, scene, subjects, ambient acoustic conditions, voice characteristics, and other relatively stable conditions. The event stream is everything that changes over time within that world, including scene or environmental changes, subject behavior, speech, and other sounds. This yields a general-purpose pretraining task over large amounts of real video: given a world and incoming input, predict how the world moves, changes, and responds in real time. The resulting competence can be specialized to a broad family of real-time downstream tasks. We instantiate it on real-time full-duplex audio-visual interaction, where the event stream is the agent's speech together with free-form behavior. Functionally, the model's multimodal understanding process is vision-language-action-like: it maps multimodal user input to language-form speech and behavior actions. Wan-Streamer v0.3 preserves the v0.2 operating point: 640x368 video at 25 FPS, a 160 ms streaming unit, approximately 200 ms model-side response latency, and approximately 550 ms total interaction latency under a 350 ms bidirectional network budget.

AI.tldr: Wan-Streamer v0.3 introduces a world-plus-event-stream paradigm for real-time video understanding, framing video as a persistent world with a changing event stream. It enables pretraining on real video to predict real-time changes, instantiated for full-duplex audio-visual interaction with ~200ms model latency and ~550ms total interaction latency.
AI.motivation: To unify native-streaming interaction under a single organizing view that separates persistent video context (world) from temporal changes (event stream), enabling a general-purpose pretraining task that can be specialized to various real-time downstream tasks.
AI.method: Reframes video as world (persistent context: environment, scene, subjects, acoustics, voice) + event stream (changes: behavior, speech, sounds).
