Uses a vision-language-action-like multimodal architecture that maps multimodal user input to language-form speech and behavior actions with 640x368@25FPS, 160ms streaming unit.
AI.result: Preserves v0.2 operating point: 640x368 video at 25 FPS, 160 ms streaming unit, ~200 ms model-side response latency, ~550 ms total interaction latency under 350 ms bidirectional network budget.
AI.conclusion: The world-plus-event-stream paradigm provides a general-purpose pretraining approach for real-time video understanding that can be specialized to tasks like real-time full-duplex audio-visual interaction.

title: BrainPilot: Automating Brain Discovery with Agentic Research
summary: Understanding the brain increasingly depends on integrating evidence across scales, modalities, and disciplines. Addressing a single research question therefore requires a coordinated sequence of operations, from surveying prior work to executing analyses and interpreting results in light of domain knowledge. AI agents promise to accelerate this process, but current agents lack domain expertise in brain science, may fabricate claims, drift during multi-step reasoning, and offer few defined points for expert intervention. These failures are especially costly in brain science, where conclusions feed into downstream scientific claims and depend on laboratory-specific expertise and careful human judgment. We present \textbf{BrainPilot} a \textbf{fully open-source} multi-agent system that accelerates brain science research with traceable logs and agent-verified results. A principal investigator (PI) agent coordinates specialist agents grounded in curated domain knowledge: a unified brain science knowledge base containing 7{,}233 indexed items and a skill library of 72 reusable methodology units across seven research domains. Every major step is recorded in the Graph of Trace, an auditable record that links subgoals, tool use, evidence, and claims and allows researchers to follow and inspect the workflow. An Auditor agent further integrates fabrication checking into the workflow. For evaluation, we run three brain science tasks from Agents' Last Exam, introduce our own benchmark, \textbf{BrainPilotBench-v0}, and present additional end-to-end case studies. Across these evaluations, BrainPilot with an open-source backbone model attains performance comparable to state-of-the-art agent framework with less costs.

AI.tldr: BrainPilot is a fully open-source multi-agent AI system for brain science research that coordinates specialist agents (guided by a PI agent), uses a unified knowledge base (7,233 items) and skill library (72 modules), maintains traceable workflows via a Graph of Trace, and incorporates an Auditor agent to prevent fabrication. It achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art frameworks at lower cost.
AI.motivation: Brain science research requires integrating evidence across scales, modalities, and disciplines, but current AI agents lack domain expertise, may fabricate claims, drift during multi-step reasoning, and offer limited points for expert intervention, which is especially costly given that conclusions affect downstream scientific claims and depend on laboratory-specific expertise.
AI.method: BrainPilot is a multi-agent system with: (1) a PI agent coordinating specialist agents; (2) a unified brain science knowledge base of 7,233 indexed items; (3) a skill library of 72 reusable methodology units across seven domains; (4) the Graph of Trace for auditable record-keeping linking subgoals, tool use, evidence, and claims; and (5) an Auditor agent for fabrication checking.
AI.result: Evaluated on three brain science tasks from Agents' Last Exam, the introduced BrainPilotBench-v0 benchmark, and end-to-end case studies. BrainPilot using an open-source backbone model achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art agent frameworks with lower cost.
AI.conclusion: BrainPilot demonstrates that a fully open-source, multi-agent architecture with domain-grounded knowledge, traceable workflows, and automated fabrication checking can accelerate brain science research while maintaining reliability and reducing cost compared to existing state-of-the-art frameworks.

title: Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning For False Negative Mitigation in 3D Medical Imaging
summary: Multimodal Contrastive Learning (CL) has shown significant performance in aligning representations across various data modalities and improving downstream tasks, especially in healthcare. It works by minimizing the distance between matched (positive) data modalities, while maximizing the distance between mismatched (negative) samples. Traditional CL frameworks typically assume instance-based correspondence within data batches, treating all non-paired samples as negatives. However, this assumption often fails in medical settings, where samples may share high-level semantic attributes, leading to false negatives that degrade representation quality. In this paper, we propose Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning (MseaCL), a CL framework trained on a pediatric cohort of 3D brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and radiology reports. The goal of this framework is to mitigate the impact of semantically similar false negative samples by incorporating semantic similarity between radiology reports, as a guiding signal during the learning process. Our results indicate that applying this framework as a pretraining stage can achieve notable improvements in downstream tasks, e.g., at least a 22.6\% increase in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of pediatric brain tumor molecular classification, demonstrating its potential for more robust and semantically aligned multimodal representations in clinical applications.

AI.tldr: MseaCL is a multimodal contrastive learning framework that addresses false negatives in medical imaging by using semantic similarity between radiology reports as a guiding signal, achieving 22.6%+ AUC improvement in pediatric brain tumor classification.
AI.motivation: Traditional multimodal contrastive learning assumes instance-based correspondence and treats all non-paired samples as negatives, but in medical settings, samples may share high-level semantic attributes, creating false negatives that degrade representation quality.
AI.method: Proposes MseaCL (Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning) trained on pediatric 3D brain MRI and radiology reports, incorporating semantic similarity between reports as a guiding signal to mitigate the impact of semantically similar false negatives.
AI.result: Applying MseaCL as a pretraining stage achieves at least 22.6% increase in AUC for pediatric brain tumor molecular classification downstream task.
AI.conclusion: MseaCL demonstrates potential for more robust and semantically aligned multimodal representations in clinical applications by addressing the false negative problem in medical contrastive learning.

title: Weakly-Supervised RGB-D Salient Object Detection via SAM-driven Pseudo Annotation and State Space Interaction-based Diffusion
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures, accepted by IEEE TMM
summary: Weakly-supervised RGB-D Salient Object Detection (SOD) is explored to reduce the heavy burden of pixel-level annotations. But scribble annotations lack the structure and details of objects, resulting in inaccurate saliency maps. In this paper, we propose a novel scribble-supervised RGB-D SOD method, consisting of a Segment Anything Model (SAM)-driven pseudo annotation generation method (\emph{SAM-PAG}) and a state space interaction-based conditional diffusion model (\emph{$S^2$Diff}). Specifically, SAM-PAG is tailored to address the issue of sparse supervision information. In SAM-PAG, we adopt the advanced SAM to expand sparse scribbles to dense pixel-level pseudo annotations through the dual-branch structure and the consistency of segmentation masks. In $S^2$Diff, we adopt the diffusion model to iteratively refine the noisy saliency maps with the guidance of conditional information, generating accurate saliency maps. Naturally, the core of our $S^2$Diff lies in the acquisition of conditional features and the denoising of saliency maps. For the former, we employ a cross-modal conditional generation module to interweave cross-modal features through frequency integration and implicit-explicit state space interaction, effectively achieving global conditional features. For the latter, we employ a context injection module to mitigate noise interference and to enhance object information with the conditional context. With the close cooperation of SAM-PAG and $S^2$Diff, our method outperforms relevant scribble-supervised methods and achieves competitive performance compared to fully-supervised methods on seven datasets. The code and results of our method are available at https://github.com/Switch457/WeakS2Diff_SOD.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scribble-supervised RGB-D Salient Object Detection method with SAM-driven pseudo annotation generation (SAM-PAG) and a state space interaction-based conditional diffusion model (S²Diff), achieving performance comparable to fully-supervised methods on seven datasets.
AI.motivation: To reduce the heavy burden of pixel-level annotations in RGB-D Salient Object Detection by using scribble supervision, while addressing the issue that scribble annotations lack structure and object details, leading to inaccurate saliency maps.
AI.method: A two-component framework: (1) SAM-PAG leverages SAM with a dual-branch structure and segmentation mask consistency to expand sparse scribbles into dense pixel-level pseudo annotations. (2) S²Diff uses a diffusion model to iteratively refine noisy saliency maps, employing a cross-modal conditional generation module (frequency integration + implicit-explicit state space interaction) for global conditional features and a context injection module for noise mitigation and object enhancement.
AI.result: Outperforms relevant scribble-supervised methods and achieves competitive performance compared to fully-supervised methods on seven datasets.
AI.conclusion: The close cooperation of SAM-PAG (dense pseudo annotation generation) and S²Diff (conditional diffusion-based refinement) effectively bridges the gap between scribble-supervised and fully-supervised RGB-D SOD.

title: Long-Context Fine-Tuning with Limited VRAM
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces model and optimizer memory, but dense attention still makes long training sequences expensive. We combine Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) with segment-wise backpropagation and tiered KV storage. Only the active segment remains differentiable in VRAM; older KV is detached into RAM or NVMe, and HGA loads a bounded set of exact historical tokens for each query block. On Qwen3-8B with 4-bit QLoRA and PG19, dense training on a 16 GB Quadro RTX 5000 fits 2,048 tokens but fails at 4,096, whereas HGA reaches 16,384 tokens with 15.28 GB peak VRAM. Under evaluation the same adapter runs through 131,072 tokens on this card; VRAM is not constant but grows gently with the resident chunk summaries, so RAM and NVMe capacity set the practical limit beyond these lengths. At the shared 2K training length, HGA-trained and dense-trained adapters obtain 2.7405 and 2.7383 nat under the same dense-attention readout, while the stock model obtains 2.9541. At this boundary HGA training is already marginally faster (217.75 vs. 207.02 tokens/s), and the HGA-to-dense throughput ratio improves from 1K to 2K; because HGA keeps the attended historical set per token approximately constant while dense work per token grows, we expect this lead to widen as context grows. Dense attention is used for the main quality and retrieval comparisons so that they measure the learned weights and remain compatible with standard generation frameworks. HGA can also be used for retrieval and generation; an optimized production-grade serving implementation is under development.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) combines segment-wise backpropagation, tiered KV storage (VRAM/RAM/NVMe), and bounded historical token access to enable ultra-long-context fine-tuning (up to 131K tokens at eval) on memory-constrained GPUs (16 GB VRAM), matching dense attention quality while improving throughput.
AI.motivation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces model/optimizer memory, but dense attention remains prohibitively expensive for long training sequences, restricting context length on commodity GPUs.
AI.method: Combines Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) with segment-wise backpropagation (only active segment differentiable in VRAM), tiered KV storage (older KV detached to RAM or NVMe), and loading a bounded set of exact historical tokens per query block.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B with 4-bit QLoRA and PG19: dense training at 2K fits 16 GB VRAM but fails at 4K; HGA reaches 16K training with 15.28 GB peak VRAM. At eval, HGA runs 131K tokens on same card. At 2K training length, HGA-trained adapter (2.7405 nat) nearly matches dense-trained (2.7383 nat), both outperforming stock (2.9541 nat). HGA is faster (217.75 vs 207.02 tokens/s) at 2K, with growing advantage as context lengthens.
AI.conclusion: HGA enables practical ultra-long-context fine-tuning on memory-limited hardware with negligible quality loss and improved throughput, with the practical limit set by RAM/NVMe capacity rather than VRAM. HGA also supports retrieval and generation; production serving implementation is underway.

title: Kernel weighted importance sampling for off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits
summary: This article presents a novel estimator for performing off-policy evaluation using only offline data for contextual bandits. The proposed estimator, Kernel-WIS is demonstrated to be asymptotically consistent and to empirically outperform strong baselines (including vanilla weighted importance sampling), particularly under complex conditions including behaviour policy miss-specification. The benefit of Kernel-WIS is derived from combining the bounded property of vanilla weighted importance sampling with the linearity of vanilla importance sampling.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Kernel-WIS, a novel off-policy evaluation estimator for contextual bandits that combines weighted importance sampling's boundedness with importance sampling's linearity. It is shown to be asymptotically consistent and outperforms strong baselines, especially under behavior policy misspecification.
AI.motivation: To develop a more robust off-policy evaluation estimator for contextual bandits that works effectively with only offline data, particularly under challenging conditions like behavior policy misspecification where existing methods struggle.
AI.method: The proposed Kernel-WIS estimator combines the bounded property of vanilla weighted importance sampling with the linearity of vanilla importance sampling, forming a kernel-based approach for off-policy evaluation.
AI.result: Kernel-WIS is proven to be asymptotically consistent and empirically outperforms strong baselines (including vanilla weighted importance sampling), especially under complex conditions involving behavior policy misspecification.
AI.conclusion: The Kernel-WIS estimator offers a superior approach to off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits by effectively merging desirable properties of existing importance sampling methods, leading to improved robustness and performance.

title: Parameter-efficient Prompt Tuning of Vision Foundation Model With Adaptive Focal Loss for Interpretable MCI Screening
summary: Mild Cognitive Impairment is a critical early stage of cognitive decline that frequently precedes Alzheimer's disease, yet its automated detection from neuropsychological drawing tests remains fundamentally constrained by data scarcity, class imbalance, and diagnostic ambiguity near clinical boundaries. Existing methodologies attempt to bypass these constraints using computationally expensive, fully fine-tuned hybrid architectures that relegate spatial explainability to a post-hoc approximation rather than an intrinsic model property. We propose a parameter-efficient framework utilizing frozen DINOv2-Small model adapted via three modality-specific learnable prompt tokens while Operating with 1.19 million trainable parameters, each token serves as a query in a shared cross-attention layer over the source image patch tokens. Crucially, spatial explainability is achieved directly through these attention maps; as a structural consequence of the architecture. Then task-conditioned embeddings fused via an attention module to quantify modality-level importance per subject. To handle boundary ambiguity, a MoCA-adapted focal loss introduced that integrates continuous cognitive scores into the training target, loss modulation, and adaptive sample weighting, strictly generalizing standard soft-label approaches. Under stratified five-fold cross-validation, the proposed architecture yields an MCI-class F1 of 0.641 and an AUC of 0.795, outperforming the computationally heavier ResViT baseline by 0.110 in MCI-class F1.

AI.tldr: A parameter-efficient framework using frozen DINOv2-Small with modality-specific learnable prompt tokens and cross-attention achieves MCI detection (F1=0.641, AUC=0.795) from neuropsychological drawing tests, outperforming heavier ResViT baseline by 0.110 in MCI F1, with intrinsic spatial explainability via attention maps and a MoCA-adapted focal loss handling boundary ambiguity.
AI.motivation: Automated MCI detection from neuropsychological drawing tests is limited by data scarcity, class imbalance, and diagnostic ambiguity near clinical boundaries. Existing methods use computationally expensive hybrid architectures with post-hoc rather than intrinsic spatial explainability.
AI.method: Frozen DINOv2-Small adapted via three modality-specific learnable prompt tokens (1.19M trainable params) with shared cross-attention over source image patches; intrinsic spatial explainability via attention maps; task-conditioned embeddings fused via attention module for modality-level importance; MoCA-adapted focal loss integrating continuous cognitive scores into training target, loss modulation, and adaptive sample weighting.
AI.result: Under stratified five-fold cross-validation: MCI-class F1 of 0.641, AUC of 0.795, outperforming computationally heavier ResViT baseline by 0.110 in MCI-class F1.
AI.conclusion: The proposed parameter-efficient framework with intrinsic explainability and boundary-aware loss function effectively addresses MCI detection challenges, significantly outperforming a heavier hybrid baseline.

title: Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization for World Models in Atari Pong
summary:
World models are usually evaluated as components of model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) systems, while the world models themselves are rarely studied in isolation.
  We examine five representative visual world-model agents in Atari Pong: DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, and STORM. After reproducing their training pipelines and matching the reported agent performance, we freeze the learned world models and evaluate them with a closed-loop rollout diagnostic: a policy trained separately from the corresponding MBRL agent interacts with each frozen model, and the generated video trajectories are inspected for visual and dynamical errors. Across all five models, the rollouts contain clear failures, including ball disappearance, incorrect ball motion, and invalid ball-paddle interactions.
  Beyond visual trajectories, we further evaluate them with pixel-space zero-shot MBRL, where a new policy is trained entirely inside a frozen world model and then evaluated in the real environment. Across all five models, the resulting policies substantially underperform those produced by the corresponding original MBRL training pipelines. The gap is particularly large for DreamerV3, whose mean return drops from -5.5 to -20.9, near the minimum Pong return of -21.
  We hypothesize that insufficient modeling of task-critical concepts, such as the ball in Pong, may contribute to these failures. We therefore propose Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization (CGSReg), an auxiliary pixel reconstruction loss applied to segmented concept regions. Experiments show that CGSReg improves both closed-loop rollouts and pixel-space zero-shot MBRL in DreamerV3, DIAMOND, and TWISTER. Its effects vary across the remaining models and evaluation metrics, indicating that CGSReg alone does not address all world-model bottlenecks.

AI.tldr: Five visual world models (DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, STORM) are evaluated in isolation on Atari Pong, revealing systematic failures in dynamics (ball disappearance, incorrect motion, invalid interactions). Pixel-space zero-shot MBRL policies trained inside frozen models severely underperform original MBRL pipelines (e.g., DreamerV3 drops from -5.5 to -20.9). The proposed Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization (CGSReg) improves rollouts and zero-shot MBRL for some models but does not fully resolve all bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: World models are typically evaluated only as components of MBRL systems, not studied in isolation. The paper aims to diagnose their standalone predictive quality and identify specific failure modes.
AI.method: Reproduce five visual world-model agents (DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, STORM) on Atari Pong; freeze learned models for closed-loop rollout diagnostics with separately trained policies and pixel-space zero-shot MBRL; propose CGSReg auxiliary loss on segmented concept regions.
AI.result: All five models produce rollouts with visual/dynamical errors. Zero-shot MBRL policies substantially underperform original training; DreamerV3 drops to near-minimum return (-20.9). CGSReg improves DreamerV3, DIAMOND, and TWISTER in some metrics but not all models/metrics.
AI.conclusion: World models have significant isolated failures (ball-related errors) even when integrated MBRL performance is matched. CGSReg provides partial improvement but does not address all world-model bottlenecks.

title: An Introduction to Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics for Engineering Applications
summary: Many engineering problems involve phenomena whose governing equations are poorly characterized or only partially known. Surrogate modeling techniques such as neural networks can capture the behavior of these systems, but they typically demand large training datasets that are difficult to obtain in engineering contexts and yield models with limited physical interpretability. The Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) method addresses both limitations by performing sparse regression over libraries of candidate nonlinear terms, recovering interpretable governing equations from comparatively small datasets. Although SINDy has been demonstrated extensively on canonical benchmark systems, its application to practical engineering problems is less widely documented. This tutorial introduces the SINDy method and progressively builds toward its main extensions, from noise-robust weak-form and ensembling-based variants to constrained and parametrizable formulations. The paper and the accompanying tutorial (available at https://github.com/paullililili/SINDy4Engineers) is organized in three parts: the first introduces the standard SINDy algorithm and progressively extends it, inviting readers without prior knowledge to follow each step and adapt the methods to their own problems; the remaining two parts present detailed case studies on (1) the system identification of an unmanned aerial vehicle and (2) a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger. Through these examples, we aim to demonstrate that SINDy is simple to implement yet flexible enough to serve as a valuable identification tool for advanced engineering applications.

AI.tldr: This tutorial introduces the SINDy method for identifying interpretable governing equations from data, covering its standard form and extensions (weak-form, ensembling, constrained, parametrizable), with case studies on UAV system identification and a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger.
AI.motivation: Engineering problems often involve poorly characterized phenomena; neural network surrogates require large datasets and lack physical interpretability. SINDy addresses both limitations by learning sparse, interpretable equations from small datasets.
AI.method: The paper presents SINDy (Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics), which performs sparse regression over libraries of candidate nonlinear terms to recover parsimonious governing equations. It covers extensions including noise-robust weak-form variants, ensembling-based approaches, constrained formulations, and parametrizable versions.
AI.result: Demonstrated through two detailed case studies: (1) system identification of an unmanned aerial vehicle, and (2) a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger, showing SINDy is simple to implement yet flexible for advanced engineering applications.
AI.conclusion: SINDy is a valuable identification tool for engineering contexts, being both simple to implement and flexible enough to handle practical problems, with accompanying open-source tutorial materials.

title: RoGS: Adaptive Meshgrid Gaussian for Large-Scale Road Surface Mapping
summary: Road surface mapping plays a crucial role in autonomous driving, supporting high-definition map generation, lane-level perception, and automatic road annotation. Recent mesh-based road surface reconstruction methods have shown promising results, but they still suffer from limited reconstruction quality and high optimization cost, especially in large-scale driving scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose ROADGS-T, a robust and efficient large-scale road surface mapping framework based on adaptive meshgrid Gaussian representation. Specifically, we model the road surface by placing 2D Gaussian surfels on a meshgrid, where each surfel explicitly stores color, semantic, and geometric information. Compared with conventional mesh-based representations and 3D Gaussian primitives, the proposed meshgrid Gaussian representation better matches the thin-surface property of roads while significantly reducing redundant primitives and overlap during optimization. To further improve representation efficiency and structural fidelity, we introduce a road-structure-aware adaptive meshgrid strategy, which allocates denser Gaussian surfels to geometrically or semantically complex regions, such as lane markings, road boundaries, and height discontinuities, while maintaining a compact representation in flat road areas. Moreover, instead of relying on a single nearest vehicle pose, we design a trajectory-consistency-guided pose-robust refinement strategy, which estimates local surface priors from multiple neighboring poses and adaptively weights pose-guided height regularization according to their geometric consistency.

AI.tldr: ROADGS-T is a meshgrid Gaussian-based framework for large-scale road surface mapping that uses adaptive 2D Gaussian surfels with explicit color, semantic, and geometric information, along with a road-structure-aware adaptive meshgrid strategy and trajectory-consistency-guided pose-robust refinement for efficient and robust road reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Existing mesh-based road surface reconstruction methods suffer from limited reconstruction quality and high optimization cost in large-scale driving scenarios, motivating the need for a more efficient and robust representation.
AI.method: (1) Modeling road surface using 2D Gaussian surfels placed on a meshgrid, storing color, semantic, and geometric information explicitly. (2) A road-structure-aware adaptive meshgrid strategy that allocates denser Gaussians to complex regions (lane markings, boundaries, height discontinuities) and compact representation to flat areas. (3) A trajectory-consistency-guided pose-robust refinement strategy that estimates local surface priors from multiple neighboring poses with adaptive weighting based on geometric consistency.
AI.result: The proposed method improves reconstruction quality and reduces redundant primitives and overlap during optimization compared to conventional mesh-based and 3D Gaussian primitive representations, while better matching the thin-surface property of roads.
AI.conclusion: ROADGS-T provides a robust and efficient solution for large-scale road surface mapping in autonomous driving, addressing key limitations of prior mesh-based and Gaussian-based approaches.

title: The Industrialization of Research ; On AI-Driven Science and Its Consequences
summary: Artificial intelligence is transforming scientific research -- not merely as a more powerful instrument, but as an autonomous participant in the research cycle itself. This transition constitutes, in the most precise sense of the term, the industrialization of research: a shift from a craft model, in which knowledge, method, and judgment are embedded in the researcher, to a pipeline model, in which these steps are decomposed, automated, and supervised. The US Department of Energy's Genesis Mission is the most ambitious current instantiation of this shift, but the fundamental questions it raises extend far beyond any single program. This essay examines seven such questions: the erosion of the intergenerational transmission of scientific competence; the growing opacity of AI-generated theories; the collapse of peer evaluation under a flood of machine-generated output; the unproven capacity of AI for paradigm-shifting discovery; the capture of the scientific agenda by political and industrial actors; the compounding of systematic errors in closed-loop pipelines; and the structural bifurcation of the global research community into incommensurable tiers. These concerns do not constitute an argument against AI-driven science -- whose demonstrated potential is real and significant. They constitute the conditions under which that potential can be responsibly pursued.

AI.tldr: This essay examines seven critical concerns arising from AI's transformation of scientific research from a craft model to an industrialized pipeline, using the DOE's Genesis Mission as a case study, while acknowledging AI's real potential and arguing these concerns define conditions for responsible pursuit.
AI.motivation: AI is transitioning from a tool to an autonomous participant in scientific research, representing an industrialization of the research process. This shift raises fundamental questions that need examination before responsible implementation.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis of seven identified concerns regarding AI-driven science, using the US Department of Energy's Genesis Mission as an illustrative case.
AI.result: Identifies seven specific risks: erosion of scientific competence transmission; opacity of AI-generated theories; collapse of peer evaluation; unproven paradigm-shifting capacity; political/industrial capture of science agendas; compounding systematic errors in closed-loop pipelines; and structural bifurcation of global research community.
AI.conclusion: These concerns do not oppose AI-driven science but rather outline the conditions under which its demonstrated potential can be responsibly pursued.

title: Evaluating covariate balance for long time horizon Markov decision processes
summary: This article explores the application of covariate balance diagnostics for detecting the presence of hidden confounding/model miss-specification in studies applying offline reinforcement learning (RL) to deriving optimal treatment recommendations. The results demonstrate that, either there is a high risk of bias within existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendations or, existing covariate balance metrics are not sufficient to assess such studies. Regardless, existing offline RL studies cannot be concluded as being statistically robust. The conclusions propose future research directions for obtaining more methodologically robust applications of offline RL to treatment recommendation problems.

AI.tldr: This paper examines covariate balance diagnostics for detecting hidden confounding in offline RL studies for treatment recommendations, finding that existing studies lack statistical robustness due to high bias risk or insufficient diagnostic metrics.
AI.motivation: To assess whether offline reinforcement learning studies for treatment recommendations are methodologically sound by detecting hidden confounding and model misspecification.
AI.method: Application of covariate balance diagnostics to evaluate hidden confounding and model misspecification in offline RL studies for treatment recommendations.
AI.result: Existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendations either have high risk of bias or current covariate balance metrics are insufficient to assess them; thus, these studies cannot be considered statistically robust.
AI.conclusion: Future research is needed to develop more methodologically robust applications of offline RL to treatment recommendation problems.

title: Beyond Single Expert: Harmonizing Diverse Visual Priors in MLLMs for Spatial Understanding
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated substantial promise in spatial understanding. Existing works typically incorporate prior knowledge extracted from a pre-trained foundation model to further enhance the spatial awareness of MLLMs. In this paper, we first reveal that when integrating diverse foundation models into MLLMs, different models provide complementary spatial priors that benefit different tasks. Motivated by this, we propose $\textbf{ViPS}$, a novel multi-model prior framework designed to fully unleash the potential of incorporating multiple $\textbf{Vi}$sual $\textbf{P}$riors from diverse models into MLLMs for $\textbf{S}$patial understanding. Specifically, ViPS introduces an Efficient Prior Proxy to generate multiple foundational priors with minimal inference overhead, and a Dynamic Prior Fusion mechanism to achieve harmonious and context-aware prior fusion and injection from the prior proxies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ViPS successfully harmonizes diverse visual priors, establishing new state-of-the-art performance across multiple complex spatial reasoning and 3D spatial understanding benchmarks. Project page: https://visual-ai.github.io/vips

AI.tldr: ViPS is a framework that integrates multiple complementary visual priors from diverse foundation models into MLLMs to improve spatial understanding, using an Efficient Prior Proxy for low-overhead inference and Dynamic Prior Fusion for context-aware integration, achieving SOTA results on spatial reasoning and 3D understanding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs often use a single pre-trained foundation model for spatial priors, but different models provide complementary spatial information beneficial for different tasks. This paper aims to harness these diverse, complementary priors to fully enhance MLLM spatial understanding.
AI.method: ViPS introduces (1) an Efficient Prior Proxy to generate multiple foundational priors with minimal inference overhead, and (2) a Dynamic Prior Fusion mechanism for harmonious, context-aware fusion and injection of these priors into MLLMs.
AI.result: ViPS achieves new state-of-the-art performance across multiple complex spatial reasoning and 3D spatial understanding benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Harmonizing diverse visual priors from multiple foundation models significantly boosts MLLM spatial understanding, and ViPS effectively realizes this integration.

title: MedFailBench: A Clinician-Built Open-Source Benchmark for Medical AI Safety Boundary Inspection
comment: 6 pages; clinician-reviewed synthetic benchmark; no patient data
summary: Most medical AI benchmarks measure whether a model knows the correct answer. MedFailBench asks a different question: which safety boundary failed? We present a clinician-built synthetic benchmark and failure atlas that labels medical AI errors by severity (1--5) and safety gate type (missed urgent escalation, unsafe remote dosing, unsafe discharge reassurance, evidence fabrication, unsafe protocol execution, source support gap). The current public release (v0.2.1) contains 44 clinician-reviewed synthetic cases with severity annotations, a live HuggingFace leaderboard preview, a safety gate taxonomy, a clinical severity rubric, and an automated pipeline for archiving model-response screening runs. No patient data, clinical validation claims, or model rankings are included. MedFailBench is released under Apache-2.0 and CC-BY-4.0 and carries the Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21205535.

AI.tldr: MedFailBench is a clinician-built synthetic benchmark and failure atlas that classifies medical AI errors by severity (1-5) and safety gate type, including missed escalation, unsafe dosing, unsafe discharge, evidence fabrication, unsafe protocol execution, and source support gaps.
AI.motivation: Most medical AI benchmarks only measure whether a model knows the correct answer, but they do not systematically identify which safety boundary failed when errors occur.
AI.method: The authors built a synthetic benchmark with clinician-reviewed cases, a safety gate taxonomy, a clinical severity rubric, and an automated pipeline for archiving model-response screening runs.
AI.result: Public release v0.2.1 includes 44 clinician-reviewed synthetic cases with severity annotations, a live HuggingFace leaderboard preview, and a safety gate taxonomy.
AI.conclusion: MedFailBench provides a structured approach to classifying medical AI errors by safety boundary type rather than just accuracy, enabling more targeted safety evaluation.

title: Learning in Infinitesimal Non-Compositional Sketches
summary: This paper develops a categorical framework -- Learning in Infinitesimal Non-Compositional Sketches (LINCS) -- as the repair of non-compositionality: failures of diagrams to factor through quotient sketches lifted to the tangent category setting. Machine learning problems are specified as sketches: graphs with commutativity conditions $\mathcal D$, limit cones $\mathcal L$, and colimit cocones $\mathcal K$, generalizing the usual scalarization of loss functions or vector space assumptions. Non-compositionality is defined purely as failure of a universal factorization problem, not as arithmetic error between the desired and actual predictions. Given a learning sketch $\mathbb S=(S,\mathcal D,\mathcal L,\mathcal K)$, whose underlying graph is $S$, and a model $D:J \rightarrow C$, the base defect is the obstruction to factorization $\mbox{Obs}(\mbox{Fact}_{\mathbb S}(D))$. The tangent lift applies the tangent functor $T$ to obtain $TD:J \rightarrow C$, and LINCS is defined as the obstruction $\mbox{Obs}(\mbox{Fact}_{\mathbb S}(TD))$ -- asking whether infinitesimal perturbations preserve the compositionality constraints.The paper also introduces Tangent Learning Sketches, which are sketches equipped with Cockett-Cruttwell tangent structure. The paper defines the INC endofunctor, which iterates the tangent lift, producing a tower $D,TD,T^2D, \cdots$ of factorization problems. ML is thereby formulated as the search for a coalgebraic fixed point where successive tangent unfoldings stabilize ($νT_{\mbox{INC}}$). Using the Aczel--Mendler theorem, we prove existence of a final INC coalgebra whenever $T_{\mbox{INC}}$ admits a set-based class realization that creates its final carrier. A detailed experimental evaluation of LINCS is underway in a number of concrete ML settings, including deep learning, large language models, and reinforcement learning, and is described in companion papers.

AI.tldr: LINCS is a categorical framework that repairs non-compositionality in machine learning problems by applying tangent functors to sketches (graphs with commutativity conditions, limit cones, and colimit cocones), formulating ML as searching for coalgebraic fixed points where tangent unfoldings stabilize.
AI.motivation: To develop a categorical framework that repairs non-compositionality failures in machine learning, moving beyond scalar loss functions or vector space assumptions by using sketches with categorical structure.
AI.method: Defines learning sketches with diagrams, limit cones, and colimit cocones; measures base defects as obstructions to universal factorization; applies tangent functor lift to obtain LINCS obstruction; introduces INC endofunctor for iterative tangent unfoldings; uses Aczel-Mendler theorem to prove existence of final INC coalgebra.
AI.result: Proves existence of a final INC coalgebra via Aczel-Mendler theorem when T_INC admits a set-based class realization creating its final carrier; LINCS is defined as the obstruction Obs(Fact_S(TD)).
AI.conclusion: ML is formulated as search for a coalgebraic fixed point where successive tangent unfoldings stabilize (νT_INC); detailed experimental evaluation in deep learning, LLMs, and RL is underway in companion papers.

title: SUFLECA: Scaling Up Feature Learning for CAD-to-image Alignment
summary: CAD-to-image alignment aims to estimate an object's 9D pose (rotation, translation, and anisotropic scale) from a single RGB image, enabling applications in robotics and augmented reality. Recent zero-shot methods use visual foundation models to match image regions to CAD models, yet typically their correspondences are appearance-driven and degrade under occlusion or sim-to-real domain shift. To address these limitations, we introduce SUFLECA (Scaling Up Feature LEarning for CAD Alignment), a weakly-supervised framework for zero-shot CAD alignment with two key contributions. First, SUFLECA scales up geometry-grounded feature learning from pretrained visual representations through Normalized Object Coordinates (NOCs) supervision on 674K images spanning 12 real and synthetic datasets, learning compact geometry-aware features that generalize across domains. Second, we propose a geometrically consistent matching algorithm that establishes reliable one-to-one CAD-to-image correspondences. Together, these contributions enable accurate, sub-second alignment per object instance without iterative pose refinement. On ScanNet25k, SUFLECA achieves 33.4%/42.3% category/instance accuracy, outperforming, with a smaller computational footprint, the strongest zero-shot baseline by 10.3/12.2 percentage points and, for the first time on this benchmark, even surpassing fully supervised methods. Code is available at: https://github.com/snt-arg/SUFLECA

AI.tldr: SUFLECA is a weakly-supervised framework for zero-shot CAD-to-image alignment that uses NOCs supervision on 674K images and a geometrically consistent matching algorithm to achieve state-of-the-art 9D pose estimation, outperforming zero-shot baselines by 10.3/12.2 percentage points and even surpassing fully supervised methods on ScanNet25k.
AI.motivation: Existing zero-shot CAD-to-image alignment methods rely on appearance-driven correspondences from visual foundation models, which degrade under occlusion or sim-to-real domain shift. The authors aim to address these limitations by learning geometry-grounded features that generalize across domains.
AI.method: SUFLECA has two key components: (1) scaling up geometry-grounded feature learning from pretrained visual representations via Normalized Object Coordinates (NOCs) supervision on 674K images from 12 real and synthetic datasets, and (2) a geometrically consistent matching algorithm for reliable one-to-one CAD-to-image correspondences.
AI.result: On ScanNet25k, SUFLECA achieves 33.4%/42.3% category/instance accuracy, outperforming the strongest zero-shot baseline by 10.3/12.2 percentage points with a smaller computational footprint, and for the first time surpassing fully supervised methods on this benchmark.
AI.conclusion: SUFLECA demonstrates that scaling geometry-grounded feature learning with NOCs supervision and geometric matching enables accurate, sub-second alignment per object instance without iterative pose refinement, advancing zero-shot CAD alignment beyond previous methods and even surpassing fully supervised approaches.

title: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Scientific Visualization Literacy
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to interpret visualizations, yet current evaluations remain largely chart-centric and provide limited evidence of understanding of scientific visualization (SciVis). We benchmark six MLLMs on the scientific visualization literacy assessment test, a standardized SciVis literacy assessment comprising 49 items based on 18 scientific visualizations and illustrations, spanning 8 techniques and 11 task types. We evaluate three closed-source and three open-source models under a closed-world protocol and compare their performance using data from 485 human participants. Results show that current MLLMs do not exhibit uniform SciVis literacy. Gemini is the strongest model overall, exceeding the human mean across the evaluated subsets, whereas the open-source models remain below the human baseline. Performance is highly uneven across techniques and tasks: models perform best on scientific illustration, search, and spatial understanding, but struggle on texture-based and integration-based visualizations and on quantitative estimation. Error analysis reveals recurring failures in fine-grained quantitative estimation, flow-direction interpretation, and grounded encoding interpretation. These findings position SciVis literacy as a necessary benchmark dimension for evaluating multimodal AI systems. Our code and model outputs are publicly available at https://github.com/patdmp/mllm-scivis-lit-benchmark.

AI.tldr: Six MLLMs are benchmarked on a scientific visualization literacy test (49 items, 18 visualizations, 8 techniques, 11 task types) against 485 humans. Gemini exceeds human mean, open-source models lag behind. Models excel at scientific illustration and spatial understanding but struggle with texture-based visualizations, quantitative estimation, and flow-direction interpretation.
AI.motivation: Current MLLM evaluations are chart-centric and lack evidence of understanding in scientific visualization (SciVis). This study aims to benchmark MLLMs on a standardized SciVis literacy assessment to fill this gap.
AI.method: Benchmarked six MLLMs (three closed-source, three open-source) on the scientific visualization literacy assessment test (49 items, 18 visualizations, 8 techniques, 11 task types) under a closed-world protocol, comparing against 485 human participants.
AI.result: Gemini is the strongest model, exceeding human mean; open-source models remain below human baseline. Performance varies significantly: best on scientific illustration, search, and spatial understanding; struggles with texture-based and integration-based visualizations, quantitative estimation, flow-direction interpretation, and grounded encoding interpretation.
AI.conclusion: SciVis literacy is a necessary benchmark dimension for evaluating multimodal AI systems. Current MLLMs do not exhibit uniform SciVis literacy and show recurring failure patterns in quantitative and interpretive tasks.

title: On-Policy Delta Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation is an alternative post-training method in reinforcement learning that alleviates the constraints imposed by reward models by providing token-level supervision from a teacher model. Although on-policy distillation has been studied and applied across various settings, its fundamental design remains underexplored. In this paper, we introduce a new distillation reward, termed the delta signal, instead of directly imitating the teacher's output distribution. The delta signal is defined as the difference between the teacher model and its base model prior to instruction tuning for reasoning capability. It therefore captures the changes induced by reasoning tuning and provides a more direct signal for transferring reasoning capabilities. Using extensive empirical evidence, we show that the delta signal substantially improves on-policy distillation and refer to the new distillation method as On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD$^2$). Experiments across mathematics, science, and code-reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that OPD$^2$ consistently outperforms conventional on-policy distillation, enabling reasoning LLMs to achieve strong performance with only a short post-training period. Code will be available at https://github.com/naver-ai/opd2

AI.tldr: This paper introduces On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD²), which uses a "delta signal" (difference between teacher model and its base model before reasoning instruction tuning) as a reward for on-policy distillation, rather than directly imitating teacher output distributions. Experiments on math, science, and code benchmarks show OPD² outperforms conventional on-policy distillation.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation's fundamental design remains underexplored. Existing methods directly imitate teacher output distributions, which may not provide the most effective supervision signal for transferring reasoning capabilities.
AI.method: Proposes OPD², which uses a delta signal defined as the difference between the teacher model and its base model (prior to reasoning instruction tuning). This captures reasoning-tuning-induced changes and serves as a more direct reward for transferring reasoning capabilities in on-policy distillation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across mathematics, science, and code-reasoning benchmarks show OPD² consistently outperforms conventional on-policy distillation, enabling strong performance with only a short post-training period.
AI.conclusion: The delta signal is a more effective supervision signal for on-policy distillation than directly imitating teacher output distributions, as it captures the specific changes induced by reasoning tuning.

title: Towards Hierarchical Structure Understanding of Newspaper Images
comment: Accepted at ICDAR 2026 Workshop on Historical Document Imaging and Processing (HIP)
summary: Understanding newspaper images remains a challenging task due to their complex, nested hierarchical structures and dense, heterogeneous layouts. In this paper, we explore two complementary approaches for newspaper structure understanding. First, we present a modular bottom-up pipeline that combines state-of-the-art open-source models: YOLO for layout detection, LayoutReader for reading order prediction, and a custom algorithm for article segmentation. This approach leverages existing robust components while maintaining flexibility and interpretability. Second, we introduce Tiramisu (Tiered Transformers for Hierarchical Structure Understanding), a novel end-to-end transformer-based architecture that explicitly models document hierarchy through an iterative tiered process. Tiramisu performs section and article separation, block localization, semantic categorization, and reading order prediction using highly parallelized attention mechanisms. Finally, we release Finlam La Liberté, a new dataset designed specifically for evaluating hierarchical information retrieval in historical newspapers. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of both approaches in reconstructing complex newspaper hierarchies, with comparative analysis highlighting their respective strengths for scalable document digitization. The Tiramisu training code, including the synthetic newspaper generator, is available at https://git.litislab.fr/tiramisu/tiramisu-newspaper-articles-extractor.

AI.tldr: This paper explores two approaches for newspaper structure understanding: a modular bottom-up pipeline (YOLO + LayoutReader + custom article segmentation) and Tiramisu, an end-to-end transformer-based architecture for hierarchical document modeling. A new dataset, Finlam La Liberté, is released for evaluating hierarchical information retrieval in historical newspapers.
AI.motivation: Understanding newspaper images is challenging due to their complex, nested hierarchical structures and dense, heterogeneous layouts, motivating the need for effective structure understanding approaches.
AI.method: Two approaches: (1) a modular bottom-up pipeline combining YOLO for layout detection, LayoutReader for reading order, and a custom algorithm for article segmentation; (2) Tiramisu, an end-to-end transformer-based architecture using tiered attention mechanisms to model document hierarchy iteratively for section/article separation, block localization, semantic categorization, and reading order prediction.
AI.result: Both approaches effectively reconstruct complex newspaper hierarchies, with comparative analysis showing respective strengths for scalable document digitization. The Tiramisu training code and synthetic newspaper generator are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: Both the modular pipeline and the end-to-end Tiramisu architecture are effective for hierarchical newspaper structure understanding, each offering complementary strengths for scalable digitization.

title: Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?
summary: AI benchmarks increasingly leverage item-level statistical models, particularly item response theory (IRT), to estimate model capabilities, rank systems, select informative examples, and diagnose benchmark quality. However, AI benchmark data often departs from the data regime of human testing, for which standard IRT estimation tools were originally developed: benchmarks typically involve fewer evaluated models, far more items, and capability distributions that may be skewed, clustered, or multimodal. We examine how these regime mismatches challenge the reliability of IRT modeling for AI evaluation. Using item parameters and capability distributions derived from six widely used LLM benchmarks, we simulate response matrices under three common IRT models and compare four estimation tools used in recent benchmark studies: marginal maximum likelihood, Markov chain Monte Carlo, variational inference, and a neural pseudo-Siamese estimator. Across 18,000 simulation conditions, we systematically evaluate computational feasibility, scalability, and the reliability of IRT inferences about model rankings, predicted performance, and item characteristics. Results show that classical estimators can become infeasible in large benchmark settings, whereas scalable estimators can produce unreliable item-level and ranking inferences with small or nonnormally distributed model sets. This study identifies when latent trait models reliably support or risk distorting AI benchmarking claims, and what sample sizes and diagnostics are needed for trustworthy use.

AI.tldr: This paper examines how standard Item Response Theory (IRT) estimation tools, originally designed for human testing, face reliability challenges when applied to AI benchmark data due to regime mismatches (fewer models, far more items, non-normal capability distributions). Through 18,000 simulation conditions across six LLM benchmarks, the authors find that classical estimators become infeasible at scale while scalable estimators produce unreliable inferences with small or non-normally distributed model sets, providing guidelines for sample sizes and diagnostics needed for trustworthy IRT-based AI evaluation.
AI.motivation: AI benchmarks increasingly use IRT for capability estimation, ranking, and quality diagnosis, but the data characteristics of AI evaluation (fewer models, more items, skewed/multimodal capability distributions) differ substantially from the human testing regimes for which IRT tools were designed, raising concerns about the reliability of these methods in AI contexts.
AI.method: The authors simulate response matrices under three common IRT models using item parameters and capability distributions derived from six widely used LLM benchmarks, then compare four estimation tools (marginal maximum likelihood, MCMC, variational inference, and a neural pseudo-Siamese estimator) across 18,000 simulation conditions, evaluating computational feasibility, scalability, and reliability of IRT inferences.
AI.result: Classical estimators become computationally infeasible in large benchmark settings, while scalable estimators produce unreliable item-level and ranking inferences when model sets are small or non-normally distributed. The study quantifies when latent trait models reliably support versus risk distorting AI benchmarking claims.
AI.conclusion: The paper identifies specific regime mismatches that challenge IRT reliability for AI evaluation and provides guidance on necessary sample sizes and diagnostics for trustworthy use of IRT in AI benchmarking.

title: RTS Smoother-Guided Learning of Physics-Based Neural Differential Models
summary: Ordinary differential equations (ODEs) are widely used to model dynamical systems in physics, biology, neuroscience, and physiology, but in many applications some equations of the dynamics are unknown and only a subset of the state variables are measured. We propose a hybrid neural--physics framework in which the known components of the ODE are kept explicit and the missing components are represented by a neural network. The proposed method consists of two stages where we alternate between state and parameter estimation and iterate until a predetermined criterion is met. Specifically, in the first step, we treat the model parameters as being known and we infer the latent states from the available measurements using a Rauch--Tung--Striebel (RTS) smoother. In the second stage, we treat the smoothed trajectories as being known and use them to estimate the neural networks' parameters through backpropagation. We evaluate the method on benchmark systems spanning linear, nonlinear, and stiff dynamics under partial state observation. Across these settings, the proposed method learns missing ODE components from incomplete measurements while exploiting and retaining interpretable mechanistic structure and improving latent-state reconstruction and long-horizon prediction.

AI.tldr: A hybrid neural-physics framework is proposed that combines known ODE components with neural networks for missing dynamics, using alternating state estimation (RTS smoother) and parameter learning (backpropagation) under partial observations.
AI.motivation: Many dynamical systems have unknown equations and only partially measured state variables, making pure mechanistic modeling infeasible while pure black-box approaches lack interpretability.
AI.method: A two-stage iterative method: (1) treat model parameters as known and infer latent states via RTS smoother; (2) treat smoothed trajectories as known and learn neural network parameters via backpropagation. Repeat until convergence.
AI.result: The method learns missing ODE components from incomplete measurements across linear, nonlinear, and stiff benchmark systems, improving latent-state reconstruction and long-horizon prediction.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid framework retains interpretable mechanistic structure while leveraging neural networks to capture unknown dynamics, effectively combining the strengths of both approaches for partially observed systems.

title: Quantifying Training Membership Information in the Hyperspherical Embedding Geometry of Face Recognition Models
summary: Face recognition models represent each face as an embedding vector on the unit hypersphere by clustering embeddings of the same identity while pushing different identities apart through angular-margin losses. Because these losses act only on training identities, non-member identities may form clusters with different geometric properties. In this paper, we quantify the magnitude of this difference and what training-time factors control it. We compute four statistics based on cluster geometry across 180 face recognition models in a factorial design over IResNet backbone size, loss head, training duration, and the number of training identities, and evaluate each configuration on nine benchmarks. Our results indicate that the number of training identities has the largest effect on member/non-member separability, while backbone and loss head contribute far less, and that, on a same-domain held-out reference, the geometric membership signal decreases monotonically as more identities are added to training. We provide an analysis of cross-domain (pose, age, quality, ethnicity) non-member benchmarks and report that these inflate the apparent membership signal. Finally, we fuse all four statistics with a learned classifier to reveal additional membership information beyond the best individual statistic.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how face recognition models trained with angular-margin losses produce different cluster geometries for member vs. non-member identities. Through a factorial study of 180 models, the authors find that the number of training identities is the dominant factor controlling member/non-member separability, while backbone size and loss head have minimal impact. The geometric membership signal decreases monotonically with more training identities on same-domain data, but cross-domain benchmarks inflate the apparent signal. A learned fusion of four geometric statistics extracts additional membership information beyond any single statistic.
AI.motivation: Face recognition models use angular-margin losses to cluster embeddings of the same identity and separate different identities on the unit hypersphere. Since these losses only optimize for training identities, non-member identities (not seen during training) may exhibit different geometric clustering properties. The paper aims to quantify this difference and identify which training-time factors most influence member/non-member separability.
AI.method: The authors conduct a factorial design experiment with 180 face recognition models varying four factors: IResNet backbone size, loss head type, training duration, and number of training identities. They compute four cluster geometry statistics for each model and evaluate on nine benchmarks (same-domain and cross-domain including pose, age, quality, ethnicity variations). They also train a learned classifier to fuse all four statistics.
AI.result: The number of training identities has the largest effect on member/non-member separability, with backbone and loss head contributing far less. On same-domain held-out reference, the geometric membership signal decreases monotonically as more identities are added to training. Cross-domain benchmarks inflate the apparent membership signal. A fused classifier reveals additional membership information beyond the best individual statistic.
AI.conclusion: The geometric properties of face embeddings differ between member and non-member identities, and this difference is primarily controlled by the number of training identities. The membership signal is dataset-dependent and can be amplified by domain shift. A multi-statistic fusion approach can better exploit this signal than any single geometric measure.

title: Plover: Steering GUI Agents through Plan-Centric Interaction
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) automation remains challenging in real-world environments, where dynamic layouts, unexpected dialogs, and evolving interface states can cause autonomous agents to drift from user intent. Recent vision-based multimodal agents improve flexibility by operating directly over screenshots and natural language instructions, but planning and adaptation often remain internal, limiting users' ability to inspect, supervise, or correct system behavior. We present Plover, a plan-centric vision-based GUI automation system that externalizes task plans and replanning as persistent, inspectable, and revisable artifacts. Through a planner--executor architecture, Plover supports explicit supervision of evolving execution, localized correction through editable plans, natural-language guidance, and screenshot-grounded interventions, while preserving prior progress during repair. A formative study with six participants informed the interaction design. We then evaluate Plover through benchmark failure-case repair and scenario-based workflow analyses. Our results show that many autonomous GUI-agent failures are structurally repairable when plans remain visible and interventions are localized, and that explicit replanning helps make GUI automation more transparent, controllable, and adaptable.

AI.tldr: Plover is a plan-centric GUI automation system that makes task plans and replanning visible, inspectable, and editable, enabling users to supervise, correct, and adapt autonomous agent behavior through localized interventions while preserving prior progress.
AI.motivation: GUI automation agents struggle in dynamic real-world environments (layout changes, unexpected dialogs, evolving states), and existing vision-based multimodal agents keep planning and adaptation internal, limiting users' ability to inspect, supervise, or correct system behavior.
AI.method: Plover uses a planner-executor architecture that externalizes task plans and replanning as persistent artifacts. It supports editable plans, natural-language guidance, screenshot-grounded interventions, and localized correction while preserving prior progress. A formative study with six participants informed the interaction design.
AI.result: Many autonomous GUI-agent failures are structurally repairable when plans remain visible and interventions are localized. Explicit replanning makes GUI automation more transparent, controllable, and adaptable.
AI.conclusion: Plover demonstrates that externalizing plans and enabling localized intervention significantly improves the transparency, controllability, and adaptability of GUI automation systems.

title: BadWAM: When World-Action Models Dream Right but Act Wrong
summary: World-action models (WAMs) are emerging as a promising foundation for embodied control: rather than predicting actions alone, they learn representations that couple action generation with future world prediction. This coupling is often viewed as a source of robustness, interpretability, and safety, as a robot's action can in principle be checked against its imagined future. In this paper, we show that this assumption is fragile. We introduce BadWAM, a unified framework for modeling and evaluating World-Action Drift Attacks: a new class of WAM-specific adversarial attacks that use small visual perturbations to break the alignment between what a WAM imagines and what it executes. BadWAM characterizes this attack surface along two natural criteria: attack strength and stealthiness. When the adversary prioritizes disruption, BadWAM instantiates an action-only adversarial attack, which directly drives the model toward task-failing actions. When the adversary additionally prioritizes stealth, BadWAM instantiates an imagination-preserving adversarial attack, which seeks to induce harmful action shifts while keeping the model's predicted future close to its clean imagination. Together, these two attacks capture a spectrum of WAM-specific failures: from overt action hijacking to stealthier cases where the model appears to imagine a plausible future but executes a desynchronized action. We evaluate BadWAM across different variants of WAMs. Results show that our attacks substantially reduce task success rates under closed-loop execution. For example, our action-only attack reduces the model performance from 96.5% to 43.1% success. The results of our imagination-preserving attack further exposes a WAM-specific vulnerability: moderate future-preserving regularization can maintain strong attack performance while reducing future imagination drift.

AI.tldr: BadWAM introduces a new class of adversarial attacks targeting World-action Models (WAMs), showing that small visual perturbations can break the alignment between imagined futures and executed actions, reducing task success from 96.5% to 43.1%.
AI.motivation: Despite WAMs being praised for robustness and safety due to their coupling of action generation with future world prediction, the authors question this assumption and demonstrate that the action-imagination alignment is fragile and exploitable.
AI.method: BadWAM proposes two types of attacks: (1) action-only adversarial attack (prioritizing disruption) that directly drives the model toward task-failing actions, and (2) imagination-preserving adversarial attack (prioritizing stealth) that induces harmful action shifts while keeping predicted future close to clean imagination.
AI.result: The action-only attack reduces task success from 96.5% to 43.1%. The imagination-preserving attack reveals a WAM-specific vulnerability: moderate future-preserving regularization maintains strong attack performance while reducing future imagination drift.
AI.conclusion: The coupling between action and imagination in WAMs is not inherently safe; BadWAM exposes a spectrum of vulnerabilities from overt action hijacking to stealthy desynchronized attacks where the model appears to imagine a plausible future but executes a different action.

title: AlphaWiSE: Adaptive Weight Interpolation for Continual Multimodal Representation Learning
summary: Multimodal models such as CLIP learn a shared embedding space for cross-modal retrieval, but continual adaptation to sequentially arriving data can disrupt the cross-modal alignment acquired from earlier phases. Conventional continual-learning methods return a single checkpoint, which commits every retrieval direction to the same stability-plasticity trade-off. We propose AlphaWiSE, a post-hoc weight-space interpolation method that composes two frozen source checkpoints. For each aligned parameter tensor identified by its checkpoint key, AlphaWiSE fits one scalar interpolation coefficient shared by all tensor entries. The coefficients are fitted on a smaller exemplar memory and used to materialize one interpolated checkpoint. The deployed model has the same architecture and parameter count as either source checkpoint, which does not require additional inference time. Extensive experiments on audio-image-text retrieval show consistent improvements over strong continual-learning baselines across multiple retrieval directions and evaluation metrics.

AI.tldr: AlphaWiSE is a post-hoc weight-space interpolation method that composes two frozen source checkpoints via scalar interpolation coefficients per tensor, fitted on exemplar memory, to improve continual multimodal learning without extra inference cost.
AI.motivation: Continual adaptation of multimodal models (e.g., CLIP) to sequential data disrupts cross-modal alignment from earlier phases, and conventional continual-learning methods with a single checkpoint force all retrieval directions into the same stability-plasticity trade-off.
AI.method: AlphaWiSE performs post-hoc weight-space interpolation between two frozen source checkpoints. For each aligned parameter tensor (by checkpoint key), one scalar interpolation coefficient is fitted (shared across all entries) using a smaller exemplar memory, then used to materialize one interpolated checkpoint with the same architecture and parameter count.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over strong continual-learning baselines across multiple retrieval directions and evaluation metrics on audio-image-text retrieval tasks.
AI.conclusion: AlphaWiSE effectively addresses the stability-plasticity trade-off in continual multimodal learning through lightweight post-hoc interpolation, requiring no architectural changes or additional inference overhead.

title: Data Driven Block Replacement Scheduling
summary: We develop data-driven algorithms for maintaining $N$ independent identical machines under a \textit{block replacement policy}, in which each machine is replaced upon failure and all machines are jointly replaced at regular intervals of length $k$. The goal is to learn the cost-minimizing interval $k^*$ from operational data when the lifetime distribution is unknown. At each decision epoch, the operator selects $k \in \{1, 2, \ldots, K\}$, observes the resulting failure history (a mixture of complete and right-censored lifetimes) and incurs a per-unit-time cost governed by the renewal function. We formulate this as a stochastic multi-armed bandit and propose Hoeffding- and Bernstein-based lower-confidence-bound algorithms achieving $O(K \log T)$ regret, matching the Lai--Robbins lower bound. Exploiting a nested observation property unique to block replacement, correlated variants attain $O((K-k^*)\log T)$ regret and require only $O(1)$ direct pulls of suboptimal arms $k < k^*$. A complementary Kaplan--Meier renewal algorithm estimates the lifetime distribution nonparametrically from censored data, achieving almost-sure policy consistency and empirically near-zero incremental regret at long horizons. We additionally analyze two average-cost MDPs: a time-elapsed formulation establishing that block replacement is optimal within its policy class for any lifetime distribution, and an age-vector formulation proving a monotone threshold structure under increasing failure rate distributions and providing a gold-standard cost benchmark. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical ordering and reveal structural cost gaps between optimal block and age-dependent replacement.

AI.tldr: The paper develops data-driven algorithms for learning the optimal block replacement interval for identical machines under unknown lifetime distributions, formulating the problem as a multi-armed bandit with regret bounds, and also analyzes MDP formulations establishing optimality and structural properties of block replacement policies.
AI.motivation: To learn the cost-minimizing block replacement interval from operational data when the machine lifetime distribution is unknown, enabling data-driven maintenance decisions without prior distributional knowledge.
AI.method: Formulates block replacement as a stochastic multi-armed bandit with Hoeffding- and Bernstein-based LCB algorithms; uses a Kaplan-Meier renewal algorithm for nonparametric distribution estimation; additionally analyzes two average-cost MDP formulations (time-elapsed and age-vector) to establish optimality and threshold structure.
AI.result: Achieves O(K log T) regret matching the Lai-Robbins lower bound; correlated variants achieve O((K-k*) log T) regret with only O(1) direct pulls of suboptimal arms k < k*; Kaplan-Meier algorithm achieves almost-sure consistency and near-zero incremental regret; MDP analyses prove block replacement optimality and monotone threshold structure under IFR distributions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed bandit algorithms are provably efficient for learning optimal block replacement intervals, and the MDP formulations provide structural insights and gold-standard benchmarks, with numerical experiments confirming theoretical predictions and revealing cost gaps between block and age-dependent replacement.

title: QuReC: All-in-One Image Restoration with Query-Specific Guidance and Local-Global Response Calibration
summary: All-in-one image restoration aims to recover clean images degraded by multiple corruption types using a single unified model. Existing methods typically rely on image-level prompts or shared guidance to handle diverse degradations. However, such a paradigm becomes inadequate when degradations are spatially heterogeneous or even coexist in mixed forms within a single image. Yet spatially adaptive guidance alone is not sufficient, since accurate restoration also requires each spatial query to reliably aggregate complementary information from local neighborhoods and global contexts. To this end, we propose QuReC, a unified framework for all-in-one image restoration. QuReC consists of a Degradation-Guided Query Reconstruction Module (DQRM) and a Local-Global Response Calibration Module (LGRCM). Specifically, DQRM matches each spatial query against a degradation prototype space to reconstruct a query-specific degradation-aware representation, thereby providing fine-grained spatially adaptive restoration guidance. To further stabilize this query-wise matching process, we introduce a weakly supervised prototype matching learning strategy to improve optimization stability and degradation semantic consistency. Meanwhile, LGRCM performs local-global dual-branch aggregation and calibrates the aggregated responses with learnable priors, improving the reliability of feature aggregation and the coordination between local detail modeling and global context modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that QuReC achieves superior performance on multiple all-in-one image restoration benchmarks. The code is released at https://github.com/zhoushen1/QuReC.

AI.tldr: QuReC is a unified all-in-one image restoration framework using a Degradation-Guided Query Reconstruction Module (DQRM) with weakly supervised prototype matching for spatially adaptive degradation guidance, and a Local-Global Response Calibration Module (LGRCM) for reliable feature aggregation, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing all-in-one image restoration methods use image-level prompts or shared guidance, which fail when degradations are spatially heterogeneous or mixed within a single image. Even spatially adaptive guidance is insufficient without reliable aggregation of local and global information.
AI.method: QuReC proposes two modules: (1) DQRM matches each spatial query against a degradation prototype space to reconstruct query-specific degradation-aware representations, with a weakly supervised prototype matching learning strategy for stability; (2) LGRCM performs dual-branch local-global aggregation with learnable priors to calibrate responses and improve coordination between local detail and global context modeling.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate superior performance on multiple all-in-one image restoration benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: QuReC effectively handles spatially heterogeneous and mixed degradations by combining fine-grained spatially adaptive guidance with reliable local-global feature aggregation, outperforming existing unified models.

title: When Words Are Safe But Actions Kill: Probing Physical Danger Beyond Text Safety in Hidden-State Risk Space
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as high-level planners for embodied agents, where linguistically benign instructions can become unsafe once grounded in the physical world. We study whether this physically grounded danger is the same safety problem as ordinary text-level content danger. Through hidden-state direction analysis and random-split null tests, we show that content danger (CD) and physical danger (PD) form separable signals in LLM representations across Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B/32B, Phi-3.5 and SmolLM2. Building on the CD/PD separability, we propose PRISM, a single-layer L2-regularized logistic probe over full hidden states. PRISM achieves 86.2--87.7\% accuracy on SafeAgentBench with 11.7--13.7\% FPR, while same-scale LLM judges over-block safe tasks at 24.7--39.0\% FPR. We further introduce PhysicalSafetyBench-1K (PSB-1K), a contrastive benchmark of 1{,}000 physical-risk pairs without direct harm keywords, to test whether methods detect physically grounded danger rather than explicit unsafe wording. On PSB-1K, PRISM reaches 99.6\% accuracy and 0.7\% FPR, whereas a Qwen2.5-3B judge rejects 67.8\% of safe tasks. PRISM also replicates on SafeText and EARBench, supporting hidden-state probing as a representation-level method for physical safety beyond text moderation.

AI.tldr: LLM hidden-state analysis reveals that physical danger (PD) and content danger (CD) are representationally separable.
