PRISM, a single-layer logistic probe, detects physically grounded danger with 86-88% accuracy on SafeAgentBench and 99.6% on the proposed PSB-1K benchmark, significantly reducing false positives compared to LLM judges.
AI.motivation: Linguistically benign instructions can become unsafe when grounded physically, but it is unclear whether this physical danger is the same as ordinary content-level safety. The paper investigates whether CD and PD form distinct representational signals in LLMs.
AI.method: Hidden-state direction analysis and random-split null tests across multiple LLMs (Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B/32B, Phi-3.5, SmolLM2); PRISM: single-layer L2-regularized logistic probe over full hidden states; introduction of PhysicalSafetyBench-1K (PSB-1K), a 1,000-pair contrastive benchmark without explicit harm keywords.
AI.result: PRISM achieves 86.2-87.7% accuracy (11.7-13.7% FPR) on SafeAgentBench vs. LLM judges at 24.7-39.0% FPR; on PSB-1K, 99.6% accuracy (0.7% FPR) vs. Qwen2.5-3B judge rejecting 67.8% safe tasks; results replicate on SafeText and EARBench.
AI.conclusion: Physical danger and content danger are representationally separable in LLMs; hidden-state probing is an effective representation-level method for physical safety that outperforms text-moderation-based LLM judges.

title: Mutable Low-Rank Sketches for Retrain-Free Recommendation
summary: A common bottleneck in two-stage recommendation is embedding staleness: when a user rates a new item, their embedding remains fixed until the next retrain cycle. We propose mutable sketches, which store each user's preferences in a KP-tree (a sparse segment tree with sum aggregation), fit a low-rank projection once, and recompute embeddings on-the-fly as ratings arrive. We prove that each new observation monotonically tightens the prediction error envelope (Theorem 1), a guarantee that FunkSVD and eALS lack. On KuaiRec, the mutable sketch achieves 0.810 RMSE at 1.8% data read vs. ALS 0.822 at 100%, with 8x faster per-batch updates. A new user receives personalized recommendations in <1 ms after their first rating, with no model retraining required. A comparison of sampling strategies across density regimes shows that the KP-tree's norm-proportional sampling provides 40-130% better item coverage on sparse data (<1% density), while uniform sampling suffices on dense matrices.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes mutable sketches using a KP-tree for on-the-fly embedding updates, achieving lower RMSE (0.810) than ALS (0.822) with only 1.8% data read, 8x faster updates, and instant personalization for new users without retraining. It provides theoretical guarantees (Theorem 1) and shows KP-tree's norm-proportional sampling improves item coverage by 40-130% on sparse data.
AI.motivation: To address embedding staleness in two-stage recommendation systems, where user embeddings remain fixed between retrain cycles despite new rating data.
AI.method: Introduces mutable sketches via a KP-tree (sparse segment tree with sum aggregation), fits a low-rank projection once, and recomputes embeddings on-the-fly as new ratings arrive.
AI.result: On KuaiRec: 0.810 RMSE at 1.8% data read vs. ALS 0.822 at 100%; 8x faster per-batch updates; new user personalization in <1 ms after first rating; KP-tree norm-proportional sampling yields 40-130% better item coverage on sparse data.
AI.conclusion: Mutable sketches with KP-tree provide a theoretically grounded, efficient alternative to traditional two-stage recommenders, eliminating embedding staleness, reducing computational cost, and enabling instant personalization.

title: DAPGNet: Dynamic Adaptive Physics-Guided Graph Diffusion Network for Hyperspectral Image Classification
comment: 9 figures and 9 tables. Pengkun Wang and Weijia Cao contributed equally to this work
summary: Hyperspectral image (HSI) classification requires reliable pixel-relation modeling under spectral variability, mixed pixels, and heterogeneous boundaries. Existing graph-based HSI classifiers usually construct graph topology from spatial proximity, superpixel connectivity, or learned feature affinity. However, the spectral physical prior carried by contiguous bands has limited influence on topology estimation and message propagation. This paper presents DAPGNet, a dynamic adaptive physics-guided graph diffusion network that injects a structure-constrained physical prior into relation-level graph learning. DAPGNet first encodes contiguous spectral responses into node-wise multiscale physical-prior representations. A two-stage graph constructor then combines spectral-spatial affinity, physical-prior consistency, and spatial distance to form a physical-prior-aware sparse topology. During graph diffusion, learned edge weights are transformed into additive attention biases, while a physical gate performs node-wise and feature-wise interpolation between graph-aggregated features and projected physical-prior features. Cross-scale fusion integrates node states from different diffusion depths, and the network is optimized with main classification, auxiliary supervision, and second-order spectral smoothness regularization. Experiments on Indian Pines, WHU-Hi-LongKou, Houston2013, and Houston2018 show that DAPGNet achieves the best OA, AA, and Kappa among representative CNN-, Transformer-, Mamba-, and graph-based baselines. It improves AA over the strongest competing method by 3.64 to 7.31 percentage points across the four datasets. Ablation and sensitivity analyses further support the complementary effects of physical-prior extraction, prior-aware topology construction, physics-gated propagation, and spectral smoothness regularization.

AI.tldr: DAPGNet is a dynamic adaptive physics-guided graph diffusion network for HSI classification that injects spectral physical priors (from contiguous bands) into graph topology construction and message propagation, achieving state-of-the-art results on four benchmark datasets with 3.64–7.31% AA improvement over the strongest competitors.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based HSI classifiers construct graph topology from spatial proximity, superpixel connectivity, or learned feature affinity, but neglect the spectral physical prior carried by contiguous bands, limiting topology estimation and message propagation.
AI.method: DAPGNet: (1) encodes contiguous spectral responses into node-wise multiscale physical-prior representations; (2) a two-stage graph constructor combines spectral-spatial affinity, physical-prior consistency, and spatial distance to build a physical-prior-aware sparse topology; (3) graph diffusion with learned edge weights transformed into additive attention biases; (4) a physical gate performs node-wise and feature-wise interpolation between graph-aggregated and projected physical-prior features; (5) cross-scale fusion integrates node states from different diffusion depths; (6) optimization with main classification, auxiliary supervision, and second-order spectral smoothness regularization.
AI.result: On Indian Pines, WHU-Hi-LongKou, Houston2013, and Houston2018, DAPGNet achieves the best OA, AA, and Kappa among CNN-, Transformer-, Mamba-, and graph-based baselines, improving AA over the strongest competitor by 3.64–7.31 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Ablation and sensitivity analyses confirm the complementary effects of physical-prior extraction, prior-aware topology construction, physics-gated propagation, and spectral smoothness regularization for HSI classification.

title: AutoSynthesis: An agentic system for automated meta-analysis
summary: Evidence synthesis is crucial for turning primary research into reliable knowledge for science, medicine, education, and policy. Yet, quantitative evidence synthesis remains largely manual and difficult to scale. Here, we introduce AutoSynthesis, an end-to-end multi-agent system for automated meta-analysis. Given a research question in natural language, AutoSynthesis formulates a search strategy, retrieves scientific literature, screens candidate studies, assesses full-text eligibility, extracts quantitative statistics, computes standardized effect sizes, and finally performs random-effects meta-analysis. AutoSynthesis further supports heterogeneity analysis to examine how effect sizes vary across moderators, as well as risk-of-bias assessment. As output, AutoSynthesis produces a transparent report aligned with PRISMA guidelines. In our application, AutoSynthesis screened over 28 studies and extracted more than 20 quantitative claims. The pooled effect estimates produced by AutoSynthesis are similar to Hedges' $g$ of expert-conducted meta-analyses, indicating close agreement with manual evidence synthesis. Together, these results show that AutoSynthesis can make quantitative evidence synthesis more scalable, thereby supporting evidence-based decision-making across disciplines.

AI.tldr: AutoSynthesis is an end-to-end multi-agent system that automates meta-analysis, from literature search to statistical synthesis, producing results comparable to expert-conducted meta-analyses.
AI.motivation: Quantitative evidence synthesis is largely manual and difficult to scale, limiting its ability to support evidence-based decision-making across disciplines.
AI.method: AutoSynthesis is a multi-agent system that takes a natural language research question, formulates search strategies, retrieves and screens literature, assesses eligibility and risk of bias, extracts statistics, computes effect sizes, and performs random-effects meta-analysis with heterogeneity analysis, outputting a PRISMA-aligned report.
AI.result: AutoSynthesis screened over 28 studies and extracted more than 20 quantitative claims. Its pooled effect estimates closely matched expert-conducted meta-analyses (Hedges' g).
AI.conclusion: AutoSynthesis can make quantitative evidence synthesis more scalable while maintaining agreement with manual synthesis, supporting evidence-based decision-making across disciplines.

title: Decoding Market Emotion from Blockchain Activity: A Data-Driven Sentiment Classifier
comment: This manuscript has been accepted for presentation at the IEEE International Symposium on Computers and Communications (ISCC 2026)
summary: The growing use of Bitcoin as a decentralized digital asset and investment tool has sparked strong interest in understanding its market behavior. This study presents a new approach to analyze Bitcoin market sentiment by combining on-chain and financial data with social media posts. Unlike models that aim to predict prices, this work focuses on explaining market sentiment using blockchain transactions, historical price data of Bitcoin, and daily Twitter sentiment classifications. The method merges sentiment trends with on-chain and financial metrics, normalized into a dataset for detailed market analysis. Multiple machine learning models were tested using cross-validation, with Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) emerging as the most reliable model for classifying sentiment, achieving an average F1-score of about 0.84. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), a game theory-based method for model interpretability, was used to quantify the contribution of on-chain features to the model's predictions, improving transparency. The results indicate that this data combination yields meaningful predictive signals and insights, supporting data-driven cryptocurrency analysis and future improvements with deep learning.

AI.tldr: This study combines on-chain data, financial metrics, and Twitter sentiment to classify Bitcoin market sentiment using machine learning, with XGBoost achieving an F1-score of 0.84 and SHAP providing interpretability of on-chain feature contributions.
AI.motivation: Growing interest in understanding Bitcoin market behavior beyond price prediction, aiming to explain market sentiment through multi-source data integration.
AI.method: Combines sentiment trends from daily Twitter classifications with on-chain blockchain transactions and historical Bitcoin price data, normalized into a unified dataset. Tests multiple ML models with cross-validation; uses XGBoost as the best classifier and SHAP for feature contribution interpretation.
AI.result: XGBoost achieved an average F1-score of approximately 0.84 for sentiment classification. SHAP analysis provided transparent quantification of on-chain feature contributions to model predictions.
AI.conclusion: The combination of on-chain, financial, and social media data yields meaningful predictive signals for sentiment analysis, supporting data-driven cryptocurrency research with potential for deep learning improvements.

title: Ray-based phase error correction for miniaturized DOE projector-based FPP under single-directional hyperbolic projection
summary: Fringe Projection Profilometry (FPP) systems using miniaturized DOE pro-jectors often suffer from severe phase artifacts due to nonlinear projection characteristics and limited pattern controllability. We propose a ray-based phase error correction framework that models phase artifacts along projection rays from the projector pinhole, incorporating projector geometry without re-lying on image-domain processing or neighboring pixels. A projector pinhole estimation method based on a single-directional hyperbolic fringe pattern is introduced, through which projector geometry can be recovered without stereo calibration. In addition, a data-efficient strategy constructs the re-finement model from a single calibration pose. Experiments on miniaturized DOE projector-based FPP systems demonstrate significant improvements in reconstruction accuracy under nonlinear projection conditions, confirming the robustness and physical consistency of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a ray-based phase error correction framework for miniaturized DOE projector-based FPP systems that models phase artifacts along projection rays using a projector pinhole estimation method with single-directional hyperbolic fringe patterns, requiring only a single calibration pose, and demonstrates improved reconstruction accuracy under nonlinear projection conditions.
AI.motivation: Miniaturized DOE projector-based FPP systems suffer from severe phase artifacts caused by nonlinear projection characteristics and limited pattern controllability, which degrade 3D reconstruction accuracy.
AI.method: A ray-based phase error correction framework that models phase artifacts along projection rays from the projector pinhole, incorporating projector geometry without image-domain processing. It uses a single-directional hyperbolic fringe pattern for projector pinhole estimation, enabling geometry recovery without stereo calibration, and a data-efficient refinement model built from a single calibration pose.
AI.result: Experiments on miniaturized DOE projector-based FPP systems show significant improvements in reconstruction accuracy under nonlinear projection conditions, demonstrating robustness and physical consistency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ray-based approach effectively corrects phase artifacts in miniaturized DOE projector FPP systems, offering a physically consistent and data-efficient solution that outperforms traditional image-domain methods.

title: teLLMe Why (Ain't Nothing but a Jam): Exploratory Causal Analysis of Urban Driving Data
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on UrbanAI. 6 pages
summary: Traffic agencies now have access to large volumes of video-derived data for studying safety and congestion. Most of these data are observational and collected without interventions, which makes causal questions such as "How would rain change traffic density?" difficult to answer. We present teLLMe, a system for exploratory causal analysis of urban driving datasets. The system starts from a structured event table built from dashcam annotations and combines causal structure learning with the PC algorithm, bootstrap-based stability checks, and query-specific effect estimation using linear regression and DoWhy. Natural-language questions are mapped to structured causal queries through a schema-aware LLM, enabling users to specify treatments, outcomes, and subpopulations. teLLMe returns a "Causal Card" that summarizes effect estimates, adjustment sets, DAG support, and assumptions, followed by a short natural-language explanation. Case studies on BDD-derived traffic events show that the system can surface plausible relationships involving weather, peak hours, and traffic density, while making uncertainty and modeling choices explicit. The system is designed as a tool for hypothesis generation and expert reasoning rather than a source of definitive causal claims.

AI.tldr: teLLMe is a system for exploratory causal analysis of urban driving datasets that combines causal structure learning, bootstrap stability checks, and LLM-based natural-language query mapping to estimate causal effects from observational dashcam data, outputting Causal Cards with effect estimates, assumptions, and uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Traffic agencies have abundant video-derived observational data but struggle to answer causal questions (e.g., "How would rain change traffic density?") because the data lack interventions. A tool is needed for exploratory causal analysis from observational driving data.
AI.method: teLLMe starts from structured event tables from dashcam annotations, uses PC algorithm for causal structure learning with bootstrap-based stability checks, estimates query-specific effects via linear regression and DoWhy, and maps natural-language questions to structured causal queries using a schema-aware LLM.
AI.result: Case studies on BDD-derived traffic events show the system surfaces plausible relationships involving weather, peak hours, and traffic density while making uncertainty and modeling choices explicit.
AI.conclusion: teLLMe is designed as a tool for hypothesis generation and expert reasoning, not for definitive causal claims, enabling exploratory causal analysis from observational driving data.

title: MAGiSt3R: Multi-Agent Feed-forward 3D Reconstruction from Monocular RGB Videos
summary: This paper presents MAGiSt3R, a multi-agent 3D reconstruction framework performing reconstruction and camera tracking for monocular RGB videos at almost 10 FPS. MAGiSt3R relies on a feed-forward model from the 3R family to process RGB videos and regress local point maps, and on a merging model, MAGMA, that combines local maps at both intra-agent and inter-agent levels to obtain the final global point map. Furthermore, MAGiSt3R performs pose graph optimization to mitigate cumulative camera drift occurring along the feed-forward pipeline. We evaluate MAGiSt3R on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its superior reconstruction and camera tracking accuracy compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: MAGiSt3R is a multi-agent 3D reconstruction framework that achieves near real-time (10 FPS) dense reconstruction and camera tracking from monocular RGB videos using feed-forward point map regression and a novel merging model (MAGMA) with pose graph optimization.
AI.motivation: To enable fast (near real-time) and accurate 3D reconstruction and camera tracking from monocular RGB videos, addressing the limitations of slower reconstruction pipelines and cumulative camera drift.
AI.method: Uses a feed-forward model from the 3R family for local point map regression from RGB videos, a merging model (MAGMA) for combining local maps at intra-agent and inter-agent levels, and pose graph optimization to reduce cumulative camera drift.
AI.result: Achieves almost 10 FPS reconstruction and camera tracking, with superior accuracy on both synthetic and real-world datasets compared to state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent framework with MAGMA merging and pose graph optimization yields state-of-the-art performance for monocular 3D reconstruction and tracking at near real-time speed.

title: SearchOS-V1: Towards Robust Open-Domain Information-Seeking Agent Collaboration
summary: Recent advances in Tool-Integrated Large Language Models have made web search a core capability of information-seeking agents. However, as interaction histories grow, agents increasingly struggle to track task progress. When search attempts fail to yield useful evidence, current single- and multi-agent systems can become trapped in repetitive loops, wasting search budgets and ultimately compromising the quality and completeness of the final output. We introduce SearchOS, a system-level multi-agent framework that turns fragile, implicit search progress into explicit, persistent, and shared state. First, we formulate open-domain information seeking as relational schema completion with grounded citations, where agents discover entities, populate attributes across linked tables, and anchor each value to source evidence. Then we design Search-Oriented Context Management (SOCM), which externalizes the evolving state into Frontier Task, an Evidence Graph, a Coverage Map, and Failure Memory. Built on SOCM, SearchOS applies a pipeline-parallel scheduling mechanism that overlaps the execution of sub-agents and continuously refills freed slots with tasks targeting unresolved coverage gaps to improve utilization and throughput. To schedule and control the execution of search agents, SearchOS introduces a Search Tool Middleware Harness that intercepts model and tool interactions to record grounded evidence and react to stalls or budget exhaustion, and provides a reusable hierarchical skill system comprising strategy and access skills to augment the agents' search process and avoid repeating failed search patterns across runs. On WideSearch and GISA, SearchOS leads all metrics among the evaluated single- and multi-agent baselines, paving the way toward robust information-seeking collaboration.

AI.tldr: SearchOS is a multi-agent framework that externalizes search progress into explicit shared state (Frontier Task, Evidence Graph, Coverage Map, Failure Memory) to prevent repetitive loops in tool-integrated LLMs, using pipeline-parallel scheduling and a Search Tool Middleware Harness, achieving state-of-the-art results on WideSearch and GISA.
AI.motivation: Current single- and multi-agent systems struggle to track task progress as interaction histories grow; failed search attempts lead to repetitive loops, wasted search budgets, and compromised output quality.
AI.method: Formulates open-domain information seeking as relational schema completion with grounded citations. Designs Search-Oriented Context Management (SOCM) with Frontier Task, Evidence Graph, Coverage Map, and Failure Memory. Applies pipeline-parallel scheduling for sub-agent execution overlap. Introduces Search Tool Middleware Harness with hierarchical skill system (strategy + access skills).
AI.result: SearchOS leads all metrics among evaluated single- and multi-agent baselines on WideSearch and GISA benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Externalizing fragile, implicit search progress into explicit, persistent, shared state is an effective paradigm for robust information-seeking collaboration in multi-agent systems.

title: Symbal: Detecting Systematic Misalignments in Model-Generated Captions
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often introduce errors when generating image captions, resulting in misaligned image-text pairs. Our work focuses on a class of captioning errors that we refer to as systematic misalignments, where a recurring error in MLLM-generated captions is closely associated with the presence of a specific visual feature in the paired image. Given a vision-language dataset with MLLM-generated captions, our aim in this work is to detect such errors, a task we refer to as systematic misalignment detection. As our first key contribution, we present Symbal, which utilizes a structured, dual-stage setup with off-the-shelf foundation models to identify systematic misalignments and summarize results in natural language. As our second key contribution, we introduce SymbalBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate automated methods on our proposed task. SymbalBench consists of 1.7 million image-text pairs from two domains (natural and medical images), organized into 420 vision-language datasets with annotated systematic misalignments. Symbal exhibits strong performance on this benchmark, correctly identifying systematic misalignments in 63.8% of datasets, a nearly 4x improvement over the closest baseline. We supplement our evaluations on SymbalBench with real-world evaluations, showing that (1) Symbal can accurately surface systematic misalignments in captions generated by four MLLMs and (2) Symbal is a powerful tool for auditing off-the-shelf image-caption datasets. Ultimately, our novel task, method, and benchmark can aid users with auditing MLLM-generated captions and identifying critical errors, without requiring access to the underlying MLLM. Code is available at https://github.com/Stanford-AIMI/Symbal.

AI.tldr: Symbal is a dual-stage framework using off-the-shelf foundation models to detect systematic misalignments (recurring captioning errors tied to specific visual features) in MLLM-generated image captions. The authors introduce SymbalBench, a 1.7M image-text pair benchmark across natural and medical domains, demonstrating Symbal achieves 63.8% detection accuracy (4x improvement over baselines) for auditing captioning errors without requiring access to the underlying MLLM.
AI.motivation: MLLMs frequently produce captioning errors that are systematically tied to specific visual features in images. These systematic misalignments undermine dataset quality, yet no automated method existed to detect them at scale. The authors aim to enable auditing of MLLM-generated captions without needing access to the original model.
AI.method: Symbal uses a structured, dual-stage pipeline with off-the-shelf foundation models: (1) first stage identifies candidate systematic misalignments by analyzing statistical associations between visual features and caption errors, (2) second stage summarizes findings in natural language. SymbalBench contains 1.7M image-text pairs from natural and medical domains, organized into 420 datasets with annotated systematic misalignments for evaluation.
AI.result: Symbal correctly identifies systematic misalignments in 63.8% of datasets on SymbalBench, achieving nearly 4x improvement over the closest baseline. Real-world evaluations confirm effectiveness across four different MLLMs and demonstrate utility for auditing off-the-shelf image-caption datasets.
AI.conclusion: Symbal provides an effective, model-agnostic approach for detecting systematic captioning errors in vision-language datasets. The novel task, benchmark, and method enable users to audit MLLM-generated captions and identify critical errors without accessing the underlying model, contributing to safer and more reliable multimodal AI systems.

title: Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda
summary: Poisoning pretraining data can introduce harmful behaviors to LMs that are difficult to detect and mitigate. Prior work on poisoning pretraining data has largely exploited established data sources such as Wikipedia, which do not represent the large scale and heterogeneity typical of pretraining corpora, and has ignored the interaction between poisoned data and data curation pipelines. We demonstrate that poisoning attacks on pretraining data are feasible beyond this limited setting through an existing web-scale content injection mechanism: public discussion interfaces. Additionally, to measure whether malicious content is included after web crawling and data curation, we introduce HalfLife, a novel analysis for estimating adversarial content inclusion in web-crawl based LM training data. We use HalfLife to explore the feasibility of poisoning pretraining corpora at web scale through open discussion interfaces. Our analysis demonstrates the importance of estimating whether poison injections are included in pretraining data, and establishes third-party webpage content as a possible vector for attacking language model pretraining.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that poisoning attacks on LM pretraining data are feasible at web scale through public discussion interfaces, and introduces HalfLife, a novel analysis for estimating adversarial content inclusion in web-crawl based training data.
AI.motivation: Prior work on poisoning pretraining data has been limited to established data sources (e.g., Wikipedia) that don't reflect the scale and heterogeneity of real pretraining corpora, and has ignored interactions with data curation pipelines. The authors aim to demonstrate feasibility beyond this limited setting.
AI.method: The authors propose an existing web-scale content injection mechanism (public discussion interfaces) for poisoning attacks. They also introduce HalfLife, a novel analysis method for estimating whether adversarial content from web crawls survives data curation pipelines and is included in LM training data.
AI.result: The analysis demonstrates the feasibility of poisoning pretraining corpora at web scale through open discussion interfaces, and establishes third-party webpage content as a possible vector for attacking language model pretraining.
AI.conclusion: Estimating whether poison injections are included in pretraining data is crucial, and third-party webpage content poses a viable attack vector for poisoning LM pretraining at scale.

title: Structural-Semantic Reciprocal Learning for Unsupervised Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification
summary: Unsupervised visible-infrared person re-identification (USVI-ReID) is challenging due to the large modality gap and the lack of cross-modal identity annotations. Progressive association paradigms have been proposed to gradually bridge the gap, but they suffer from two critical bottlenecks: reliance on ambiguous global representations and unchecked propagation of pseudo-label noise in an open-loop manner. To address these issues, we propose Structural-Semantic Reciprocal Learning (SSRL), a framework that transforms open-loop association into a self-correcting closed-loop system. Structurally, we introduce Fine-grained Structural Decoupling (FSD) to extract discriminative body-part primitives as reliable spatial anchors, complementing ambiguous holistic silhouettes with spatially consistent structural details. Semantically, we design a Closed-loop Semantic Calibration (CSC) mechanism that reconstructs shared semantic prototypes at each epoch and feeds them back into the training loop, effectively filtering pseudo-label noise before the next clustering cycle. Through the reciprocal interaction between structural and semantic learning, SSRL achieves robust cross-modal representation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the competitive performance of SSRL against state-of-the-art USVI-ReID methods on both SYSU-MM01 and RegDB, notably surpassing several supervised counterparts on RegDB.

AI.tldr: SSRL introduces Structural-Semantic Reciprocal Learning for unsupervised visible-infrared person re-identification, transforming open-loop progressive association into a self-correcting closed-loop system via Fine-grained Structural Decoupling (FSD) for discriminative spatial anchors and Closed-loop Semantic Calibration (CSC) for noise filtering, achieving state-of-the-art performance on SYSU-MM01 and RegDB datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing progressive association paradigms in USVI-ReID suffer from reliance on ambiguous global representations and unchecked propagation of pseudo-label noise in an open-loop manner.
AI.method: Proposes SSRL with two key components: (1) Fine-grained Structural Decoupling (FSD) extracts discriminative body-part primitives as spatial anchors; (2) Closed-loop Semantic Calibration (CSC) reconstructs shared semantic prototypes each epoch and feeds them back into training to filter pseudo-label noise, forming a self-correcting closed-loop system through reciprocal interaction between structural and semantic learning.
AI.result: Achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art USVI-ReID methods on SYSU-MM01 and RegDB datasets, and notably surpasses several supervised counterparts on RegDB.
AI.conclusion: The reciprocal structural-semantic learning paradigm effectively addresses the open-loop noise propagation problem in unsupervised cross-modal re-identification, demonstrating that closed-loop self-correction is a viable path toward robust USVI-ReID.

title: Falsifiable Release Gates for Self-Improving Systems
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures. Software, gate suite, run artifacts, and TLA+ specification are open source

We describe falsifiable release gates, and a methodology to build and validate such systems, such that every new capability must pass a pre-specified, machine-verifiable acceptance suite before it ships, and a fixed set of standing invariants is preserved at each gate. A purposely broken model gives the shortest counterexample, so the checker has teeth, is apparent. The self-enhancement loop is positively Constrained: the entire write surface is policy rules, tightening changes. may auto-apply loosening changes always require a human merge and a proposal autoclosed is one that mispredicts its own effect; We publish the acceptance measured results for all the seven gates, define precisely the scope of each claim (a bounded of the coordination skeleton (not the learned components) and free the runtime, either command line tools and the gate suite, so the results reproduce, and gates can run against other agent frameworks. Reviewers may repeat the single command central non-bypass in seconds.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a methodology for falsifiable release gates in self-improving AI agent runtimes, applied to Antahkarana. Every new capability must pass machine-verifiable acceptance tests before shipping, with standing invariants checked at each gate. The system achieves exhaustive machine-checking over 1M reachable states, with a constrained self-enhancement loop where tightening changes auto-apply but loosening requires human approval. Results for seven gates are published with reproducible command-line tooling.
AI.motivation: Current safety claims on self-improving agent runtimes are self-graded (policy files, guardrails, README commitments) and lack rigorous, machine-verifiable validation. The authors aim to replace subjective safety claims with falsifiable, reproducible release gates.
AI.method: The authors designed a methodology of falsifiable release gates: each new capability must pass a pre-specified, machine-verifiable acceptance suite before shipping, with standing invariants preserved at each gate. Applied to Antahkarana (an open runtime) via seven gates from basic observability to a self-governing loop. Actions require a safety-critical capability token from a control ring, exhaustively machine-checked over 1M reachable states (bounded model) and re-checked against execution traces. The self-enhancement loop is positively constrained: tightening changes auto-apply, loosening requires human merge; proposals that mispredict their own effect auto-close.
AI.result: Acceptance measured results for all seven gates are published. A purposely broken model yields the shortest counterexample, demonstrating the checker has teeth. Scope is precisely defined: bounded to the coordination skeleton (not learned components). The runtime, command-line tools, and gate suite are released freely for reproducibility. Reviewers can run a single command to verify non-bypass in seconds.
AI.conclusion: Falsifiable release gates provide a rigorous alternative to self-graded safety claims for self-improving agent runtimes. The methodology is applied successfully to Antahkarana with seven gates, reproducible tooling, and exhaustive state-space checking over the coordination skeleton.

title: Divergent Gaze Patterns in Artistic Viewing: Spatial and Temporal Signatures of Attention Across Autistic Individuals, Artists, and Neurotypical Observers
summary: How different populations visually explore artworks bears on cognitive science and on accessibility design, yet most eye-tracking work in autism has used social scenes rather than art, and has analysed where the eyes land while ignoring when and in what order. We present a comparative free-viewing study across three groups, autistic adults (ASD), trained artists, and neurotypical observers, who each viewed 30 paintings for 15s. We introduce a directed, metric-grounded framework that compares groups along two complementary axes: a spatial axis, in which one group's fixation-density map predicts another's fixations under six saliency metrics (AUC-Judd, NSS, CC, SIM, KL, Information Gain); and a temporal axis, in which individual scanpaths are compared with MultiMatch, ScanMatch, a foveal-disc IoU score (FDISS), and dynamic time warping (DTW). Fixations are extracted uniformly for all groups with a dispersion-threshold algorithm. Three results converge. (i)Artists and neurotypicals are almost indistinguishable in both space (density-map correlation CC=0.96) and time (they form the most alignable scanpath pair), whereas ASD gaze diverges from both. (ii)ASD attention is dissociated: it matches artists' wide spatial exploration (dispersion, explored area) but carries a distinct temporal signature, shorter fixations, less dwell, and the most idiosyncratic (least self-consistent) scanpaths of any group. (iii)ASD gaze is not selectively artist-like on any metric; if anything it is marginally closer to neurotypical. Together these findings indicate that autistic viewing of art is a distinct, group-specific attentional profile in both space and time, and they motivate population-conditioned models of aesthetic attention. We release all analysis code and per-stimulus results.

AI.tldr: In a comparative free-viewing study of art, autistic adults (ASD) show a distinct attentional profile in both spatial fixation patterns and temporal scanpath dynamics, diverging from both trained artists and neurotypical observers; artists and neurotypicals are nearly indistinguishable, while ASD gaze combines wide spatial exploration (similar to artists) with shorter fixations and more idiosyncratic temporal sequences.
AI.motivation: Prior eye-tracking research on autism focused on social scenes rather than art, and primarily analyzed where people look (spatial fixations) without considering when and in what order (temporal scanpaths). This study addresses both gaps by introducing a metric-grounded framework that jointly captures spatial and temporal dimensions of visual exploration in art viewing.
AI.method: Three groups (ASD adults, trained artists, neurotypical controls) freely viewed 30 paintings for 15s. Fixations were extracted uniformly using a dispersion-threshold algorithm. Spatial analysis used six saliency metrics (AUC-Judd, NSS, CC, SIM, KL, Information Gain) to compare fixation-density maps. Temporal analysis compared scanpaths via MultiMatch, ScanMatch, foveal-disc IoU score (FDISS), and dynamic time warping (DTW).
AI.result: (i) Artists and neurotypicals are nearly indistinguishable (density-map CC=0.96); ASD diverges from both. (ii) ASD shows wide spatial exploration like artists but with shorter fixations, less dwell, and the most idiosyncratic scanpaths. (iii) ASD gaze is not selectively artist-like; it is marginally closer to neurotypical. ASD exhibits a distinct group-specific attentional profile.
AI.conclusion: Autistic viewing of art constitutes a distinct attentional profile in both space and time, motivating population-conditioned models of aesthetic attention. All analysis code and per-stimulus results are released.

title: CRISP: Constrained Refinement via Iterative Squeezing Process for Robust Medical Image Segmentation under Domain Shift
comment: X pages, 3 figures, 3 tables; submitted to AAAI 2027
summary: Distribution shift in medical imaging remains a central bottleneck for the clinical translation of medical AI. Failure to address it can lead to severe performance degradation in unseen environments and exacerbate health inequities. Existing methods for domain adaptation are inherently limited by exhausting predefined possibilities through simulated shifts or pseudo-supervision. Such strategies struggle in the open-ended and unpredictable real world, where distribution shifts are effectively infinite. To address this challenge, we adopt the "Rank Stability of Positive Regions" as a working assumption under distribution shift, and use it to derive robust spatial hints for source-only segmentation. Guided by this assumption, we propose CRISP, a model-agnostic framework that, unlike deployment-time adaptation, requires no test-time parameter updates and no target-domain data--a target-free, plug-in refinement framework that segments with frozen weights. Rather than using ranking to directly output masks, CRISP exploits the stability of probability rankings under distribution shift to derive robust spatial priors. Via latent feature perturbation, perturbation-invariant high-grade regions define a high-precision (HP) core, while voxels that remain potentially foreground under at least one perturbation define a high-recall (HR) support; these dual priors are then recursively refined under perturbation. We then design an iterative training framework that progressively squeezes HP and HR toward the final segmentation. Extensive evaluations on multi-center cardiac MRI and CT-based lung vessel segmentation demonstrate CRISP's superior robustness, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods with striking HD95 reductions of up to 0.14 (7.0% improvement), 1.90 (13.1% improvement), and 8.39 (38.9% improvement) pixels across multi-center, demographic, and modality shifts, respectively.

AI.tldr: CRISP is a target-free, plug-in refinement framework that uses the stability of probability rankings under distribution shift to generate robust spatial priors (high-precision core and high-recall support) via latent feature perturbation, then iteratively refines them toward segmentation without requiring test-time adaptation or target-domain data.
AI.motivation: Distribution shift in medical imaging causes severe performance degradation and health inequities in clinical AI deployment. Existing domain adaptation methods are limited by predefining shifts or using pseudo-supervision, which fail in the open-ended, unpredictable real world where shifts are effectively infinite.
AI.method: CRISP adopts "Rank Stability of Positive Regions" as a working assumption. It uses latent feature perturbation to derive two robust spatial priors: perturbation-invariant high-grade regions (high-precision core) and voxels foreground under at least one perturbation (high-recall support). These dual priors are recursively refined under perturbation via an iterative training framework.
AI.result: On multi-center cardiac MRI and CT-based lung vessel segmentation, CRISP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving HD95 reductions of up to 0.14 (7.0%), 1.90 (13.1%), and 8.39 (38.9%) pixels across multi-center, demographic, and modality shifts respectively.
AI.conclusion: CRISP provides a model-agnostic, target-free, plug-in refinement solution that demonstrates superior robustness to distribution shifts without requiring test-time parameter updates or target-domain data, offering a practical path for clinical translation of medical AI.

title: ARMOR++: Agentic Orchestration of a Multi-Domain Primitive Set for Transferable Attacks on Deepfake Detectors
summary: The reliability of deepfake detectors frequently degrades under black-box adversarial transfer, as these models often rely on fragile, architecture-dependent forensic cues. Existing transfer attacks often lack semantic awareness and struggle to maintain effectiveness under strict no-query constraints, particularly when perturbations are transferred from convolutional surrogates to transformer-based targets. To address these limitations, this paper introduces ARMOR++, a robust multi-agent framework designed for high-transferability deepfake evasion. The framework leverages the Qwen2.5-VL Vision-Language Model (VLM) to supply spatial semantic priors, while the Qwen3 Large Language Model (LLM) orchestrates primitive selection, adaptive hyperparameter reparameterization, and entropy-regularized perturbation mixing. By integrating five complementary primitives, spanning dense optimization, saliency-based methods, spatial transformations, frequency-domain perturbations, and block-structured modifications, ARMOR++ effectively targets heterogeneous inductive biases. Rigorous evaluation on the AADD-2025 benchmark demonstrates that ARMOR++ significantly outperforms existing agentic and non-agentic baselines across both low- and high-quality image regimes. Statistical analysis confirms a substantial gain in blind-target Attack Success Rate (ASR) over the state-of-the-art agentic baseline, with further performance advantages evidenced against non-agentic benchmarks and under robust defensive configurations. These findings highlight a significant residual reliability gap in current deepfake detector deployments and demonstrate the efficacy of agentic orchestration in identifying latent vulnerabilities.

AI.tldr: ARMOR++ is a multi-agent framework using Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3 LLMs to generate high-transferability adversarial perturbations that evade deepfake detectors under black-box settings, significantly outperforming existing methods on the AADD-2025 benchmark.
AI.motivation: Deepfake detectors are unreliable under black-box adversarial transfer due to reliance on fragile, architecture-dependent forensic cues. Existing transfer attacks lack semantic awareness and struggle when perturbations transfer from convolutional models to transformer-based targets under no-query constraints.
AI.method: ARMOR++ uses Qwen2.5-VL for spatial semantic priors and Qwen3 LLM for orchestrating primitive selection, adaptive hyperparameter reparameterization, and entropy-regularized perturbation mixing across five complementary perturbation primitives: dense optimization, saliency-based, spatial transformations, frequency-domain, and block-structured modifications.
AI.result: On the AADD-2025 benchmark, ARMOR++ significantly outperforms agentic and non-agentic baselines in both low- and high-quality image regimes, with substantial gains in blind-target Attack Success Rate (ASR) over state-of-the-art agentic baselines and under robust defensive configurations.
AI.conclusion: There is a significant residual reliability gap in current deepfake detectors, and agentic orchestration is effective at identifying latent vulnerabilities across heterogeneous model architectures.

title: HoloGeo: Mitigating Landmark Bias in Geo-localization via Evidence-Driven Reasoning
summary: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have significantly improved image geo-localization, yet existing models remain susceptible to landmark bias, causing them to overlook geographical cues or form spurious correlations, ultimately resulting in inaccurate localization. To systematically investigate this issue, we first design two quantitative metrics, Bias Intensity (BI) and Bias Harmfulness (BH), to characterize the impact of landmarks exerted on model reasoning, and establish a comprehensive benchmark, LandmarkBias-3K. To mitigate landmark bias, we further propose an evidence-driven reasoning framework, HoloGeo, to improve the reliability of geo-localization. HoloGeo is supported by a high-quality dataset, BF-30k, annotated with structured multi-evidence bias-free reasoning chains. By incorporating multi-dimensional rewards, HoloGeo explicitly encourages balanced attention over diverse visual cues and achieves evidence-driven joint reasoning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HoloGeo not only maintains excellent performance on IM2GPS3K and YFCC4k but also significantly outperforms existing open-source VLMs on LandmarkBias-3K, validating its effectiveness for robust geospatial reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies landmark bias in VLMs for geo-localization, proposes metrics (BI, BH) and a benchmark (LandmarkBias-3K) to measure it, and introduces HoloGeo, an evidence-driven reasoning framework with a bias-free dataset (BF-30k) and multi-dimensional rewards, achieving robust geo-localization.
AI.motivation: Existing VLMs for image geo-localization suffer from landmark bias—over-relying on landmarks while ignoring other geographical cues or forming spurious correlations—leading to inaccurate localization. The paper aims to systematically measure and mitigate this bias.
AI.method: (1) Design two metrics: Bias Intensity (BI) and Bias Harmfulness (BH). (2) Build LandmarkBias-3K benchmark. (3) Propose HoloGeo, an evidence-driven reasoning framework using a high-quality bias-free dataset BF-30k with structured multi-evidence reasoning chains, trained with multi-dimensional rewards to encourage balanced attention and joint reasoning over diverse visual cues.
AI.result: HoloGeo maintains excellent performance on IM2GPS3K and YFCC4k and significantly outperforms existing open-source VLMs on LandmarkBias-3K.
AI.conclusion: The proposed metrics and framework effectively characterize and mitigate landmark bias, validating HoloGeo as a robust approach for geospatial reasoning in VLMs.

title: Motion-Conditioned Multi-View Fusion for Myocardial Infarction Localization from Echocardiography
summary: Myocardial infarction (MI) remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Echocardiography (Echo) is a widely available modality for MI assessment, where regional wall motion abnormality is a key indicator. Prior learning based methods for myocardial motion analysis often use handcrafted descriptors or densely supervised estimation, but the need for extensive annotation limits applicability. Foundation models have recently improved vision-based Echo analysis; however, most methods operate on single views and segment-level localization remains unreliable under view-dependent ambiguity, especially in apical views. To address this, we propose MCF-Net, a novel motion-guided multi-view fusion framework that fuses myocardial motion cues with foundation model representations to localize infarction. Visual features are extracted using EchoPrime, a pretrained Echo foundation model shared across dual views. Cardiac motion is modeled with extremely sparse supervision: a single annotated template frame is transferred across videos to initialize point tracking, avoiding dense labels. Motion-derived segment-aware soft masks provide coarse spatial priors that selectively enhance features for challenging myocardial segments. A motion-conditioned fusion mechanism then integrates motion and vision across views, refining predictions without overriding strong appearance cues. On segment-level MI localization, MCF-Net achieves 72.4\% F1 and 84.9\% accuracy, outperforming state-of-the-art motion-only, vision-only, and fusion baselines.

AI.tldr: MCF-Net is a motion-guided multi-view fusion framework that combines myocardial motion cues (via extremely sparse supervision) with foundation model representations (EchoPrime) for segment-level myocardial infarction localization in echocardiography, achieving 72.4% F1 and 84.9% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for myocardial motion analysis rely on handcrafted descriptors or dense supervision requiring extensive annotation. Foundation models improve Echo analysis but operate on single views and suffer from unreliable segment-level localization under view-dependent ambiguity, particularly in apical views.
AI.method: MCF-Net extracts visual features using EchoPrime (a pretrained Echo foundation model) shared across dual views. Cardiac motion is modeled with extremely sparse supervision by transferring a single annotated template frame across videos for point tracking. Motion-derived segment-aware soft masks provide coarse spatial priors to enhance features for challenging segments. A motion-conditioned fusion mechanism integrates motion and vision across views without overriding strong appearance cues.
AI.result: On segment-level MI localization, MCF-Net achieves 72.4% F1 score and 84.9% accuracy, outperforming state-of-the-art motion-only, vision-only, and fusion baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed motion-guided multi-view fusion with sparse supervision effectively addresses view-dependent ambiguity and reduces annotation burden, improving segment-level infarction localization over existing approaches.

title: Online Neural Space Time Memory for Dynamic Novel View Synthesis
comment: 15 pages. Preprint. Project page with demos and video results: https://nst-mem.github.io
summary: Online novel view synthesis from multi-view streaming videos faces a fundamental trade-off: maintaining a persistent, long-horizon memory to reconstruct temporarily occluded regions while operating under strict real-time constraints. While Test-Time Training (TTT) offers a powerful memory mechanism, standard models mandate gradient-based memory updates at every frame to adapt to the changing motion in dynamic scenes. The computational cost of heavy memory updates precludes real-time application and can lead to instability over long contexts. Given that memory updates are more demanding than memory application and video content is largely redundant, we propose to decouple the frequencies of these two processes. Our approach performs periodic memory updates while applying the memory on a per-frame basis, using cross-view attention to manage deformations between the prior memory state and the current frame. To lock in the historical context, we introduce two critical mechanisms: an auxiliary Memory Loss that forces persistent internalization of the scene, and a Memory Caching strategy that regularizes active weights against catastrophic drift. Our method demonstrates real-time, state-of-the-art performance on scenes with dynamic human motion as well as minute-scale online memorization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes decoupling memory update frequency from memory application frequency in online novel view synthesis, using periodic updates with per-frame application, cross-view attention, Memory Loss, and Memory Caching to achieve real-time, state-of-the-art performance on dynamic scenes.
AI.motivation: Online novel view synthesis from multi-view streaming videos faces a trade-off between maintaining long-horizon memory for occluded regions and meeting strict real-time constraints. Standard TTT models require gradient-based memory updates at every frame, which is computationally prohibitive for real-time applications and unstable over long contexts.
AI.method: The method decouples memory update and application frequencies: periodic memory updates with per-frame memory application. It uses cross-view attention to handle deformations between prior memory and current frame. Two mechanisms—Memory Loss (forcing internalization of scene structure) and Memory Caching (regularizing active weights against catastrophic drift)—lock in historical context.
AI.result: Achieves real-time, state-of-the-art performance on dynamic human motion scenes and minute-scale online memorization.
AI.conclusion: By exploiting the redundancy in video content and the asymmetry between memory update and application costs, the proposed frequency-decoupled approach enables real-time online novel view synthesis with robust long-term memory.

title: MeanFlowNFT: Bringing Forward-Process RL to Average-Velocity Generators
comment: Project Page: https://harahan.github.io/meanflownft-project-page/, GitHub: https://github.com/Harahan/MeanFlowNFT, Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/Harahan/MeanFlowNFT
summary: MeanFlow generators achieve fast few-step sampling by predicting average velocities over time intervals, making them attractive for efficient generation. Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a powerful way to align diffusion and flow models with human preferences and task-specific objectives. In particular, DiffusionNFT offers an efficient forward-process RL framework that does not require reverse-process trajectories or likelihood estimation. However, applying such RL methods to MeanFlow remains underexplored. DiffusionNFT optimizes instantaneous velocities, whereas MeanFlow samples with average velocities. To bridge this gap, we introduce MeanFlowNFT. Inspired by the MeanFlow identity, which bridges average and instantaneous velocities, we construct an induced instantaneous-velocity predictor. We apply the DiffusionNFT objective to this predictor, making reward optimization well-defined for MeanFlow. Sampling remains based on the average velocity, preserving MeanFlow's fast few-step generation. We further prove that MeanFlowNFT inherits DiffusionNFT's strict policy-improvement guarantee. Experiments on image and video generation show that MeanFlowNFT consistently improves baselines. Moreover, it outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL-tuned few-step generators on most metrics ($6$ of $8$ on SD3.5-M), and can even surpass multi-step RL-tuned diffusion while using only a few sampling steps. For instance, on Wan 2.1, $4$-step MeanFlowNFT reaches a VBench score of $84.33$, surpassing $50$-step LongCat-Video RL ($82.57$).

AI.tldr: MeanFlowNFT bridges Reinforcement Learning alignment to MeanFlow generators by constructing an induced instantaneous-velocity predictor, enabling reward optimization while preserving fast few-step sampling, with strict policy-improvement guarantees and strong empirical results on image and video generation.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning (RL) has proven powerful for aligning diffusion and flow models with human preferences, but existing RL methods like DiffusionNFT optimize instantaneous velocities, whereas MeanFlow generators use average velocities for sampling, creating a fundamental gap that prevents applying such RL alignment to MeanFlow models.
AI.method: Inspired by the MeanFlow identity (bridging average and instantaneous velocities), MeanFlowNFT constructs an induced instantaneous-velocity predictor, applies the DiffusionNFT objective to this predictor, while keeping sampling based on average velocity to preserve fast few-step generation.
AI.result: MeanFlowNFT consistently improves baselines on image and video generation tasks, outperforming prior state-of-the-art RL-tuned few-step generators on 6 of 8 metrics on SD3.5-M, and surpassing multi-step RL-tuned diffusion (e.g., 4-step MeanFlowNFT achieves 84.33 VBench on Wan 2.1 vs. 82.57 for 50-step LongCat-Video RL).
AI.conclusion: MeanFlowNFT successfully extends RL-based alignment to MeanFlow generators, inheriting DiffusionNFT's strict policy-improvement guarantee while preserving fast few-step sampling advantages.

title: Hierarchical Denoising For Multi-Step Visual Reasoning
summary: Video models are evolving into vision foundation models, yet they still lack human-like multi-step reasoning. Streaming autoregressive diffusion models are efficient but limited in reasoning, while bidirectional diffusion enables global revision with high inference costs due to dense frame-level denoising. Both paradigms struggle to achieve logical consistency and low-latency streaming for complex reasoning tasks. We propose HDR (Hierarchical Denoising for Visual Reasoning), a unified framework that integrates hierarchical latents into causal video generation for multi-step reasoning. HDR organizes video latents into a tree-structured hierarchy, enabling coarse-to-fine reasoning before streaming output. Coarse denoising layers preserve uncertain hypotheses for global planning, while finer layers progressively refine them into concrete visual states. A sparse hierarchical attention pattern (SHAP) further reduces temporal attention costs. We introduce a level-stratified multi-step video reasoning benchmark with out-of-distribution cases, covering six tasks: maze navigation, Tower of Hanoi, one-line drawing, sliding puzzle, Sokoban, and water pouring. Compared with streaming autoregressive diffusion baselines, HDR improves success from 34.22 to 60.29 (76.2% relative gain) and increases average progress from 76.00 to 89.56, demonstrating more consistent reasoning trajectories. HDR maintains low-latency streaming at 0.70 seconds per latent, achieving 54.2 times faster inference than bidirectional diffusion. It also retains 82.9% of full-data performance with only 2% training data, compared with 52.0% for bidirectional diffusion. Real-world robot experiments further demonstrate HDR's potential for physical interaction and world modeling. Project demo: https://hierarchical-diffusion-reasoning.github.io/.

AI.tldr: HDR introduces hierarchical denoising into causal video generation for multi-step reasoning, achieving 76.2% relative gain over streaming autoregressive diffusion baselines and 54.2x faster inference than bidirectional diffusion while maintaining low-latency streaming.
AI.motivation: Existing video models lack human-like multi-step reasoning: streaming autoregressive diffusion models are efficient but limited in reasoning capability, while bidirectional diffusion enables global revision but suffers from high inference costs due to dense frame-level denoising. Both paradigms struggle to achieve logical consistency and low-latency streaming for complex reasoning tasks.
AI.method: HDR integrates hierarchical latents into causal video generation, organizing video latents into a tree-structured hierarchy for coarse-to-fine reasoning. Coarse denoising layers preserve uncertain hypotheses for global planning, while finer layers progressively refine them into concrete visual states. A sparse hierarchical attention pattern (SHAP) reduces temporal attention costs.
AI.result: HDR improves success from 34.22 to 60.29 (76.2% relative gain) and increases average progress from 76.00 to 89.56 over streaming autoregressive diffusion baselines. It achieves 0.70 seconds per latent latency (54.2x faster than bidirectional diffusion) and retains 82.9% of full-data performance with only 2% training data (vs 52.0% for bidirectional diffusion).
AI.conclusion: HDR demonstrates that hierarchical denoising in causal video generation effectively bridges the gap between logical reasoning and low-latency streaming, with strong performance on out-of-distribution multi-step reasoning benchmarks and promising real-world robot experiments for physical interaction and world modeling.

title: SAGA: Schema-Aware Grounding for Agentic Text-to-SPARQL Generation
summary: Complex knowledge base question answering (KBQA) is commonly approached through either information retrieval over a question-specific subgraph or semantic parsing into an executable logical form. We study the latter paradigm. Recent large language model agents make semantic parsing interactive: they alternate between reasoning, querying the knowledge base, and extending a partial SPARQL query. This interleaving reduces reliance on one-shot generation, but makes the quality of \emph{KB grounding} depend on what the interaction tools expose. Existing agents retrieve or prune candidate properties mainly through lexical relevance and instance-level observations, without systematically conditioning on entity types, property domains and ranges, or the expected answer type. We call this failure mode \emph{type-blind grounding}. It enlarges the grounding search space and often produces plausible-looking but semantically incompatible triple patterns that execute to empty results. We propose SAGA (\underline{S}chema-\underline{A}ware \underline{G}rounding for \underline{A}gentic Text-to-SPARQL Generation), a training-free framework that turns property exploration into a schema-constrained grounding operation. SAGA maintains a persistent bidirectional type state, filters known-incompatible property candidates at construction time, presents the remaining graph patterns in a compact schema-annotated format, and handles missing schema information permissively through empirical and trace-local evidence. Across nine benchmark settings over Wikidata and Freebase, SAGA achieves the highest F1 on all nine settings and the highest exact-match accuracy on eight, while reducing empty-result queries across all reported Wikidata settings.

AI.tldr: SAGA is a training-free, schema-aware framework for agentic text-to-SPARQL generation that uses persistent bidirectional type states and property domain/range constraints to reduce type-blind grounding errors, achieving state-of-the-art F1 across nine benchmark settings on Wikidata and Freebase.
AI.motivation: Existing interactive KBQA agents retrieve or prune candidate properties mainly through lexical relevance and instance-level observations, without systematically conditioning on entity types, property domains/ranges, or expected answer types. This "type-blind grounding" enlarges the search space and produces semantically incompatible triple patterns that often yield empty results.
AI.method: SAGA turns property exploration into schema-constrained grounding by: (1) maintaining a persistent bidirectional type state, (2) filtering known-incompatible property candidates at construction time, (3) presenting graph patterns in a compact schema-annotated format, and (4) handling missing schema information permissively through empirical and trace-local evidence.
AI.result: Across nine benchmark settings over Wikidata and Freebase, SAGA achieves the highest F1 on all nine settings and the highest exact-match accuracy on eight, while reducing empty-result queries across all reported Wikidata settings.
AI.conclusion: Schema-aware grounding that explicitly leverages type constraints substantially improves the quality and reliability of agentic text-to-SPARQL generation over existing type-blind approaches.
